title: Robot Learning on Discrete Surfaces: Theory and Applications
authors: Matteo Dalle Vedove,Fares J. Abu-Dakka,Luigi Palopoli,Daniele Fontanelli,Matteo Saveriano
abstract:
All the objects composing our world are enclosed within surfaces. Yet, most robot learning and motion generation frameworks treat surfaces as constraints ignoring their intrinsic geometry. This gap is acute for polyhedral meshes—the standard output of CAD and 3D reconstruction—whose discrete geometric structure remains unexploited.
In this paper, we propose a unified discrete Riemannian framework that enables robot learning directly on polyhedral surface meshes. Using discrete differential geometry, we define logarithmic and exponential maps, parallel transport, and ambient-space projections that remain well-defined across faces, edges, and vertices.
We instantiate the framework in three learning paradigms: (i) Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs), an improved exponential-map computation and a fixed-tangent-cone forcing-term encoding with parallel transport yield better cross-surface generalisation and stability over prior mesh-based approaches. (ii) Gaussian Process (GP), a geodesic-based kernel with practical admissibility control, enables regression at arbitrary mesh locations without smoothness assumptions. (iii) Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM), mesh-native operators improve generative quality over spectral baselines while reducing training time.
The framework is validated in simulation against state-of-the-art methods and demonstrated on two real-robot scenarios: generalising user-drawn trajectories across different surfaces and planning polishing motions on RGB-D-reconstructed surfaces.
introduction:
In real applications, robots have to learn how to physically interact with objects and their environment. Sometimes this is required for manipulation purposes (e.g., grasping, pick-and-place, insertion), and sometimes for manufacturing operations (e.g., wiping, finishing, drawing, grinding, cutting, inspecting). A common trait of all these operations is that they are not executed in free space: in the vast majority of cases, they entail continuous contact with a surface enclosing the target object, where friction effects and geometric irregularities play a significant role. This raises a fundamental question: can a learning process for such tasks be truly effective if the geometric properties of the contact surface are ignored?
This issue has been often overlooked in the literature. Most existing Learning from Demonstration (LfD) and motion generation frameworks assume that skills evolve in flat Euclidean spaces and can be directly transferred to surfaces. When task complexity increases, surface constraints are typically recovered a posteriori through projection methods [1], impedance control, or local parameterisation. While effective in structured and repeatable settings, treating surface geometry as an external constraint—rather than an intrinsic component of the learning process—often results in poor generalisation when the underlying structure changes.

In recent years, geometry-aware learning methods have been proposed for some classes of Riemannian manifolds, such as rotations or symmetric positive-definite matrices [2, 3, 4, 5], for which researchers have developed tools and methods to learn robot skills in non-Euclidean spaces. These formulations rely on differential operators—such as exponential and logarithmic maps, and parallel transport—that enable learning and control directly in the tangent space. However, extending these methods to surface-based skills remains an open issue, as surfaces encountered in real applications are rarely available as smooth manifolds. In most cases, surfaces are obtained from CAD models, perception pipelines, or 3D reconstruction tools [6], for which the most natural representation is a 3D polyhedral mesh. Such discrete representations exhibit non-differentiable singularities at edges and vertices and do not admit the smooth structure assumed by classical Riemannian learning frameworks.

The absence of a smooth representation creates a significant gap between geometry-aware robot learning theory and its practical applicability to discrete manifolds. Although surfaces can be studied through the lens of differential geometry, constructing smooth representations for objects with arbitrary topology is generally intractable [7]. At the same time, naïve discretisation of smooth manifold operators on meshes either requires restrictive assumptions on surface smoothness or leads to inconsistencies and ill-defined behaviour at singularities. As a result, existing approaches often rely on local approximations, ad hoc embeddings, or spectral smoothness assumptions that limit robustness and hinder generalisation [8, 9, 10].

Paper Contribution.  In this work, we take a more direct route to fill this gap by developing a discrete Riemannian framework for robot learning directly on polyhedral surface meshes. Starting from discrete differential geometry [11], we construct
geometrically consistent approximations of key Riemannian
operators—including logarithmic and exponential maps, parallel
transport, geodesic distance, and ambient-space projections—that remain well-defined across faces, edges, and vertices of a mesh. Unlike prior mesh-based formulations [9], which leave edge and vertex singularities unaddressed and rely on local approximations of the exponential map (valid only for small displacements), our operators are built on the straightest-geodesic principle [12] and are equipped with tangent-cone projections that handle all singular loci. Building on this geometric foundation, we show how three established learning frameworks can be naturally extended to discrete surfaces: (i) geometry-aware Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) with a fixed-tangent-cone forcing-term encoding that replaces the local parameterisations used in [9, 13], (ii) geodesic-distance-based
Gaussian Processes (GPs) with controllable kernel admissibility, and (iii) Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM) with mesh-native operators replacing the spectral premetrics of [4]. These formulations yield motion and function representations that generalise across surfaces with different curvature, topology, and discretisation resolution, removing the need for smoothness or spectral assumptions.

To summarize, our main contributions are as follows:

A discrete Riemannian operator framework on polyhedral meshes—including tangent cones, straightest-geodesic exponential maps, and ambient-space projections—that explicitly handles edge and vertex singularities left unaddressed by existing mesh-based
methods [9, 8], enabling consistent geometric computations directly on discrete surface representations like polyhedral meshes.

A reformulation of geometry-aware DMPs on meshes that encodes forcing term in a fixed tangent cone and reconstructs it via parallel transport during execution, replacing the local, velocity-aligned parameterisation of [9] and eliminating the limit-cycle drift it induces on curved surfaces.

A geodesic-distance-based GP formulation on meshes that enables kernel regression at arbitrary surface locations—including face interiors—without smoothness or density requirements, overcoming the vertex-restriction and resolution-sensitivity of Laplace–Beltrami-based kernels [10].

An extension of RFM to discrete polyhedral surfaces using geodesic premetrics, improving generative quality and reducing training time relative to the spectral baselines of [4].

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Section II analyses the state of the art. After a quick recall of foundation knowledge (Sec. III), we present the unified approach for geometry-aware learning on discrete surfaces in Sec. IV. Section V provides simulation results and comparisons with the state-of-the-art, while Sec. VI provides experiments on a real robot highlighting the strengths of our approach. We conclude in Sec. VII with some limitations of the approach and final remarks.

1. A discrete Riemannian operator framework on polyhedral meshes—including tangent cones, straightest-geodesic exponential maps, and ambient-space projections—that explicitly handles edge and vertex singularities left unaddressed by existing mesh-based
methods [9, 8], enabling consistent geometric computations directly on discrete surface representations like polyhedral meshes.

2. A reformulation of geometry-aware DMPs on meshes that encodes forcing term in a fixed tangent cone and reconstructs it via parallel transport during execution, replacing the local, velocity-aligned parameterisation of [9] and eliminating the limit-cycle drift it induces on curved surfaces.

3. A geodesic-distance-based GP formulation on meshes that enables kernel regression at arbitrary surface locations—including face interiors—without smoothness or density requirements, overcoming the vertex-restriction and resolution-sensitivity of Laplace–Beltrami-based kernels [10].

4. An extension of RFM to discrete polyhedral surfaces using geodesic premetrics, improving generative quality and reducing training time relative to the spectral baselines of [4].

title: Towards Physical Underwater Robotic Assistance for Scuba Diver Movement in Confined Spaces
authors: Demetrious T. Kutzke,Junaed Sattar
abstract:
Scuba divers are taught to control their depth to avoid rapid ascents and descents, which could result in serious injuries such as gas embolisms and barotrauma.
However, many underwater tasks necessitate lateral control, maintaining distance between subsea structures such as coral reefs, submerged drilling instrumentation, or unexploded ordnance.
In this work, we discuss a first-of-its-kind wearable robotic solution providing thruster-actuated directional guidance to a diver, as distinct from prior propulsive-assistance exoskeletons.
We introduce Robotic Assisted Diver Movement in Confined Spaces (RADMCS), a wearable robot that assists divers in maintaining a fixed distance from subsea structures by leveraging perception techniques in monocular depth estimation and force-feedback from submersible thrusters to provide haptic feedback. Its small and compact form factor creates a foundational platform that could be expanded to include more sophisticated control and navigation behaviors.
We present results from Institutional Review Board (IRB) in-water studies with eight human scuba diver participants on threshold sensitivity tests in both a closed-water swimming facility and ocean environments; distance-maintaining experiments in a closed-water facility; and form, fit, and function testing in the ocean.
We demonstrate that relatively low thrust values (≈10\approx 10% of maximum) allow robotic direction of a human’s movement using the physical sensation of the robot’s guidance.

title: ChunkVLA-AM: Parallel Action Chunking for Vision-Language-Action Robot Control in Additive Manufacturing
authors: Zhugang Liu,Kaichuang Zhang,Jinman Zhang,Pu Sun,Martha Asare,Jose Hernandez,Maxim Ermolinsky,Efren Saenz,Qi Lu,Jinghao Yang
abstract:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and action generation, offering new opportunities for automation in additive manufacturing (AM).
However, deployment in AM remains challenging because adapting these models to unseen robot embodiments is costly, and performance can degrade under environment changes.
In this work, we present a framework for deploying OpenVLA-OFT on a FAIRINO FR3 robot in a fixed AM workcell.
A data pipeline converts monocular real-world demonstrations into OpenVLA-compatible TFDS/RLDS datasets to support adaptation to the FR3 embodiment. At runtime, each inference request predicts an eight-step chunk of 7-D actions. The FR3 executes each chunk open loop before capturing a new observation, providing closed-loop feedback between chunks. The system uses a cloud–edge architecture in which the FR3 client streams observations to a remote inference server through a FastAPI interface.
In 42 physical A-to-B object-transfer trials, evenly split between red and blue targets, the system succeeded in 39 (92.9%). All three failures occurred during final placement, when insufficient release-height control caused the object to topple. An illumination sweep identified a low-error luminance range of 85–125 on a 0–255 scale, with the lowest mean spatial error at 95.
introduction:
Additive manufacturing (AM) has become an important production paradigm for rapid prototyping, customized medical devices, aerospace components, and high-value industrial parts [1, 2, 3]. Beyond deposition itself, practical AM workflows require inspection, part retrieval, build-plate handling, post-processing, and occasional intervention after process failures. These operations can expose human operators to process-specific risks: fused deposition modeling (FDM) may emit ultrafine particles and volatile organic compounds during heated thermoplastic extrusion [4, 5], while selective laser melting (SLM) involves fine metallic powders and particulate-matter hazards [6]. Robotic automation is therefore attractive for AM workcells because it can improve repeatability and reduce human exposure during inspection, transfer, and failure response. However, conventional rule-based robot programs are difficult to reuse across different printers, robot platforms, camera configurations, lighting conditions, object poses, and defect types such as FDM warping, inter-layer delamination, SLM porosity, lack-of-fusion holes, and cracks [7, 8, 9].

Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a possible route toward more flexible AM robotic systems. By mapping visual observations and natural-language task descriptions directly to robot actions, VLA policies can represent tasks such as “retrieve the printed part,” “inspect the warped edge,” or “move the build-plate sample to the cooling area” without requiring a separate perception pipeline and a handcrafted state machine. Recent systems including RT-1, RT-2, Open X-Embodiment, and OpenVLA have shown that large-scale robot datasets, vision-language backbones, and action-token prediction can support general manipulation and transfer across tasks and embodiments [10, 11, 12, 13]. This capability is relevant to AM because the robot must interpret both the visual manufacturing context and the language instruction while generating manipulation commands within a constrained workspace.

Despite this potential, transferring a VLA model to an AM workcell is not a straightforward model-deployment problem. The first difficulty is migrating demonstrations and action interfaces across robot platforms. Robot datasets often differ in image resolution, observation structure, sampling rate, episode organization, coordinate frames, state definitions, and gripper conventions. Their action spaces may also represent joint positions, joint velocities, absolute Cartesian poses, or relative end-effector motion. Even when two platforms expose action vectors of the same dimension, the individual elements may have different physical meanings, units, ranges, or normalization rules. RLDS and TFDS provide a common structure for organizing episodic robot data, but they do not by themselves resolve these embodiment-specific differences [14, 15]. As a result, transferring an existing VLA pipeline to a platform such as the FAIRINO FR3 requires more than renaming dataset fields. Coordinate transformations, action semantics, gripper commands, and normalization statistics must all be defined consistently before the model can be trained and safely deployed.

The second difficulty is robustness to changes between the demonstration environment and the deployed AM workcell. Lighting intensity, illumination direction, camera exposure, background clutter, camera viewpoint, and object pose may vary between data collection and execution. Reflective build plates, dark polymer parts, shadows cast by the robot, and changes in printer illumination can further alter the visual appearance of the part and the gripper. These variations are especially relevant when the model is adapted using demonstrations collected under a fixed camera and lighting configuration. Because a VLA policy predicts actions directly from image observations, it may associate the required motion with incidental visual features of the training environment instead of the task geometry. A policy that succeeds under the original lighting condition may therefore become less reliable when the workcell appearance changes, even though the physical task remains the same.

In this work, we present ChunkVLA-AM, a reproducible OpenVLA-OFT-based deployment pipeline for FR3-based AM post-print retrieval. To make embodiment adaptation explicit, we construct a conversion pipeline that transforms monocular FR3 demonstrations, Cartesian end-effector states, binary gripper commands, language instructions, and episode metadata into OpenVLA-compatible TFDS/RLDS episodes. The pipeline defines the coordinate frames, action semantics, and normalization procedure required by the target FR3 system, while LoRA is used to avoid full-parameter fine-tuning. For robot control, we adopt a horizon-HH action-chunk interface and use H=8H=8 in the reported physical tests, allowing the model to predict short-horizon motion sequences in a single request. The FR3 client then applies action denormalization, workspace clipping, unsafe-action rejection, and chunk-wise replanning after execution of the returned actions. This implementation focuses on the system-level adaptation and deployment required to use an action-chunked VLA policy in a fixed AM workcell and to evaluate its behavior under changes in lighting and object pose.

title: FlashDexRetarget: Accelerating Dexterous Manipulation Data Generation through Multi-Motion Retargeting
authors: Kyungmin Lee,Sibeen Kim,Dongyoon Hwang,Yoonsang Oh,Donghu Kim,Youngdo Lee,I Made Aswin Nahrendra,Jaegul Choo,Hojoon Lee
abstract:
Human hand-object demonstrations offer a reusable source of dexterous robot manipulation data, but transferring them across embodiments requires physically feasible retargeting. Existing physics-based approaches face limitations in retargeting success, motion-specific training efficiency, or both. To address these limitations, we introduce FlashDexRetarget, an RL-based framework for high-success, efficient dexterous motion retargeting. To make the demonstrated interaction easier to learn, we combine object point-cloud observations, hand-object distance features, and future trajectory encodings with complementary rewards that supervise object motion and reference hand-object relationships. To further accelerate learning, we employ separate left- and right-hand actor critic networks and adapt the off-policy algorithm, FlashSAC to dexterous motion tracking. On a benchmark of 50 motions spanning single-object and two-object interactions, FlashDexRetarget achieves a 90% success rate, approximately 2.5×\times that of the evaluated sampling-based baselines, while requiring up to 100×\times less training compute than the evaluated RL-based baselines. Evaluations on both XHand and Sharpa Wave Hand show consistent gains, and component-wise ablations examine the contributions of our design choices. Beyond the 50-motion benchmark, experiments with 200, 500, and 1,000 motions demonstrate that our method remains stable at larger scales and produces successful retargeted motions more efficiently as the training set grows.
Qualitative replay results using real-world-captured demonstrations further illustrate the applicability of our framework to recorded human manipulation.
Videos and code are available at davian-robotics.github.io/FlashDexRetarget.
introduction:
Learning dexterous manipulation requires large amounts of robot interaction data.
Human hand-object demonstrations [2, 3, 4] provide a promising source of such data, as diverse manipulation behaviors can be collected at scale without directly operating a robot.
To use these demonstrations for robot learning, however, human motions must be translated into actions executable by a target robot hand.
Physics-based retargeting addresses this issue by adapting human demonstrations to the morphology and actuation of the robot in simulation, while leveraging physical contact to reproduce the demonstrated object motion.
To make large human motion datasets practical sources of robot data, retargeting must achieve high success at low compute cost.

Existing physics-based retargeting methods adopt a single-reference formulation, optimizing each demonstration independently.
Sampling-based methods [5, 6] search directly over action sequences through simulated rollouts, but high-dimensional actions and long contact sequences make this search challenging under a finite simulation budget.
RL-based methods [7, 8, 9] instead learn closed-loop policies to track the demonstrated hand-object interaction, but train a separate policy for each reference.
Despite their difference in optimization strategies, both approaches retarget each demonstration independently, causing computational cost to grow linearly with the number of demonstrations.

To avoid this repeated optimization, we study multi-reference tracking, where a single reference-conditioned policy is trained jointly across many demonstrations.
By sharing learning across references, this formulation has the potential to amortize training cost over an entire dataset while retaining accurate tracking.
Multi-reference tracking has been effective for humanoid whole-body motion [10], but dexterous manipulation introduces additional challenges.

First, object shapes and hand-object configurations vary across demonstrations, requiring the policy to distinguish interaction geometries. Second, reconstructed human demonstrations contain contact errors, making exact contact matching unreliable. Third, multi-reference training broadens the state distribution, increasing the need for model capacity and effective experience reuse. Finally, for bimanual motions, the two hands may play different roles with asymmetric signals.

To address these challenges, we introduce FlashDexRetarget, an RL
framework for multi-reference dexterous retargeting.
First, we condition the policy on object geometry and KK future reference frames to distinguish diverse interactions across references.
Second, we replace exact contact matching with distance-based interaction
rewards to provide dense hand-object supervision despite imperfect contact
reconstruction.
Third, we adopt the off-policy learner FlashSAC [11] and
increase its replay and critic capacity to support learning across a broader
multi-reference distribution.
Finally, we use separate left- and right-hand actor critic networks to
handle the distinct roles and learning signals of the two hands.

We evaluate FlashDexRetarget on 50 hand-object motions from TACO, OakInk2, and HOT3D [2, 3, 4] using XHand and Sharpa Wave Hand as target embodiments.
Against sampling-based and RL-based baselines, we measure the fraction of successfully retargeted demonstrations as a function of total training compute.
A single FlashDexRetarget policy retargets 90% of the benchmark using about 30 GPU-hours, compared with about 46% success at about 3,000 GPU-hours for CHORD [7].
This corresponds to approximately 100×100\times lower training compute and a 44-percentage-point improvement in retargeting success.
Ablations examine how hand-object interaction objectives, off-policy training and capacity scaling, and left and right hand networks contribute to these gains in the multi-reference setting.
We further show that the number of successfully retargeted trajectories continues to grow as the dataset scales.
We also validate the retargeted trajectories through real-world replay.

Our main contributions are:

We introduce FlashDexRetarget, an RL framework that jointly retargets human hand-object demonstrations through multi-reference tracking with a single policy.

We combine object point-cloud observations, hand-object interaction objectives, off-policy learning with larger replay and model capacities, and left and right hand actor-critic networks for joint dexterous tracking.

We evaluate on 50 motions and two robot embodiments, achieving approximately 100×100\times lower training compute and 44 percentage points higher success than CHORD, with ablations and real-world replay.

title: World Motion Models: Flexible Sequence Modeling of SE(3) Trajectories
authors: Jiahui Lei,Qianqian Wang,Trevor Darrell,Angjoo Kanazawa
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight). Url:this https URL
abstract:
Equipping artificial agents with spatial intelligence requires a comprehensive generative prior over the dynamic 3D world.
We propose World Motion Models (WMMs) that capture “what was, is, and will be where across time” via sparse SE(3) pose trajectories.
WMMs are built on the observation that elements of dynamic scenes can be well approximated by a set of rigid SE(3) trajectories, a minimal yet expressive primitive for 4D modeling.
This representation unifies articulated objects, human bodies, hand-object interactions, piecewise-rigid scene dynamics, camera motion, and even robot states and actions into a single shared space. Given this representation, we cast the joint distribution of these entities as a flexible sequence modeling problem, utilizing flow-matching with per-token noise levels. Coupled with a context token mechanism for non-sequential conditioning, this formulation supports any-to-any marginal conditioning across an arbitrary number of entities and time steps. Tasks such as future prediction, motion infilling, model-predictive control, inverse kinematics, cross-embodiment retargeting, and policy learning all reduce to the application of different masks over the same network. Experiments on 6 diverse applications of 3D vision and robotics demonstrate the versatility and flexibility of WMMs with strong performance.
introduction:
The world that surrounds us is inherently three-dimensional and highly dynamic—a 4D space where perception and interaction are fundamentally tied to movement. Physical actions are achieved by moving limbs or end-effectors, generating forces that translate into the motion of objects, while other agents dynamically navigate and act within this same environment. As humans, we naturally develop a strong prior over these moving entities: we intuitively anticipate how others will move, plan the physical motions required to achieve a desired goal, and foresee the physical consequences of our own actions.
To act and reason in the physical world, intelligent systems benefit from the same capability: a generative prior over the 4D world that captures the evolution of “what” and “where” across time.

In this work, we present a unified generative model which provides a general prior over the dynamic 3D world. Our approach is highly flexible with minimal assumptions and handles unstructured scenes and arbitrary object categories. By supporting various prompting modes, a single model enables diverse inference tasks ranging from world modeling (e.g., action-conditioned/free future prediction) to complex planning (e.g., motion infilling, inverse dynamics).

To build such a prior, we first need a unified representation that expresses the dynamic world in a physically grounded manner.
Our insight is that complex, dense motion of the physical world can be compactly approximated by a sparse set of moving coordinate frames — specifically S​E​(3)SE(3) trajectories. Most entities of interest naturally reduce to this format: the dense flow of thousands of mesh vertices on a human or robot collapses into tens of joint trajectories [60, 36]; cameras and rigid objects track as single moving frames; and even non-rigid scene dynamics can be represented as interpolations of a small S​E​(3)SE(3) motion basis [85, 43, 49]. We therefore adopt the S​E​(3)SE(3) trajectory as our basic language for what is where across time.
These S​E​(3)SE(3) trajectories subsume prior point trajectories in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} but can be far sparser, replacing, for instance, the flow of thousands of mesh vertices with the tens of joint poses of a SMPL human [60] or a robot [36]. We further impose no category-specific structure: every entity is treated equally as a pose proxy, generalizing class-bound representations (SMPL [60], MANO [80], URDFs) to any unstructured scene.
It is also orthogonal to video-based world modeling [9, 92, 70, 3, 103], which captures dynamics implicitly through color changes on a screen, entangling the underlying 3D motion with appearance, lighting, and viewpoint changes. In short, the S​E​(3)SE(3) trajectory provides a highly compact, physically grounded 3D abstraction for modeling arbitrary motion.

The question now becomes: how do we learn a generative prior over these S​E​(3)SE(3) trajectories? Since motion naturally unfolds over time, this is inherently a sequence modeling problem. Traditionally, this is treated as a strictly causal task: a standard world model or dynamics model predicts future states conditioned on past history and actions. However, humans can perform non-causal inference as well, such as determining the actions required to achieve a specific goal (inverse dynamics) or planning intermediate motions between waypoints. The inference type varies widely across applications. To support these diverse inference schemes, we propose World Motion Models (WMMs), flow-matching generative models with per-token noise levels. Inspired by Diffusion Forcing [15] and discrete diffusion [69, 2], WMMs treat each 6D S​E​(3)SE(3) pose at a given time step as an independent token, assign each its own noise level, and denoise the entire token field in a single shared forward pass.

Once trained, a WMM admits inference over arbitrary numbers of entities and time steps simply by dictating which tokens are clean (the condition) and which are noised (the prediction). Given past tokens, it acts as a future predictor p⁡(s′|s)p(s^{\prime}|s); applied to action tokens, it becomes a feed-forward policy p⁡(a|s)p(a|s); and when both past states and actions are provided, it acts as an action-conditioned dynamics model p⁡(s′|s,a)p(s^{\prime}|s,a) supporting model-predictive control. Ultimately, WMMs realize any p⁡(unknown|known)p(\text{unknown}|\text{known}). By simply changing what is known, the exact same network transitions seamlessly between serving as a policy, an action prior, and a world model.

While standard trajectory modeling assumes a strictly consecutive temporal horizon, many practical tasks require reasoning beyond it. For example, planning a complex interaction often relies on an abstract goal state situated arbitrarily far in the future. Similarly, tasks like cross-embodiment retargeting require inferring correspondences between trajectories, such as those of a human and a robot. Providing a few paired demonstration frames from outside the current episode serves as an in-context template that tells the model “what is what.” To support these non-consecutive anchors, we enhance the flexibility of WMMs by introducing a set of context S​E​(3)SE(3) tokens. Rather than being bound to the continuous physical timeline of the current episode, they are assigned to a decoupled context timeline with its own learnable positional embeddings. Mechanically, these context tokens are treated identically to real trajectory tokens, meaning they can seamlessly condition the model or be generated themselves.

Together, this general S​E​(3)SE(3) formulation and our flexible sequence modeling enable WMMs to demonstrate broad versatility across applications, including robot policies and model-predictive control (MPC), scene future prediction, human-object interaction generation, and multi-embodiment humanoid retargeting (Sec. ), all with SOTA performance.

Contributions. We propose a general formulation that uses the sparse S​E​(3)SE(3) trajectory as a unified representation for 4D world modeling.
To learn a flexible generative prior over this space, we introduce WMMs, flexible flow-matching models with per-token noise levels. By supporting any-to-any marginal conditioning alongside a context token mechanism, WMMs deliver strong performance across diverse 3D vision and robotics tasks.

title: Query-Conditioned Articulation Estimation from a Single Image
authors: Abdelrhman Werby,Fabio Scaparro,Kai O. Arra
comment: Code and video are available atthis https URL
abstract:
Enabling robots to estimate the kinematic parameters of articulated objects unlocks a wide range of capabilities for interaction and manipulation. The estimation has to happen from the information the robot currently observes, often just a single RGB image of an object it has never seen before.
Current single-image approaches couple articulation part segmentation with articulation estimation, making their predictions vulnerable to missed detections and incorrect part associations, and they regress metric 3D geometry that a single view fixes only up to scale.
We present QueryArt, a model that estimates articulation parameters from a single RGB image, a 2D query point, and camera intrinsics. QueryArt is trained to estimate the 3D articulation geometry relative to the queried point and in units of its depth, which keeps its target identifiable from the image alone. A single depth measurement at the query point then supplies the scale and recovers the metric parameters. We train QueryArt on a curated mixture of synthetic and real-world articulation datasets. We evaluate QueryArt on several benchmarks and compare it against recent baselines. QueryArt outperforms recent baselines on most articulation metrics, including on out-of-distribution data. To demonstrate the model’s capabilities in real-world settings, we evaluate QueryArt on a mobile manipulator across 57 manipulation trials spanning 16 object parts and five viewpoint classes, achieving a 70.2% success rate. We provide code and videos at: https://abwerby.github.io/queryart/.
introduction:
Robots deployed in human-centered environments must interact with articulated objects such as doors, cabinets, drawers, and appliances [1, 2]. Successfully manipulating such objects requires estimating their underlying kinematic model, including the joint type, motion axis, and axis location. These parameters support a wide range of downstream capabilities, from navigating through closed doors to searching for objects inside cabinets and drawers. Ideally, a robot should infer them for an unseen object before physical interaction, using only the observations available from its current viewpoint.

Single-view articulation estimation methods [3, 4, 5, 6] jointly detect and segment movable parts and estimate their motion parameters from a single image. This formulation couples articulation estimation with part localization; as a result, a localization failure propagates directly to the kinematic prediction. Recent approaches [7, 8] instead predict a 3D interaction trajectory from a single image using a learned motion prior, but their output is not parameterized by an explicit revolute or prismatic joint model and therefore does not guarantee kinematic consistency by construction. Both families of methods regress metric 3D geometry directly from the image, although a single view determines the scene only up to scale.
Methods such as USDNet [9] operate on complete 3D scene point clouds and jointly predict articulated-part segmentation and motion attributes; however, they require prior scene exploration. Video-based methods [10, 11] infer articulation by observing the articulated object in motion, requiring the object to be manipulated or observed in multiple states before its articulation can be estimated.

To this end, we present QueryArt, a model for estimating articulation parameters from a single calibrated RGB image and a 2D query point on the articulated part (Fig. 1). It predicts the joint type, the 3D motion axis, and the query-relative axis location, normalized by the query point’s depth. This normalization makes the target invariant to uniform scaling of the scene. At inference time, obtaining the query point’s depth provides the metric scale, removing the need for the model to infer absolute size from appearance. Conditioning on an interaction point decouples the question of where to interact from the question of how the selected point moves, allowing the query to originate from a human click or an independent affordance-grounding system [12, 13].
The model combines a frozen visual foundation encoder [14], deformable attention [15], and lightweight articulation-specific heads. QueryArt is trained on a curated mixture of two synthetic and three real-world articulation datasets. When the query point metric depth is available, a deterministic lifting step recovers the metric 3D motion axis.
Across held-out splits of four training datasets and two datasets excluded from training entirely, QueryArt improves over recent single-image baselines on most articulation metrics, and 57 trials on a mobile manipulator show that its predictions are accurate enough to open furniture the model has never seen, at a 70.2% success rate.

Our main contributions are:

A query-conditioned formulation that models articulation estimation as regression of normalized articulation geometry, given a single calibrated RGB image and a 2D query point.

An efficient architecture that combines high-resolution frozen visual foundation features and lightweight prediction heads with a compact, physically structured axis-hinge representation.

An extensive evaluation on synthetic and real-world articulation benchmarks, including out-of-distribution data, demonstrating improved articulation estimation over recent baselines.

Real-robot experiments showing that the predicted parameters support analytic motion generation and manipulation of previously unseen objects.

1. A query-conditioned formulation that models articulation estimation as regression of normalized articulation geometry, given a single calibrated RGB image and a 2D query point.

2. An efficient architecture that combines high-resolution frozen visual foundation features and lightweight prediction heads with a compact, physically structured axis-hinge representation.

3. An extensive evaluation on synthetic and real-world articulation benchmarks, including out-of-distribution data, demonstrating improved articulation estimation over recent baselines.

4. Real-robot experiments showing that the predicted parameters support analytic motion generation and manipulation of previously unseen objects.

title: ActiveWAM: Evidence-Aware Active Vision for World-Action Models
authors: Renjun Wu,Luzhou Ge,Xuesong Li
abstract:
Active vision manipulation requires a policy to control both its camera and its
end-effectors, yet camera motion determines which evidence remains visible within
finite observation windows. Acquiring a new view can displace task-critical cues,
while retaining a view forgoes potentially useful observations. We formulate this
as an evidence-aware retain–acquire problem and present ActiveWAM, a unified
world–action model that learns observation and manipulation jointly. To this end,
we propose training-time inversion which constrains a frozen video prior by
task-bearing source evidence and visible temporal changes, eliminating the need
for test-time inversion or candidate ranking. At deployment, the policy generates
bimanual and pan/tilt actions—including stay and reacquisition behaviors—from
view-aware history, and updates context from newly measured RGB observations.
Future-video prediction serves as a co-training signal, while action generation
requires neither future-video decoding nor optimal viewpoint annotations. We
introduce RoboTwin-AV, a 50-task benchmark with executable pan/tilt control and
automatically generated demonstrations. ActiveWAM improves TAVIS out-of-distribution
success by up to 17.0 percentage points over the strongest baselines, achieves 20.0
additional points over Fast-WAM on RoboTwin-AV, and outperforms it by 26.7 points on real-world physical kitchen tasks.
introduction:
General-purpose manipulation requires robots to both acquire task-relevant visual evidence and act on it. Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies connect observations and instructions to commands [1, 2], while World–Action Models (WAMs) additionally learn the visual consequences of those commands [3, 4, 5]. In bimanual manipulation, coordinated arm actions change the scene while camera actions determine which spatial relations remain visible within the policy’s finite observation window.

Useful observation is not equivalent to removing occlusion. During approach, a view should expose object–end-effector relations; during placement, the destination becomes equally important. Even in an unobstructed workspace, moving a well-positioned camera can discard context. The appropriate observation behavior includes retaining a good view, not only searching for a better one. We call this the retain–acquire problem: a policy must preserve task-critical evidence in its recent representation while acquiring or reacquiring physical evidence when the current view is insufficient.

Recent benchmarks demonstrate that active camera control depends on task structure rather than universal heuristics. AV-ALOHA evaluates active, static, and wrist cameras in bimanual tasks [6]; TAVIS studies conditional selection, search, and waiting behaviors under distribution shifts [7]; AVR combines viewpoint and focal-length control [8]; See2Act couples action refinement to target-centric views [9]. These results establish that observation control cannot rely on fixed rules and expose a temporal challenge: changing the view can acquire new evidence while removing previously useful evidence.

Pretrained representations [10, 11] and domain randomization [12] support visual transfer, yet history still mixes task evidence with appearance and camera motion. Stem-OB uses diffusion inversion to improve visual generalization [13], but a generic transform neither specifies which historical evidence must survive nor preserves temporal changes that can overturn earlier decisions.

We address the joint question: how can a world–action model learn to retain task-relevant evidence while controlling which evidence it acquires next? Our key insight is to couple a task-selective training transformation with executable observation actions through the same demonstrated continuation. The transformation changes the representation of an observed history; head and arm actions change the physical observation stream. Neither substitutes for the other: transforming a history cannot reveal an unobserved surface, and moving a camera cannot by itself ensure that a previously seen cue remains available.

We present ActiveWAM, an evidence-aware active vision WAM that combines task-guided history inversion with unified head–arm generation (Fig. ActiveWAM: Evidence-Aware Active Vision for World-Action Models). Training-Time Inversion (TTI) uses a frozen video prior constrained by task-bearing source evidence and visible temporal changes. A view-aware history adapter represents camera identity, pose, exposure time, and validity alongside current RGB. The policy learns from raw and transformed conditions with identical original targets. Future-video prediction provides a co-training signal; deployment uses raw observations to generate one head–arm trajectory, without online inversion, candidate ranking, or manually annotated optimal viewpoints.

To evaluate this retain–acquire coupling at bimanual-task scale, we introduce RoboTwin-AV, an active vision benchmark extension of RoboTwin 2.0 [14] retaining all 50 task definitions while adding executable pan/tilt control, synchronized RGB, and automatically generated demonstrations. We evaluate on the independently released TAVIS benchmark and use RoboTwin-AV for large-scale controlled comparisons, complemented by fixed-camera generalization tests and physical trials.

Our contributions are threefold:

We formulate active vision manipulation as evidence-aware retain–acquire behavior and introduce task-guided inversion that preserves task evidence and visible temporal changes within a finite history window while transferring the training signal to a raw-input policy.

We propose ActiveWAM, a unified policy that generates executable head–arm actions from view-aware history, including stay and reacquisition behaviors; future-video prediction is used as a co-training signal rather than a required test-time output.

We introduce RoboTwin-AV, a 50-task benchmark extension with executable pan/tilt control, and evaluate the retain–acquire interaction through factorial control, collector-shift tests, external baselines, and physical bimanual manipulation.

1. We formulate active vision manipulation as evidence-aware retain–acquire behavior and introduce task-guided inversion that preserves task evidence and visible temporal changes within a finite history window while transferring the training signal to a raw-input policy.

2. We propose ActiveWAM, a unified policy that generates executable head–arm actions from view-aware history, including stay and reacquisition behaviors; future-video prediction is used as a co-training signal rather than a required test-time output.

3. We introduce RoboTwin-AV, a 50-task benchmark extension with executable pan/tilt control, and evaluate the retain–acquire interaction through factorial control, collector-shift tests, external baselines, and physical bimanual manipulation.

title: Beyond Leaderboard Scores: A Deployment-Focused Protocol for Interpretable Tracking Evaluation in Pedestrian-Centric Environments
authors: Dominik Wojcikiewicz,Diego Paez-Granados
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: supplementary video provided as ancillary material. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
abstract: Mobile robots operating among pedestrians need trajectories that become available quickly, remain spatially credible through missed observations, preserve identity, and fit within an embedded computing budget. Aggregate tracking scores provide limited insight into when and how trajectories fail, while varying detector inputs can confound tracker and detector quality. We present a deployment-focused, tracker-only evaluation protocol that uses shared detections to isolate tracker behavior and directly evaluates initialization, detector-gap continuation, identity recovery, close-neighbor association, and load-dependent tracker-step runtime, while Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA) is retained as a complementary aggregate measure. We apply the protocol to the JackRabbot Dataset and Benchmark (JRDB) using six open-source trackers and our lightweight Pedestrian Reference Tracker (PedRefTrack), together with a GT-assisted variant that estimates the remaining tracker-side gap under idealized association and motion. Under fixed detections, the non-GT trackers span only 24.26%–29.67% HOTA yet exhibit markedly different capability profiles. After 1.0 s without detector support, no tracker without GT assistance maintains spatially correct, same-identity output in more than half of eligible cases, making missing-observation continuation the dominant limitation among the tested properties. Close-neighbor failures are smaller and increase mainly at the shortest separations. Tracker-step runtime on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin is heavy-tailed and load-sensitive, causing several trackers to fall below the 10 Hz real-time target in crowded frames. The protocol provides a reproducible way to characterize tracker behavior and deployment suitability in pedestrian-centric environments. Code and evaluation scripts are released at https://github.com/SCAI-Lab/tracker_eval.
introduction:
Robots operating in pedestrian-centric spaces such as hospitals, airports, and transit hubs need more than isolated pedestrian positions. A robot path planner uses recent trajectories to estimate walking direction and speed, predict near-term motion, assess collision risk, and choose socially compliant paths [1, 2, 3]. Tracking output must therefore arrive with limited delay, preserve identity, remain credible through missed observations, and be computed within the robot’s control cycle. Whether a tracker is suitable for deployment depends on its temporal behavior and failure conditions, not only on aggregate tracking accuracy.

Most 3D multi-object tracking (MOT) systems are developed and evaluated on autonomous-driving datasets centered on roadway geometry and vehicle-mounted sensing [4, 5]. Pedestrian-centric navigation presents a different operating regime in which people are observed at close range, nonlinear walking motion is common, and frequent partial occlusions arise from the crowd itself [6, 7, 8]. Performance established in the driving regime therefore does not by itself characterize the challenges faced by a mobile robot moving among pedestrians. Moreover, aggregate MOT scores summarize performance over an entire test set, providing limited insight into how tracker behavior relates to sequence complexity and deployment-relevant situations [9, 10]. Attributing these differences to tracker design is further complicated when evaluation is performed with different input detections, since scores then reflect both detection and tracking behavior. Shared detections are established in 2D MOT benchmarking [11, 12], but their use is generally not enforced by 3D MOT and robot-centric pedestrian-tracking benchmarks [13, 14, 15, 6].

We therefore propose a deployment-focused, tracker-only protocol that evaluates tracker behavior under shared detections (Fig. 1) with embedded runtime across input loads. Eligible events are defined from GT and detection information so every tracker is evaluated under identical conditions.

Rather than introducing a new composite tracking score, the protocol complements HOTA with directly interpretable success profiles for initialization, continuation through detector gaps, post-gap identity recovery, and close-neighbor association, while separately profiling tracker-step runtime as a function of input load on embedded hardware. As part of the protocol, we implement PedRefTrack, a lightweight pedestrian-oriented reference tracker, together with a GT-assisted variant that uses GT identity and displacement to idealize association and motion estimation, exposing the remaining performance gap associated with these factors. We instantiate the protocol on JRDB [6] to provide an evaluation of how established tracking methods handle deployment-relevant challenges in a pedestrian-centric robot setting. A supplementary video provides an overview of the protocol and case-study results.

title: Learning a Resolution-Consistent Jacobian Field for Bio-Inspired Rigid-Soft Finger
authors: Tianyou Liang,Haisen Zeng,Shanjun Chen,YiMing Zhu,Zhongyue Lu,Zirong Luo
comment: including supplementary material. Under review at Robotics and Autonomous Systems
abstract:
Bio-inspired tendon-driven rigid-soft coupled dexterous fingers exhibit strong nonlinearity
and configuration-dependent sensitivity, making accurate modeling challenging. In discrete-time
control, Jacobian-based kinematic algorithms typically rely on point-wise local linear approximations,
which makes their performance sensitive to sensor sampling frequency and controller update frequency.
To address this issue, we propose Jacobian Flow Matching (JFM), a structured learning framework based on Conditional
Flow Matching (CFM), to learn a resolution-consistent Jacobian field that models actuation-to-motion
transitions as a dynamical flow. The proposed framework supports both single-step prediction and continuous
rollout via ODE integration, enabling consistent inference across temporal resolutions. Experiments on a
tendon-driven rigid-soft finger show that the proposed method suppresses outlier errors and improves
single-step prediction accuracy, reducing the global average RMSE by over 53% compared with a baseline
discrete Jacobian learning approach. For long-horizon prediction, trajectories recovered via ODE integration
achieve higher fidelity under sparse sampling (Stride = 8), reducing the RMSE median by 14.43% and the error
variance by 24.87%. These results demonstrate that the learned flow-based Jacobian field provides an effective
local model for offline multi-step trajectory optimization in rigid-soft coupled nonlinear systems.
introduction:
Rigid-soft coupled dexterous fingers promise versatile manipulation in cluttered and constrained
settings [10, 1], yet reliable precision control remains difficult in practice. Unlike rigid-link
manipulators, bio-inspired underactuated fingers exhibit strong actuation coupling and compliance-induced
nonlinearities and hysteresis, so the mapping from actuation inputs to fingertip motion can change sharply
with configuration and operating conditions (e.g. tendon routing) [5].

Conventional approaches largely fall into two categories. Model-based methods derive kinematic or
quasi-static mappings from finger design and calibrated parameters, and then apply feedback control
using analytical Jacobians or locally linearized models [3, 17]. While attractive for their interpretability,
analytic transmission models are hard to maintain for tendon-driven soft underactuated fingers: tendon-sheath
friction exhibits pronounced hysteresis and is often modeled under simplifying assumptions, which can limit
accuracy and generalization across configurations and operating conditions [6, 7]. In practice, this often
necessitates repeated identification or retuning when hardware routing, load, or wear changes [8].

However, learning-based control still faces a train-test gap under practical deployment. First, most data-driven models
are tightly coupled to specific input conditions—whether step size, sampling rate, or command magnitude—and their
performance degrades significantly when these conditions change. Second, the actuation-motion coupling of tendon-driven
rigid-soft fingers varies markedly with configuration and operating conditions [13], yet prevailing approaches
focus on learning a direct pointwise Jacobian function while overlooking the holistic structure of the underlying
Jacobian field—making them brittle under finite command increments and sparse sensing.

What is needed is not merely a pointwise local map, but a resolution-consistent Jacobian field:
a Jacobian field that varies smoothly over the configuration space and remains consistent across sensing
and control resolutions, so that its integrated predictions remain stable as the sampling interval changes.
This shifts the core technical challenge from improving pointwise prediction accuracy alone to enforcing
field-level consistency under deployment resolution changes.

To address this issue, we propose Jacobian Flow Matching (JFM), a Conditional Flow Matching (CFM)-based
framework for learning resolution-consistent Jacobian fields. Our main contributions are as follows:

Resolution-consistent Jacobian field for rigid-soft finger kinematics: We formulate the actuation-motion
relationship of rigid-soft coupled fingers as a smooth, configuration-dependent Jacobian field rather than a pointwise
local map. The learned field is designed to remain consistent across sensing and control resolutions, improving motion prediction under discrete sampling.

Resolution-consistent Jacobian field for rigid-soft finger kinematics: We formulate the actuation-motion
relationship of rigid-soft coupled fingers as a smooth, configuration-dependent Jacobian field rather than a pointwise
local map. The learned field is designed to remain consistent across sensing and control resolutions, improving motion prediction under discrete sampling.

JFM learning of within-step Jacobian evolution: We introduce a JFM training scheme that supervises
the within-step evolution of the Jacobian field using adjacent observations. By normalizing
the step interval and enforcing intermediate-time consistency, the proposed model supports both pointwise prediction and
continuous-time rollout inference within a unified framework.

Evaluation under sparse sampling: We benchmark prediction and rollout fidelity across strides and horizons,
and further present open-loop trajectory optimization to show that the learned field provides a useful local model for multi-step
trajectory optimization.

title: SonarVoxNet: Diver Detection in 3D Bounding Box using 3D Sonar
authors: Eugene Park,Jiwon Lee,Seyoung Kan,Trung Dong,Xiaomin Lin,Jane Shin
abstract: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) assisting human divers must continuously track not only the diver’s 3D position but also their full-body orientation. However, vision-based perception is unreliable underwater, and forward-looking sonar – despite being widely used – discards the elevation information needed for orientation estimation, posing a fundamental limitation. Recently commercialized 3D sonar preserves elevation but produces sparse, noisy returns, and existing detectors are built for dense LiDAR data and for targets that remain upright and rotate only about the yaw axis (e.g., vehicles, pedestrians), making them unable to represent a freely pitching and rolling diver. To address this gap, we present two contributions. First, SonarVoxNet adapts a voxel-based encoder and an anchor-free center-based detection head to 3D sonar data, replacing the conventional yaw-only rotation representation with a continuous 6D rotation parameterization to predict full 9-DoF oriented bounding boxes—to our knowledge, the first 3D sonar diver detector to do so. Second, Diver3D is the first public 3D sonar dataset with full 3D orientation labels for divers in diverse, non-upright poses, collected at a natural cave-diving site. Through controlled ablations over the backbone and detection head, we show that the dominant factor behind accurate 3D sonar-based diver detection is the transition from yaw-only rotation to full-SO(3) rotation. This transition substantially improves detection accuracy and reduces orientation error. These results demonstrate that full-body diver orientation is recoverable from 3D sonar alone, laying the groundwork for future work on diver pose estimation and diver-robot interaction.
introduction:
Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are increasingly deployed to assist marine operations, from infrastructure inspection to scientific exploration; however, many tasks still require a human diver in the loop. For an AUV to safely and usefully assist such a diver, it must continuously track the diver’s position and 3D body orientation – a prerequisite for any context-aware human-robot interaction underwater. However, vision-based perception [1, 2], despite its success on land, is poorly suited to this task: light attenuation, scattering, and turbidity frequently render optical cameras unreliable underwater. The community has therefore turned to acoustic imaging, and in particular forward-looking sonar (FLS), which has been extensively used for detecting objects on the seabed.

Applying FLS to diver monitoring, however, exposes a fundamental geometric bottleneck: FLS projects 3D spatial structure onto a single 2D acoustic plane, discarding elevation. This loss is often tolerable for rigid, seabed-bound objects, but not for a diver, whose 3D orientation in the water column is precisely the quantity of interest.

This limitation motivates volumetric sensing, recently made practical by the commercialization of 3D sonar sensors, which preserve elevation alongside range and azimuth. The transition from 2D to 3D acoustic data[3], however, trades one bottleneck for several new ones. Acoustic returns from a non-rigid human body are sparse, non-uniform, and corrupted by multipath noise, causing architectures built for dense LiDAR and RGB data[4, 5] to fail. Just as importantly, the detection heads built for such dense sensors assume that targets are upright and rotate only about the vertical (yaw) axis. This assumption is violated outright by a free-swimming diver, who pitches and rolls continuously; a yaw-only detector can localize a diver while completely misrepresenting the out-of-plane orientation that HRI most depends on.

We note that this paper targets diver detection – an oriented 3D bounding box capturing position, size, and full-body orientation – rather than per-joint skeletal pose estimation, which we view as a subsequent problem that first requires solving accurate 3D-oriented detection. To the best of our knowledge, there is no existing 3D sonar method that recovers even the coarse body orientation of a diver using real 3D sonar, and there is no existing 3D sonar dataset that captures divers in sufficiently diverse, non-upright poses to train or evaluate one.

To address the aforementioned gaps:

We present SonarVoxNet, which adapts a VoxelNet [6] volumetric encoder and a CenterPoint [7] anchor-free head to sparse, noisy 3D sonar returns, replacing yaw-only output with a continuous 6D rotation parameterization [8]. To our knowledge, this is the first 9-DoF diver detector for 3D sonar.

We present Diver3D, comprising 2 hours, 37,010 frames, and 34,568 annotated instances across 36 scenes, collected at Blue Grotto, a natural spring cave-diving site near Gainesville, FL, where divers exhibit realistic pitch and roll rarely seen in pool settings. To our knowledge, this is the first public 3D sonar dataset with full 3D orientation labels for human divers.

Through a controlled backbone-and-head ablation, we show that adopting full-SO(3) rotation, rather than yaw-only, is the dominant factor behind accurate 3D detection on sonar data, outweighing backbone choice. We further show that a sonar-specific, orientation-preserving augmentation strategy yields additional gains in detection accuracy and orientation fidelity, and we release our full evaluation protocol as an open baseline for underwater 3D perception research.

1. We present SonarVoxNet, which adapts a VoxelNet [6] volumetric encoder and a CenterPoint [7] anchor-free head to sparse, noisy 3D sonar returns, replacing yaw-only output with a continuous 6D rotation parameterization [8]. To our knowledge, this is the first 9-DoF diver detector for 3D sonar.

2. We present Diver3D, comprising 2 hours, 37,010 frames, and 34,568 annotated instances across 36 scenes, collected at Blue Grotto, a natural spring cave-diving site near Gainesville, FL, where divers exhibit realistic pitch and roll rarely seen in pool settings. To our knowledge, this is the first public 3D sonar dataset with full 3D orientation labels for human divers.

3. Through a controlled backbone-and-head ablation, we show that adopting full-SO(3) rotation, rather than yaw-only, is the dominant factor behind accurate 3D detection on sonar data, outweighing backbone choice. We further show that a sonar-specific, orientation-preserving augmentation strategy yields additional gains in detection accuracy and orientation fidelity, and we release our full evaluation protocol as an open baseline for underwater 3D perception research.

title: ReCo: Response-Consistent Locomotion with Policy-Aware MPC for Legged Manipulation
authors: Kuankuan Sima,Yichao Gao,Chenxi Gu,Kefan Zhao,Lin Zhao
abstract: Continuous legged manipulation requires accurate end-effector tracking while the base keeps walking. Combining reinforcement learning (RL) with model predictive control (MPC) suits this task: the learned policy provides robust locomotion, while MPC coordinates the base and arm to compensate for tracking errors. However, MPC can compensate only for base motion that it can predict, and a learned policy’s command response varies with gait phase, contact, and payload. We present ReCo, a framework that couples response-consistent locomotion with policy-aware MPC for legged manipulation. Response shaping trains the policy to respond to commands consistently and repeatably across randomized dynamics. An identified closed-loop response model then lets MPC jointly plan locomotion commands and arm motion. On the simulation benchmark, ReCo reduces position and orientation root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 28.7% and 27.4% relative to the best baseline for each metric. Real-world experiments demonstrate onboard continuous legged manipulation with coordinated base and arm motion.
introduction:
A quadruped equipped with an arm can bring manipulation capabilities to environments that are difficult for conventional mobile platforms to traverse. Tasks such as inspection, scanning, and tool positioning can require the robot to track a world-frame end-effector (EE) trajectory while walking. Every step moves the arm’s supporting frame: base translation, attitude changes, and gait oscillations all propagate to the EE. Continuous legged manipulation therefore requires coordination throughout locomotion, beyond repositioning the base to extend the arm’s workspace (Fig. 1).

Robust locomotion and precise manipulation place different demands on control. Reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled quadrupeds to traverse challenging terrain under uncertain contact conditions and dynamics [1, 2, 3, 4]. Model-based control explicitly represents task geometry, motion constraints, and future references, supporting coordinated locomotion and manipulation [5, 6]. Learned whole-body controllers also demonstrate effective leg–arm coordination [7, 8]. However, (i) model-based control relies on accurate contact and dynamics models, which are hard to maintain on uneven terrain with uncertain contact, and (ii) learned whole-body control balances task-space accuracy and stability within one reward, which can require retuning across terrains, payloads, and disturbances.

A modular alternative assigns locomotion to RL and base–arm coordination to model predictive control (MPC) [9]. In such architectures the key difficulty lies at the interface: the manipulation planner must predict how the policy-controlled base will move under candidate locomotion commands. To MPC, the base is a closed-loop subsystem whose command response can vary with gait phase, contact conditions, and payload. To the locomotion policy, arm motion changes the dynamics it must stabilize. Assuming that a commanded velocity or posture is realized immediately neglects these interactions. Even an accurate mean-velocity model can miss the periodic height and attitude motion that propagates to the EE.

Our key insight is that a locomotion policy should be trained not only to be robust but also to be predictable by the planner that commands it. Locomotion supplies sustained displacement and disturbance recovery, while the arm supplies fast local corrections within its workspace and actuator limits; a planner can exploit this division of labor only if the base response is repeatable. A consistent delay can be compensated by feedforward, whereas a variable delay cannot. We therefore seek a locomotion response that a low-order model can predict over a useful horizon.

We present ReCo, a framework that couples response-consistent locomotion with policy-aware MPC for legged manipulation. Our contributions are:

A training method that makes the command response of a locomotion policy repeatable through reference tracking, phase repeatability, steady-state gain, and cross-domain consistency rewards.

A policy-aware MPC that jointly plans locomotion commands and arm motion for continuous world-frame EE SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) tracking, where an identified closed-loop response model with a gait-periodic component serves as the predictive interface to the learned policy.

Simulation and hardware experiments in which ReCo reduces position and orientation root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 28.7% and 27.4% relative to the best of five baselines for each metric, response shaping lowers normalized prediction mean squared error (MSE) by 59.6%, and the full system runs onboard.

1. A training method that makes the command response of a locomotion policy repeatable through reference tracking, phase repeatability, steady-state gain, and cross-domain consistency rewards.

2. A policy-aware MPC that jointly plans locomotion commands and arm motion for continuous world-frame EE SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) tracking, where an identified closed-loop response model with a gait-periodic component serves as the predictive interface to the learned policy.

3. Simulation and hardware experiments in which ReCo reduces position and orientation root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 28.7% and 27.4% relative to the best of five baselines for each metric, response shaping lowers normalized prediction mean squared error (MSE) by 59.6%, and the full system runs onboard.

title: Completion Aware Guidance for World Action Models
authors: Seungyeon Kim,Junhoo Lee,Baekseung Kim,Minkyu Kim,Nojun Kwak
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) predict visual futures and robot actions, yet they remain susceptible to task-incomplete imagination, where plausible, action-consistent predictions omit the transition needed for task completion. In this paper, we show that this failure is not inherent to the world model backbone, but emerges when adapted for short-chunk control, which can repeatedly favor plausible local continuations over task-completing transitions. To address this, we introduce Completion Aware Guidance (CAG), a training-free sampling method that guides generation toward task completion. Across representative WAMs, CAG improves success from 64% to 70% on a RoboTwin 2.0 subset and from 69% to 75% in zero-shot simulation, while reducing task-incomplete imagination from 79% to 40%.
introduction:
Robot tasks unfold through changes in the world state, and therefore require temporal understanding of what is likely to happen after an action is executed. Vision–language–action policies [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] predict actions from the current observation, yet the resulting future changes are difficult to infer from observed images alone. World Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by using video generative models to jointly predict a visual future and the actions that realize it [6, 7, 8]. However, generating visual futures with aligned actions does not guarantee task success.

Interestingly, as shown in Fig. 1, we find that WAMs exhibit task-incomplete imagination, generating visually coherent, instruction-relevant futures while omitting the state transitions required for task completion. For example, given a pick-and-place instruction, the imagined video may move an object above its target but continue holding it instead of releasing it, and the predicted actions follow this future, resulting in task failure. This differs from a corrupted video or video–action misalignment in that both modalities agree on a plausible continuation that does not complete the task.

In this paper, we ask why WAMs exhibit task-incomplete imagination and how this failure can be addressed. We argue that it arises from an objective mismatch between the fixed-horizon video-generation objective for video-backbone pretraining and the short-horizon video-action prediction objective for WAM fine-tuning. Under the former objective, video diffusion models jointly predict an instruction-following trajectory over a fixed horizon, whereas WAMs predict video-action chunks that are executed and regenerated from the observation. Because the WAM objective does not require the current phase to be completed within each horizon, the state transition required for task completion can be repeatedly deferred.
As a result, although the video backbone can generate instruction-following trajectories, this capability is not reliably elicited when needed.

To address this mismatch, we introduce Completion Aware Guidance (CAG), a training-free sampling method for WAMs. CAG strengthens the conditioning of instruction tokens most relevant to the current video–action prediction, steering the current chunk toward the required state transition without retraining the WAM. Across DreamZero and Fast-WAM [6, 7], CAG improves the average task success rate from 64.4% to 70.0% on a RoboTwin 2.0 subset and from 69% to 75% in zero-shot simulation. More importantly, in a representative manipulation setting exhibiting task-incomplete imagination, CAG further reduces the incidence of this failure from 79% to 40%.

title: OpenSpace Lab Solution to the IROS 2026 Indoor Exploration Competition
authors: Yuxuan Zhang,Dong Li,Zezhou Sun,Yuxuan Xu,Siyu Teng,Yuchen Li,Jianjian Yang,Long Chen
comment: this https URL
abstract:
This report presents the OpenSpace Lab’s solution to the Competition on Intelligent Information Gathering for Single and Multi-Robot Systems Workshops, organized as part of the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026. Our team reached 1st place in the Single-Robot Public Track and 3rd place in both the Single- and Multi-Robot Private Tracks.
The single-robot framework utilizes pre-trained map completion predictions for global planning to prioritize unexplored areas. To reconcile map coverage with limited operation time, we introduce a remaining-time-based exploration strategy that integrates homing constraints into the decision-making process.
For multi-robot exploration, we utilize a utility-driven target selection strategy that balances observation gains, movement costs, and budget constraints, leveraging shared map and intent data to eliminate redundant search and maximize coordination efficiency.
Our solution reached a 61.04% coverage rate in the Single-Robot Public Track, while reaching 39.53% and 39.91% coverage in the Single- and Multi-Robot Private Tracks, respectively.
An extended full-length paper based on this report is currently being prepared for submission, and the source code will be released upon acceptance of the full manuscript at https://github.com/OpenSpace-Lab/Indoor-Exploration-IROS2026.
introduction:
Robotics exploration is a fundamental capability for autonomous robots, aiming to guide robotic actions through the real-time evaluation of information gain to maximize environmental information collection within minimal temporal budgets [8]. This capability underpins a wide spectrum of applications, ranging from indoor search and wild rescue to underwater surveying and planetary exploration [6]. Progressively, the target of quantified information extends beyond conventional geometric representations, such as point clouds and signal sources, to high-level spatial semantic representations and field-based environmental resources [7, 2].

Despite extensive research in autonomous robotic exploration, existing methods predominantly treat execution time or path length as a passive evaluation metric after mission completion, rather than an active constraint governing real-time decision-making. In many critical real-world scenarios, such as battery-constrained rovers exploring the lunar south pole or search-and-rescue agents operating in hazardous environments, time-bounded exploration is paramount. Under these strict temporal budgets, robots must not only maximize information gathering within a finite horizon, but also continuously evaluate the time cost of returning to a base station or communications hub to deliver collected data. However, incorporating explicit, hard time constraints into real-time frontier evaluation and path planning remains largely unaddressed in current exploration frameworks [1, 3].

The Indoor Exploration Competition11
1
https://github.com/BYU-FROST-Lab/indoor-exploration-competition, hosted by Seungchan Kim and Brady Moon at the IROS 2026 Workshop on Intelligent Information Gathering for Single and Multi-Robot Systems22
2
https://frostlab.byu.edu/IIG-workshop/, evaluates autonomous agents under realistic operational constraints. The competition provides scale-dependent step budgets and strictly requires robots to return to the base station range to upload gathered map data.

To address these challenges, our team, OpenSpace Lab, developed specialized solutions for both single- and multi-robot tracks. The single-robot strategy generates candidate goals based on immediate observations and leverages pre-trained map completion to prioritize exploration sequences. Adapting to varying step budgets, it dynamically adjusts goal selection and pathing rules. The multi-robot extension reduces redundant search by initializing dispersed exploration directions and incorporating shared teammate goals alongside historical trajectories. Both strategies monitor remaining steps against estimated homing costs to guarantee timely return and data delivery. Detailed formulations of these methods are presented in Section 2.
