title: ALFRED: Requirement-driven development of an open-source mobile manipulator for long-term plant monitoring
authors: Ciarán Miceal Johnson,Christopher Quail,Garry Ellard,Alistair McConnell,Steve Tonneau,Fernando Auat Cheein
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Tracking seasonal change in crops and forests requires observing the same plants repeatedly. Ground robots can do this at close range, and a manipulator gives their sensors more viewpoints. Yet the robots behind long-term field datasets are rarely released with their design files, and how a robot’s own structure limits arm reach and occludes its sensors is seldom compared between builds. We present ALFRED, an open-source mobile manipulator built from commercially available components. It carries a six-degree-of-freedom arm, LiDAR, RGB-D cameras, RTK GNSS and an IMU on an Ackermann-steered base, all mounted on a reconfigurable aluminium strut frame, and runs containerised ROS software. It was developed through four builds against six requirements for repeated outdoor deployment: durability, modularity, repairability, sensing reach, endurance and reproducibility. Model-based analysis of the last three builds shows the usable share of the arm’s reachable poses rising from 34.0% to 60.0% and then 66.1%, and ray casting shows that only the final build keeps the frame-mounted LiDAR’s horizontal view clear both forwards and backwards. ALFRED completed a year of monthly forest surveys (528 traversals) without missing a scheduled collection. This was despite battery degradation, reconfiguration for another researcher’s study, and the parallel development of ALFRED 2.0 for autonomous crop-row operation, with each switch between builds taking about six hours. The deployment also showed that mechanical modularity is only as dependable as the robot description that tracks it. Design files, bill of materials, robot descriptions, containers and build documentation are openly released.
introduction:
Crop growth models simulate crop development from weather, soil and management practices, but numerous uncertainties compromise their performance (Dlamini et al., 2023). Data assimilation can reduce this uncertainty using in-season measurements of crop traits (Huang et al., 2016). Acquiring those measurements conventionally requires manual and often destructive sampling, which is slow, labour-intensive and costly (Atefi et al., 2021). Destructive sampling is also unsuitable for monitoring a crop continuously through its growth cycle: the plant is removed or damaged, and the gap it leaves alters the plants either side of it, which partially compensate for its loss (Pavek and Thornton, 2006). Non-destructive measurement, by contrast, allows the same plants to be measured repeatedly and their growth tracked over time (Poorter et al., 2023).

Satellites and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) both provide in-season observations for crop model data assimilation, and each makes a different trade-off between coverage and detail (Wang et al., 2024). Satellites cover whole regions, but their resolution is coarse and cloud cover can leave long gaps between usable images during the growing season (Matese et al., 2015; Whitcraft et al., 2015).UAVs offer finer spatial resolution and more flexible revisits than satellites, at the cost of coverage (Bazrafkan et al., 2025). However, they view the crop from above or at an oblique angle, so lower leaves, stems and internal canopy structure are often occluded in dense or tall crops (Zhang et al., 2026). Low-altitude multi-rotor flight adds a further problem, since rotor downwash can deform flexible plants and alter the canopy geometry being measured Shi et al. (2021). Unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) do not suffer from the same issue and can sense plants at close range, where more information can be acquired about individual organs, and adding a manipulator allows cameras to be positioned and oriented at the best viewpoints (Atefi et al., 2021). Because the end effector can be swapped, a single mobile manipulator can be reconfigured for different tasks (Guri et al., 2024), allowing several kinds of data to be collected from the same plants. This article focuses on mobile manipulators of this kind.

Long-term experiments and data collection place additional demands on the platform. The platform must be able to operate outdoors all year round, be reconfigurable as sensing requirements change, and maintainable and repairable. Further demands arise when the platform is needed for other experiments, as happens when it is shared between projects, or during planned upgrades, which must be built and validated without missing scheduled data collections. Existing research shows that long-term deployment of agricultural robots is achievable (Bender et al., 2020; Polvara et al., 2024), as are modular platforms (Grimstad and From, 2017; Guri et al., 2024). However, these studies rarely discuss the rapid prototyping required before and during sustained, repeated deployment, or compare successive prototype builds against desirable characteristics to quantify their improvements. Additionally, reachability analysis (Zacharias et al., 2007; Vahrenkamp et al., 2013) and LiDAR placement (Kim and Park, 2020; Hu et al., 2022) are common tools in manipulation and autonomous driving, but are rarely used as development tools to compare agricultural robot prototypes.

This paper presents the Autonomous Leaf and Forestry Research Exploration Device (ALFRED), a mobile manipulator assembled from commercially available components for repeated close-range sensing of crops and forests. It was developed through four builds, each motivated by a requirement its predecessor failed to meet, against six design requirements: outdoor durability, modularity and reconfigurability, repairability, sensing reach and coverage, endurance, and reproducibility by others. The last two builds are ALFRED, an aluminium strut-frame robot that collected a year of monthly forest surveys, and ALFRED 2.0, which adds a second frame layer, a second computer and real-time kinematic (RTK) positioning for autonomous crop-row operation. Since the authors had no access to farmland, forestry served as a proxy, testing the platform’s ability to capture seasonal and structural change in living plants over a full annual cycle. For the same reason, ALFRED 2.0’s crop-row operation used artificial plants set out in rows in a field.

The contributions of this article are:

the presentation of a modular platform used in three experiments in the course of a year all requiring significantly different builds while not missing scheduled data collection in a year long experiment

a requirement-traced account of the four builds, recording the failure behind each design change

a model-based comparison of the last three builds, in which the usable share of the arm’s reachable workspace rises from 34.0% to 60.0% and 66.1%, and the visibility of the frame-mounted LiDAR is compared across build, task, and arm posture

an open release of the design files, robot description, and containerised software

The remainder of this article is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews data assimilation into crop models, mobile manipulators for repeated crop sensing, and the use of reachability and visibility analysis as design tools. Section 3 introduces ALFRED and ALFRED 2.0 together with the ForestYear3D and ROWCAST experiments they were built for, and Section 4 describes the hardware and software shared by both builds and the differences between them. Section 5 states the six design requirements and Section 6 introduces the four prototypes. Sections 7 to 10.4 then assess every build against each requirement in turn, including the model-based comparison of manipulator reach and sensor visibility in Section 10. Section 11 sets out the limitations and future work, and Section 12 concludes.

1. the presentation of a modular platform used in three experiments in the course of a year all requiring significantly different builds while not missing scheduled data collection in a year long experiment

2. a requirement-traced account of the four builds, recording the failure behind each design change

3. a model-based comparison of the last three builds, in which the usable share of the arm’s reachable workspace rises from 34.0% to 60.0% and 66.1%, and the visibility of the frame-mounted LiDAR is compared across build, task, and arm posture

4. an open release of the design files, robot description, and containerised software

title: Continue, Abort, or Fall: Viability-Aware Policy Selection (VAPS) for Safe Humanoid Acrobatics
authors: Siwei Ju,Lu Liu,Jan Peters,Oleg Arenz
abstract:
Dynamic humanoid motions such as flips risk hardware damage due to suboptimal policies, disturbances or sim-to-real gaps. A motion tracking policy offers no way out once the maneuver leaves its reference, and a backup policy needs to take over to protect the hardware for a minimum-damage landing.
Which backup to use matters as much as when to switch.
We present Viability-Aware Policy Selection (VAPS), which treats safety as a policy-conditioned, receding-horizon decision.
Besides a protective fall policy, we also train an abort policy which can abort the motion at any time, landing on its feet.
At every control step, learned predictors estimate whether the nominal tracking policy and the abort policy remain viable over a short horizon, and a least-sacrificial hierarchy keeps the most task-ambitious behavior that remains viable.
In simulation with randomized disturbances, VAPS sharply reduces head contact and hand contact, which are the dominant sources of hardware damage, with both a Unitree G1 and a LimX Oli; on the LimX Oli, we validate the viability predictors and the full VAPS controller for side-flip motions.
VAPS Pareto-dominates the strongest single-network alternatives we could train, including an end-to-end safe-tracking policy and students distilled from VAPS’s own oracle-routed decisions, in both task success and head impact.
We also show that VAPS is a powerful framework to supervise undertrained policies and protect the hardware.
introduction:
Humanoid robots are increasingly capable of highly dynamic whole-body behaviors, including running, jumping, and acrobatics [1, 2], but deploying such maneuvers safely remains difficult. Sim-to-real gaps, disturbances or suboptimal policies are common reasons for deployment failure and cause significant hardware damage, especially for highly dynamic acrobatic motions.

Humanoid acrobatics are typically learned as reference-tracking policies [2]. A tracking policy is rewarded for staying close to its reference, and its training episodes terminate as soon as it strays from it; at deployment, once the maneuver has left the reference, a backup must take over. Most existing safety mechanisms nonetheless cast this intervention as a binary choice between continuing the nominal controller and activating a single backup policy or safety shield, which either steers the robot back to a safe region [3, 4, 5] or executes a safe fall [6]. Highly dynamic acrobatics are fast and short, lasting only one to two seconds. When something goes wrong, there is little time left to correct or recover, only to abort safely.
Depending on the severity of the deviation, a robot that has left its reference may still be able to abort the motion with a controlled landing on its feet rather than a fall, whereas even a learned safe fall can cause serious damage at these speeds.
A single switch is therefore too coarse, particularly in the intermediate regime where the maneuver is already lost but a controlled landing is not.
Folding execution and recovery into one policy [7, 8] does not restore the missing granularity either.

We address these challenges with policy-conditioned, receding-horizon viability: whether a state is safe depends on which closed-loop behavior runs next, and should be judged over a short, continuously re-evaluated window rather than by a single guess for the end of the episode. We instantiate this as Viability-Aware Policy Selection (VAPS), which selects among the nominal tracking policy and backups ordered by decreasing task ambition: an abort policy that seeks a controlled feet-first landing, and a protective-fall policy that minimizes harm once upright recovery is no longer viable. A policy-dependent predictor, which encodes a short observation history, re-estimates each behavior’s short-horizon viability at every control step, and VAPS preserves the most ambitious behavior that remains viable. As the predictor judges the state and the candidate behavior rather than the cause of risk, the same mechanism recovers a mature policy from disturbances, supervises a new and unproven one, and handles a stop request issued by an operator or a workspace monitor. As hardware failures are expensive to collect, all failure cases are generated in simulation, and each state is reloaded under every candidate behavior.

We summarize our main contributions as follows:

Least-sacrificial safety. VAPS formulates intervention during a dynamic maneuver as a selection over an ordered hierarchy of behaviors: continue, abort, and protective fall, committing to the smallest sacrifice of task ambition that remains viable.

Policy-conditioned, receding-horizon viability. We learn viability predictors for the nominal policy and the abort policy from counterfactual rollouts and evaluate them continuously from proprioceptive history.

Analysis of single-policy alternatives. We investigate monolithic alternatives, including end-to-end RL policies and students distilled from VAPS with DAgger, and show that VAPS dominates all of them.

Hardware validation. We develop and test VAPS in simulation on Unitree G1 and LimX Oli, deploy it and validate the sim-to-real transfer on LimX Oli.

1. Least-sacrificial safety. VAPS formulates intervention during a dynamic maneuver as a selection over an ordered hierarchy of behaviors: continue, abort, and protective fall, committing to the smallest sacrifice of task ambition that remains viable.

2. Policy-conditioned, receding-horizon viability. We learn viability predictors for the nominal policy and the abort policy from counterfactual rollouts and evaluate them continuously from proprioceptive history.

3. Analysis of single-policy alternatives. We investigate monolithic alternatives, including end-to-end RL policies and students distilled from VAPS with DAgger, and show that VAPS dominates all of them.

4. Hardware validation. We develop and test VAPS in simulation on Unitree G1 and LimX Oli, deploy it and validate the sim-to-real transfer on LimX Oli.

title: Is Success All You Need? Investigating the Impact of Input Perturbations on VLA Behaviour in Tabletop Manipulation Tasks
authors: Sophie Higham,Riccardo Andrea Izzo,Matteo Matteucci,Alessandro Suglia
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved high task success rates on robot manipulation task benchmarks. More recently, there has been an emphasis on evaluating the robustness of VLA models to perturbations. However, this robustness is still predominantly measured through Task Success Rate (TSR). In this work, we propose a benchmark-agnostic evaluation framework to measure the behavioural robustness of models by characterising how successful trajectories are executed under perturbation. We implement this methodology by extending the widely-used LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. Across three state-of-the-art VLA models, four LIBERO task suites and seven perturbation conditions, we evaluate changes in both typical successful behaviour and its variability, including metrics of motion smoothness, efficiency and gripper behaviour. We find that perturbations can alter the behaviour of successful trajectories, a phenomenon which cannot necessarily be inferred from TSR alone. Across LIBERO suites, we identify cases where state-of-the-art VLA models achieve comparable TSR under the same perturbation condition, yet behaviour on successful trajectories diverges substantially. Therefore, to have a more robust assessment of task performance, we argue that suitable measures of robustness should capture not only whether a task is completed, but also how the robot behaves while completing it. When evaluating the robustness of VLA models, TSR may be complemented by behavioural evaluation metrics that characterise the nature and variability of successful task execution by robots.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [1] have emerged as a prominent paradigm in robotics, with the ability to map visual observations, natural language instructions and proprioceptive states directly to motor commands. Building upon large-scale pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs), VLAs have progressed rapidly in recent years, demonstrating generalisation to unseen objects and language instructions [2, 3]. Such models have shown strong performance across robotic tasks, including tabletop manipulation [4, 5, 6]. More recently, increasing attention has been given to the robustness of VLA models, which have shown brittleness to environmental variations such as altered scene lighting and visual distractors [7, 8]. A number of works investigate this by introducing perturbations to the evaluation data, along dimensions including scene lighting and language instruction [7, 8, 9, 10]. However, this robustness is typically measured by binary task success rate (TSR). Focussing primarily on TSR enables straightforward comparison; however, it may obscure other critical failures which aren’t captured by this binary outcome alone [11, 12].

In their work on AI agent reliability, Rabanser et al. argue that once agents are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably face environmental perturbations, but that ”robust agents should maintain comparable performance despite such perturbations” [11]. We argue that, for embodied AI systems, the notion of comparable performance should account for the fundamentally embodied nature of the application. The decisions and control outputs of embodied AI agents translate into physical actions, which can have significant real-world consequences [13]. Beyond binary TSR alone, behavioural metrics may more suitably reflect the deployability of VLA models. We consider a number of such metrics. The jerkiness of the trajectory may be important, as large acceleration changes can lead to higher mechanical stress and manipulator wear [14, 15]. Behavioural metrics also matter from a human acceptability perspective. Sheidlower et al. [16] found that task completion speed data, a marker of efficiency, was requested by users. Additionally, perceived reliability and predictability are central factors affecting trust [17], and unexpected behaviour from robots can degrade the trust that users may have in the technology [18]. In addition to TSR, we argue for the inclusion of behavioural metrics, which we find can offer greater insight into the comparative robustness of VLA models.

We identify a gap in the evaluation of VLA and embodied AI models. Work exists which either (i) evaluates the trajectory behaviour beyond binary task success, or (ii) measures robustness to perturbations using task success as the primary metric. To our knowledge, these two practices have not yet been combined. As a result, current robustness evaluation cannot determine whether a policy’s behaviour has meaningfully degraded when it continues to complete a task successfully. Two policies may achieve identical success rates under perturbation, while exhibiting substantially different trajectory quality. A demonstrative example is given in Figure 1. Motivated by this gap, we propose a framework for evaluating the behavioural robustness of VLA models under perturbation by calculating metrics of motion smoothness, efficiency and gripper behaviour, to complement TSR. With this evaluation framework, we aim to answer the following research questions:

RQ1: How does the typical behaviour of successful trajectories change under input perturbation?

successful trajectories?

We implement this framework by extending the LIBERO [19] and LIBERO-Plus [7] benchmarks. While we use these benchmarks as an experimental testbed given their wide adoption [6, 7], the proposed behavioural evaluation is benchmark-agnostic and could be applied to other benchmarks, as long as trajectory-level state and action information can be retrieved (e.g. MetaWorld) [20].

Thus, through this work, we:

Propose a benchmark-agnostic behavioural evaluation methodology that complements task success rate with trajectory-level behaviour metrics, enabling practitioners to derive a more complete performance assessment of the robustness of VLA models, and implement it on the popular LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. The metrics comprise the duration, total gripper movement, Cartesian jerk, joint jerk, Cartesian path length, and joint path length observed for the trajectories.

Demonstrate that for state-of-the-art VLA models, robustness of task success does not necessarily equate to robustness of successful execution behaviour. Under perturbations, successful trajectories can change substantially even when task success is preserved.

title: Cross-entropy optimization with prioritized constraints
authors: Francisco Roldan Sanchez,Pau de las Heras Molins,David Fridovich-Keil,Georgios Bakirtzis
abstract: When constraints conflict, an optimizer must determine which requirements to preserve and which to relax. On the one hand, a priority ordering specifies which requirements take precedence. On the other hand, penalty-based formulations encode their relative importance through numerical weights. Depending on these weights, a solution can improve its weighted score while violating intended priorities. We introduce TierCEM, a variant of the cross-entropy method that incorporates strict constraint priorities directly into elite selection without requiring per-constraint importance weights. TierCEM works by sequentially filtering sampled candidates, from highest- to lowest-priority constraint. If and when a constraint eliminates all remaining candidates, TierCEM returns to the last nonempty set and selects elites with the smallest violations of that blocking constraint, recursively preserving satisfaction of all higher-priority constraints. We evaluate TierCEM on 2D navigation and contact-rich pushing tasks in proprioceptive and learned world-model settings. Experiments show that reversing the constraint ordering changes which constraints are violated under conflict. Prioritizing progress toward the task objective also enables TierCEM to relax lower-priority constraints when they would otherwise prevent further progress.
introduction:
When constraints have different priorities, optimizing a scalarized objective turns the priority order into a weighted trade-off and the optimizer can sacrifice a higher-priority constraint to reduce lower-priority violations. In autonomous driving, for example, better lane keeping must not compensate for a collision when collision avoidance takes precedence (Censi et al., 2019). A priority ordering among possibly conflicting constraints makes that distinction explicit. Satisfying a lower-priority requirement must not sacrifice a higher-priority requirement that could otherwise be preserved.

Incorporating multiple constraints into a single optimization problem is often achieved by combining the task objective and constraint penalties into a scalar score, making constraint priorities dependent on numerical trade-offs between the competing terms (Ma et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2023; Kushwaha et al., 2025). Under that task objective, an improvement in objective value or lower-priority penalties can compensate for a higher-priority violation. Preventing such compensation requires weights calibrated to both the prescribed ordering and the scales and attainable values of the competing terms, making constraint satisfaction sensitive to that calibration (Imanov et al., 2026).

Sampling-based optimizers such as the cross-entropy method (CEM) (Botev et al., 2013) and model-predictive path integral (MPPI) (Williams et al., 2017) provide a natural setting for candidate-wise constraint evaluation. In standard CEM, the top ℓ\ell candidates according to a ranking metric are called elites and are used to update the sampling distribution in an iterative fashion. We propose the tiered CEM (TierCEM), which implements ordered constraint relaxation directly in CEM’s elite selection logic through a priority-relaxation cascade (cf. Figure 1). At each iteration, TierCEM filters sampled candidate solutions from highest- to lowest-priority constraint. If a filter eliminates every remaining candidate, the cascade returns to the preceding nonempty elite set and selects samples with the smallest violations of the blocking constraint. If all filters retain candidates, those that maximize the distance to the boundary of the lowest-priority constraint are selected as elites.

The selected elites then determine the next sampling distribution through the standard CEM update. The constraint ordering thus governs which requirements are preserved and which violation guides relaxation when the current sample batch contains no jointly satisfying candidate, without per-constraint importance weights.

We evaluate TierCEM in the context of trajectory optimization, where different constraint orderings lead to distinct behavioral tradeoffs.
In a controlled two-dimensional navigation problem with explicit dynamics, geometric conflicts prevent simultaneous satisfaction of all spatial constraints while also reaching the goal. Reversing the constraint ordering changes which spatial constraint is violated.
We then evaluate contact-rich manipulation in the Push-T environment (Chi et al., 2024), optimizing action sequences through a frozen latent-space world model and evaluating constraints with learned decoder heads that predict constraint violation.
World model-based experiments reproduce the priority-dependent relaxation observed in the controlled setting: changing the ordering changes which constraint is violated, even when future states and constraint satisfaction are evaluated using imperfect learned predictions.

title: Ex vivo breach detection using electrical conductivity during robotic pedicle drilling in the spine
authors: Jorge Andrés Pérez Velásquez,François Teyssere,Thibault Chandanson,Quentin Grimal,Brahim Tamadazte
abstract: Purpose: Pedicle screw placement is technically demanding in scoliosis treatment. High precision is required due to limited visibility, anatomical variability, and the risk of complications. Although robotic systems assist CT-based planning and execution, they still rely on ionizing intraoperative imaging and complex registration. This study proposes robotic pedicle drilling with real-time preventive breach detection using electrical bioimpedance sensing.
introduction:
Pedicle Screw Placement (PSP) is a surgical procedure used to treat various spinal pathologies, such as scoliosis, spinal trauma, or spinal instability. Drilling the pedicles for screw positioning is a challenging procedure. Failure can lead to injuries, such as major vessels (aorta, vena cava) or the spinal cord Esses et al. (1993). The literature reports a complication rate in the case of screw mispositioning of up to 18% Tang et al. (2014). Indeed, the main risk arises during the pedicle preparation phase, when the surgeon defines a drilling trajectory that is considered optimal and safe for the patient. The surgeon has no means of real-time, in-depth visualization of the vertebra and therefore relies primarily on skill and experience. For example, in scoliosis (Fig. 1 left), which is characterized by severe three-dimensional deformities of the spinal column, identifying the entry point for each pedicle screw is particularly challenging. This often leads to high rates of pedicle screw misplacement, and approximately 7% of these mispositioned screws may result in medial or lateral breaches (Fig. 1, right). Lateral breaches can damage vascular structures, causing significant bleeding and potentially life-threatening complications Lopera et al. (2010). When medial breaches occur into the spinal canal, they can expose the spinal cord to risk and lead to neurological consequences ranging from paraparesis to complete paralysis Mac-Thiong et al. (2013). The literature reports that most breaches are classified as ”A” or ”B” under the Gertzbein and Robbins classification Gertzbein and others (1990). In this well-established classification, the position of a transpedicular screw is graded from ”A” to ”E” based on the extent of pedicle cortex breach: grade ”A” corresponds to a fully intrapedicular position without cortical violation, grade ”B” to a breach of less than 2 mm, grade ”C” to a breach of 2–4 mm, grade ”D” to a breach of 4–6 mm, and grade ”E” to a breach greater than 6 mm or a screw located outside the pedicle.

To improve the accuracy of pedicle screw placement and prevent breaches, various techniques have been proposed in the literature. First, patient-specific 3D-printed guides generated from preoperative imaging have been introduced as templates to assist PSP procedures Sheha et al. (2019). Several studies also report the use of different non-visual exteroceptive or proprioceptive sensors, including vibroacoustic, accelerometric, torque, and force sensors Seibold et al. (2021); Massalimova et al. (2023); Saghbiny et al. (2024). However, most solutions rely on image-based navigation, using fluoroscopy or CT scans.

Furthermore, robotic assistance in spinal surgery was first introduced in 2004, marking a major advancement in the field, which primarily uses navigation systems to optimize pedicle screw placement Bozic et al. (2003). Most of the available robotic systems are integrated with stereotactic navigation systems Kia and Esmende (2021). The SpineAssist system, developed by Mazor Robotics, was the first robotic system for spinal surgery to receive FDA (Food and Drug Administration) approval. Over the years, significant advances have been achieved, with the latest generation, Mazor X®, incorporating a camera to assess the surgical environment and improve accuracy Ringel et al. (2012). Another widely used robotic system is ROSA Spine®, which operates according to similar shared-control principles Lefranc and Peltier (2016). The most recent system, ExcelsiusGPS®, integrates real-time intraoperative imaging and enables screw placement without the use of guidewires Zygourakis et al. (2018).

Although navigation and robotic systems have improved spinal surgery, they remain limited by usability, cost, and accuracy. Respiratory motion and small patient movements during pedicle preparation can introduce substantial registration errors Shuman et al. (2022). Moreover, these systems improve trajectory planning but do not fully prevent pedicle breaches. To address this limitation, we developed a robotic platform for pedicle screw placement that integrates a SpineGuard® bioelectrical conductivity sensor, hereafter referred to as the DSG sensor, which is already used clinically Bai et al. (2013); Yurube et al. (2022). A threaded drill bit with a pyramidal sensorised tip operating at 25 Hz was mounted on a custom motorized drilling system attached to Kurobot’s end effector.

A real-time algorithm uses adaptive conductivity thresholds and a dual-alert mechanism to stop drilling before a breach occurs. The system was evaluated ex vivo on fresh pig vertebrae through 51 drillings, achieving preventive detection in all trials. The mean error remained within [-1, +1.4] mm, and 100% of drillings were graded ”A” or ”B” according to the Gertzbein and Robbins classification.

title: Continual Learning for 6-DoF Grasp Synthesis via Experience and Demonstrations
authors: Giulio Schiavi,Andrei Cramariuc,Michael Pantic,Roland Siegwart
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026
abstract:
Most current grasp synthesis systems are trained offline and remain fixed during deployment. While this works well when deployment conditions resemble the training data, performance can degrade when robots encounter conditions they have not seen before, such as unfamiliar objects. In this work, we present a continual-learning framework for single-view 6-DoF grasp synthesis for a parallel-jaw gripper in cluttered scenes. Rather than finetuning a large parametric model, our method adapts through memory in a learned embedding space: grasp outcomes update future grasp scores, while optional user demonstrations are recalled and transferred to new scenes as additional candidate grasps. We evaluate our method in simulation and in extensive real-world experiments comprising over 1500 grasp trials. We show that our method matches the performance of existing 6-DoF grasping baselines even before adaptation, improves online on unseen objects from categories absent or underrepresented during training, and supports long-horizon continual learning with limited forgetting. In real-world experiments, our method reaches over 90% success rates on several challenging object categories after only 50 online grasp attempts.
Videos and code at https://giuschio.github.io/cl_grasping/.
introduction:
Current 6-DoF grasp synthesis systems can generate grasps in cluttered scenes with impressive reliability. Most do so by training parametric models on large offline datasets of synthetic or real-world grasp examples [6, 1, 10, 3, 29]. Once trained, however, these models are typically frozen during deployment, and can still fail when the robot encounters conditions that are poorly covered by the training distribution, such as unfamiliar object geometries that were absent or underrepresented during training. One promising direction is to let grasping systems continue learning on site from the feedback available to them, such as grasp outcomes and occasional user demonstrations.

In this work, we present a continual-learning framework for 6-DoF grasp synthesis. As in many prior works [10, 30], our system (Figure 1) has two main components: a proposal module that generates candidate grasps and a scoring module that ranks them for execution. Unlike standard learned grasping systems, however, both modules can change during deployment through memory. Instead of using a parametric grasp scorer that remains fixed after training, we use a memory-based scorer in a learned embedding space, so new grasp outcomes immediately influence future scores. We also augment heuristic grasp proposals with lightweight recall from user demonstrations, transferring previously shown grasps to geometrically similar regions in new scenes. Together, these mechanisms let the system combine offline experience, deployment trials, and demonstrations into a single adaptive system. In addition, because adaptation only requires adding entries to memory, each update is simple and practical to apply on site, without requiring gradient-based retraining.

We evaluate our method in simulation and on a real robot and compare it with common 6-DoF grasping baselines. Our method achieves strong offline performance, improves online through deployment experience on unfamiliar objects, and supports long-horizon continual learning with limited forgetting. In real-world experiments comprising over 1500 grasp trials, online adaptation improves performance across challenging object categories and reaches over 90% success on several of them.

title: Interaction-Stiffness-Guided Basis Allocation in Dynamic Movement Primitives for Efficient Skill Transfer
authors: Chan Xu,Silu Chen,Dehao Wang,Xiyu Chen,Dexin Jiang,Chi Zhang,Guilin Yang,Chenguang Yang,Zaojun Fang
abstract: Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) provide a compact and stable formulation for trajectory representation and generalization in robot skill learning. However, their predefined basis layout limits the allocation of approximation capacity according to stage-dependent precision requirements. To address this issue, this article proposes Stage-Criticality-Guided Dynamic Movement Primitives (SC-DMPs) with adaptive basis allocation for precision-critical skill learning. Operator-robot interaction stiffness and a trajectory-consistency cue derived from cross-demonstration task-space variability are integrated to construct a stage-criticality index. Guided by this index, basis centers are redistributed in normalized time through inverse cumulative criticality and mapped to the canonical phase domain, while their bandwidths are refined to adjust local approximation support. This enables denser and more flexible representation at high-criticality stages while retaining sparser allocation elsewhere. Experiments on handwriting trajectories and three real-robot tasks show that the inferred criticality is concentrated in geometrically demanding and task-constrained regions. Comparisons with DMPs, ProMPs, ProDMP, GP-MP, and KMP demonstrate improved trajectory reproduction, endpoint generalization, and task-critical accuracy while retaining a compact model and the stable structure of classical DMPs.
introduction:
Learning from Demonstration (LfD) has emerged as an effective paradigm for transferring dexterous human motion skills to robots, especially in settings where explicit programming is difficult or costly [1]. Representative applications include fine insertion, tight-clearance assembly, and other operations with stringent precision requirements [2]. In such tasks, the robot must not only reproduce the overall shape of the demonstrated trajectory, but also maintain high geometric accuracy at critical local stages, which are often less tolerant to error than other segments [3]. Accordingly, achieving global fidelity and local accuracy at task-critical stages is central to precision-oriented trajectory learning [4].

Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) are one of the most representative trajectory-encoding frameworks in LfD, owing to their compact dynamical formulation, stability guarantees, and convenient spatiotemporal modulation [5]. Classical DMPs represent demonstrated motions through stable dynamical systems, where nonlinear forcing terms encode task-specific trajectory profiles [6]. In particular, the forcing term is approximated by basis functions preset along the canonical phase variable, where the basis layout is associated with the resulting reproduction performance [7]. Although this design is generally effective, it provides limited stage-wise adaptability for precision-critical skill representation [8]. Trajectory adaptability and tracking accuracy can be improved by integrating DMPs with model predictive control, reinforcement learning, and adaptive or neural feedback [9, 10, 11]. However, such approaches may require additional environmental information or interaction, online computation, or specialized controller design, while local approximation errors introduced during trajectory encoding are not directly addressed [12].

By contrast, representation-level methods modify movement primitives to improve trajectory reproduction and generalization, primarily through probabilistic or kernel-based formulations and parameter refinement. The former represents demonstrated trajectories and their uncertainty through probability distributions or kernel mappings, as in ProMPs [13], ProDMP [14], GP-MP [15], and KMP [16]. However, local reproduction fidelity is typically regulated through covariance structures, kernel design, or hyperparameter settings, without explicitly allocating approximation support according to stage-dependent precision requirements. The latter refines movement-primitive parameterization by adjusting the number, locations, widths, or forms of basis functions, providing more explicit control over local approximation support [17, 18]. Among these refinements, basis-center redistribution relocates approximation support without increasing the basis number or altering the stable DMP dynamics, making it an efficient strategy for precision-critical skill learning [19]. Existing methods refine trajectory representations based on curvature, variance, recovered temporal structure, or mutual-information-based timestep weights [20, 21, 22]. These criteria characterize trajectory structure or informativeness but do not necessarily indicate task-imposed motion tolerances. For example, peg-in-hole insertion may follow a geometrically simple path yet require high positioning accuracy under tight clearances [23].

In precision-oriented physical interaction, increased stiffness may accompany stronger regulation of positional deviations, providing task information that is not evident from trajectory geometry alone [24, 25]. Robot-environment contact stiffness can reveal such constraints during sustained contact, but its force-displacement-based estimation may be unreliable in noncontact, weak-contact, or contact-transition stages [26, 27]. Operator-robot interaction stiffness can instead be estimated from muscle activation and upper-limb configuration without requiring robot-environment contact-force measurements, making it available across different stages of kinesthetic teaching [28, 29]. Existing stiffness-aware skill learning methods primarily incorporate stiffness or compliance into task execution through variable-impedance profiles, compliant dynamical systems, or programmed interaction behaviors [30, 31, 32]. Alternatively, operator-robot interaction stiffness can serve as a task-informed cue for trajectory representation. Although informative, it may not fully characterize task criticality on its own, since some dynamic or periodic manipulation tasks may instead depend on compliant behavior [33, 34]. Accordingly, operator-robot interaction stiffness and cross-demonstration trajectory consistency may offer complementary cues for characterizing stage-dependent reproduction requirements.

In this work, operator-robot interaction stiffness and a trajectory-consistency cue derived from cross-demonstration variability are integrated to construct a stage-criticality index. Based on this index, Stage-Criticality-Guided Dynamic Movement Primitives (SC-DMPs) redistribute basis centers and adapt their bandwidths to allocate approximation support according to stage-dependent reproduction requirements. The main contributions are as follows.

A physically motivated stage-criticality index is formulated by integrating operator-robot interaction stiffness and cross-demonstration task-space variability, providing an interpretable estimate of stage-wise reproduction-fidelity requirements.

A criticality-guided basis allocation strategy is developed by redistributing centers through inverse cumulative criticality and adapting bandwidths to refine local support in high-criticality stages.

Comprehensive experiments on handwriting trajectories and real-robot tasks compare SC-DMPs with DMPs, ProMPs, ProDMP, GP-MP, and KMP, demonstrating improved trajectory reproduction, generalization, and task-critical accuracy while retaining a compact model.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section II formulates a probabilistic model of multiple demonstrations. Section III develops the stage-criticality index and SC-DMPs method. Section IV validates the effectiveness of the proposed method. Finally, Section V concludes this article.

title: PROMO: Preference-conditioned Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Quadrupedal Robots
authors: Amr Mousa,Rifny Rachman,Neil Karavis,Michele Caprio,Richard Allmendinger
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics. Project website, code, and videos:this https URL
abstract:
Quadrupedal locomotion requires balancing conflicting objectives such as command tracking, stability, and energy efficiency, yet conventional reinforcement learning (RL) hard-codes these priorities into a fixed scalar reward at training time.
We present PROMO (Preference-Conditioned Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning), a semantic multi-objective framework that makes this trade-off an explicit runtime input to a single locomotion policy. PROMO conditions the policy on deployment-facing preferences while keeping embodiment-specific locomotion priors fixed, thereby separating operator intent from reward-shaping terms required for viable gait generation.
Compared with fixed-objective controllers, multi-objective baselines, and independently trained specialists, PROMO achieves objective specialization and robustness from a single deployable policy.
Across 100100 sampled preferences in simulation, 6767 behaviors are non-dominated under exact Pareto dominance, with a mean preference–objective correlation of 0.8430.843, demonstrating broad Pareto coverage and predictable preference response.
The same policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree Go2, where preference changes alone reduce specific energy by up to 30.4%30.4\%, position error by 38.7%38.7\%, and peak body-attitude deviation by 59.0%59.0\% relative to the balanced preference.
These results establish preference-conditioned multi-objective RL as a practical runtime interface for adaptive legged locomotion, extending its role beyond offline Pareto-set construction.
Open-source code and videos are available at https://amrmousa.com/promo/.
introduction:
Robotic locomotion via  rl (rl) has moved quadrupeds from controlled demonstrations toward agile and deployable systems [1, 2, 3]. Most learned controllers, however, optimize a scalar reward that fixes the trade-off among command tracking, stability, energy efficiency, and locomotion regularization. This is restrictive in long-horizon autonomy, where terrain, payload, mission urgency, operator intent, or hardware state can change which objective should dominate.

After training, a robot can receive new motion commands, but the objective trade-off governing how those commands are executed remains locked. Changing that trade-off usually requires a reward redesign, policy retraining, or controller switching. The deployment challenge is therefore to learn robust locomotion while making the underlying objective priorities selectable after training.

morl (morl) provides a principled basis for adapting trade-offs by representing distinct objectives through vector-valued rewards and optimizing their utility under a preference [4, 5, 6]. However, directly treating locomotion reward terms as independent objectives creates a fundamental mismatch with learned locomotion. Robotic rewards typically combine many shaping terms for posture, contact timing, smoothness, joint limits, and other requirements for viable motion [2, 3, 7]. Making each term an objective yields a high-dimensional Pareto space that becomes harder to optimize as dimensionality grows [8], while exposing low-level coefficients that do not express behavioral intent.

This objective-definition problem is central to deployable robotic morl: the optimized dimensions need not coincide with the components used to shape a robust controller. We therefore separate a compact semantic objective vector—tracking, stability, and efficiency—from fixed locomotion priors. This keeps embodiment-specific requirements internal to the controller and makes the preference vector a meaningful runtime interface rather than a reformulation of the full reward function.

Behavior-conditioned locomotion addresses flexibility through a different interface. Methods such as Walk These Ways [9] expose gait descriptors that specify how the robot should move through morphology, timing, or stance parameters. Preference-conditioned control instead specifies what the robot should prioritize, leaving the physical gait realization to the policy. This distinction matters for deployment: semantic preferences should retain their meaning across commands, disturbances, and operating conditions rather than become handcrafted gait-tuning variables.

These observations motivate  promo (promo), a preference-conditioned morl framework that turns a fixed reward trade-off into a runtime semantic behavior interface. A single policy is conditioned on preferences over three deployment-facing objectives—tracking, stability, and efficiency—while embodiment-specific locomotion priors remain fixed.

The resulting preference vector is both a deployment-time control input and an interpretable representation of behavioral intent. Rather than manipulating latent gait codes or implementation-level reward weights, the operator specifies why behavior should change—for example, by prioritizing stability over tracking—and the policy learns how to realize that trade-off.

We evaluate whether this interface is controllable in simulation and remains preference-responsive after zero-shot transfer to hardware. In simulation, promo remains competitive at the balanced operating point while providing tracking, stability, and efficiency specialization from a single policy, with lower failure rates than the evaluated preference-conditioned and specialist baselines. A dense 100-preference study shows that these anchor behaviors lie within a broader controllable interface. On a Unitree Go2, changing only the preference produces large, directionally consistent changes in tracking, stability, and energy efficiency across five trials per condition. To our knowledge, this is the first real demonstration of semantic preference-conditioned morl on a robotic platform, moving morl from offline Pareto optimization toward an operator-facing mechanism for adaptive robot behavior.

Our core contributions are:

A semantic locomotion interface.
We formulate runtime-adjustable quadruped control as preference-conditioned morl over tracking, stability, and efficiency, making the objective trade-off an explicit deployment-time input that represents operator intent.

Objective/prior factorization for controllable locomotion.
We address the mismatch between vector-valued morl objectives and dense robotic reward design by separating operator-facing semantic objectives from fixed embodiment-level locomotion priors. Ablations show that this factorization is critical for controllability and reliability: the fixed-prior formulation attains a 6%6\% fall rate under challenging evaluation conditions, whereas alternative designs increase it to as much as 21.8%21.8\% and degrade preference controllability.

Zero-shot semantic morl on a real quadruped.
We provide, to our knowledge, the first real-robot demonstration of semantic preference-conditioned morl for locomotion. A single policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree Go2 and modulates tracking, stability, and efficiency through preference alone. Relative to a balanced configuration, preference modulation reduces specific energy by up to 30.4%30.4\%, position error by up to 38.7%38.7\%, and peak body-attitude deviation by up to 59.0%59.0\%.

Open-source implementation and complete experimental suite.
We release the implementation of promo together with all evaluated baselines, experimental tasks, evaluation protocols, and ablation studies, enabling reproduction of the complete experimental pipeline and facilitating future benchmarking and extensions.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III formulates promo and describes its training and deployment. Sections IV and V evaluate the framework in simulation and on the Unitree Go2 robot, respectively. Section VI discusses the implications and limitations, and Section VII concludes the paper.

title: ColoACT: Multi-Cue Action Chunking for Smooth Autonomous Colon Navigation on a Self-Propelled Endoscopic Robot
authors: Jian Hu,Shujing He,Leixin Chang,Zongze Li,Ding Huang,Chaoyang Shi,Chengzhi Hu
abstract: Autonomous colonoscopic navigation can reduce operator burden and the risk of loop formation or tissue trauma, but remains challenging due to deformable anatomy, weak-texture and specular endoscopic visuals, and contact-rich viscoelastic interactions. Existing methods either rely on geometry-driven pipelines, which are efficient and interpretable yet brittle due to manually engineered features and switching logic, or adopt learning-based policies, whose inferred depth/geometry can become temporally inconsistent or overly smooth under weak texture and specular highlights while simulation-trained variants (e.g., deep reinforcement learning) may further suffer from a sim-to-real gap. We propose ColoACT, an autonomous navigation system that integrates an RGB-D-E based Action Chunking Transformer policy (ColoACT policy) for a compact self-propelled Bevel-Gear-Based Endoscopic Robot (BGER). The ColoACT policy augments RGB with estimated relative depth and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to enhance fold-ridge saliency and other high-frequency geometric cues, and enables smooth continuous control of the BGER by predicting overlapping action chunks and fusing them via temporal ensembling. In different ex-vivo porcine colons (approximately 60 cm), our system achieves success rates of 85.4% and 72.5% in straight and curved segments, respectively, and achieves 70% success in 90-degree turns and 60% in double-bend sequences, with feasibility further demonstrated in challenging triple-bend segments. The project page is available at: https://Adamhu1.github.io/ColoACT/.
introduction:
Endoscopic examination remains the gold standard for the prevention and early diagnosis of colorectal diseases[1]. While traditional colonoscopy is widely adopted, it still suffers from a steep learning curve, limited automation, and risks of loop formation or tissue trauma during navigation[2]. Robotic endoscopic systems are therefore being explored to improve navigational safety and consistency[3], and to reduce the cognitive and physical burden on physicians.

Autonomous colonoscopic navigation is challenging due to large anatomical variability with frequent bends and collapses[4], weak texture and specular highlights, and strongly nonlinear, time-varying interactions[5] between the endoscope and viscoelastic tissue[6]. These factors demand a closed-loop policy that is robust under imperfect perception and contact disturbances while producing smooth, stable motion. Existing robotic navigation solutions fall into geometry-driven pipelines[7, 8, 9] and learning-based approaches[10, 11, 12]. Geometry-driven methods are often efficient and interpretable, but their reliance on manually engineered features and switching logic can make the behavior brittle under challenging visual conditions and contact-rich interactions.
Learning-based strategies derive policies directly from data and can handle nonlinear dynamics. However, they remain limited by unreliable geometric cues under weak-texture/specular observations[13], where learned depth/geometry can be temporally inconsistent or overly smooth and obscure fine topographic structures[14], and by sim-to-real gaps in simulation-trained variants (e.g., reinforcement learning) due to difficulty of faithfully modeling viscoelastic, contact-rich colon interactions[15, 16].

To address the challenges of robustness under weak-texture conditions, smooth control consistency, and the sim-to-real gap, we propose ColoACT, a holistic navigation system that integrates an RGB-D-E input that combines appearance (RGB) and geometry (RGB with estimated relative depth and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map) based Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) policy for smooth, continuous closed-loop control and a compact self-propelled Bevel-Gear-Based Endoscopic Robot (BGER) designed to provide the mechanical and visual stability required by learning-based navigation. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first imitation-learning-based navigation policy for a self-propelled colonoscopic robot in ex-vivo tests. We validate the full system in ex-vivo porcine colons, achieving success rates of 85.4% in straight and 72.5% in curved segments (∼\sim60 cm). The system further succeeds in highly tortuous anatomies, successfully negotiating sharp 90-degree turns (70%) and double-bend paths (60%), and remains feasible even in extreme triple-bend scenarios. The contributions of this work are as follows:

We proposed an RGB-D-E ACT navigation policy (ColoACT Policy) that leverages multi-cue geometric representations to improve robustness in challenging colonic environments, while generating smooth and stable actions.

We proposed an RGB-D-E ACT navigation policy (ColoACT Policy) that leverages multi-cue geometric representations to improve robustness in challenging colonic environments, while generating smooth and stable actions.

We design a compact self-propelled BGER mechanism that ensures transmission stability and supports reliable visual feedback for autonomous control.

We demonstrate system-level validation of ColoACT on ex-vivo porcine colons, showing strong performance across straight, curved, and complex tortuous segments.

title: EIDA: Execution-Interface Dynamics Adaptation for Real-to-Sim-to-Real Robot Navigation
authors: Yiwei Qian,Shanze Wang,Qingyuan Hu,Xinming Zhang,Wei Zhang
abstract: Simulation-to-robot transfer can fail when velocity commands produce motion and feedback that differ from those modeled during policy training. We present execution-interface dynamics adaptation (EIDA), which fits these responses from target-platform execution data without reconstructing actuator dynamics. A model of body-frame pose increments updates simulator geometry, while a separate model predicts the velocity feedback observed by the policy; a short history of velocity feedback is included in the policy input. The fitted models are used within a lightweight GPU-parallel simulator. On the full Jackal and Go2 validation sets, the fitted models reduced position and yaw prediction errors relative to the simulator’s predefined motion model. Across 100 benchmark navigation environments evaluated in a separate physics-based simulator, EIDA achieved the highest success rate and navigation score among the compared learned policies, both with and without global guidance. Feedback ablations further supported the need to match policy-facing velocity estimates. On a physical Unitree Go2, EIDA reached the goal without collision in all 20 static-scene trials, compared with 4 of 20 for the baseline. These results show that execution-interface adaptation can improve navigation transfer without detailed actuator simulation.
introduction:
Efficient and reliable autonomous navigation is fundamental to the safe
operation of mobile robots in complex environments. Deep reinforcement
learning (DRL) can acquire behaviors for collision avoidance and goal reaching
through large-scale interaction [1, 2], while
GPU-parallel simulation substantially reduces navigation policy training
time [3]. However, strong performance in simulation does
not ensure effective transfer to a physical robot.

This transfer gap involves both perception and execution. Prior studies improve
robustness to visual appearance and sensing errors [4, 5], but action modeling and collision handling also affect how
well simulation predicts physical navigation performance [6].
Velocity commands pass through a platform-specific low-level controller, with
the resulting motion and feedback affected by actuator response, control
latency, and recent commands. Identical commands can therefore produce
different trajectories in simulation and physical execution, potentially
causing drift, turning overshoot, or collisions. At higher speeds, less time is
available for closed-loop correction, making small response errors more
consequential.

Robustness to dynamics mismatch can be improved by training across varied
simulation parameters and adapting their distribution with real
experience [7, 8]. Reproducing
detailed actuator and contact dynamics is another option, but increases
computational cost without ensuring better transfer. Truong et
al. [9] showed that simplified motion models fitted from
real execution can outperform slower, more detailed simulation in navigation
transfer. In local navigation, collision avoidance and goal progress depend on
pose evolution relative to the environment. This motivates modeling that
evolution together with the velocity feedback available to the policy.
Can navigation policies trained in a lightweight simulator transfer to a
physical robot without reconstructing detailed low-level actuator dynamics?

This paper addresses this question through execution-interface dynamics
adaptation (EIDA), as illustrated in Fig. 1. Using target-system execution data, EIDA fits body-frame pose
increments to update simulator geometry and a separate causal model to predict
the velocity feedback available to the policy. Recent velocity observations
help the policy account for history-dependent execution responses. At
deployment, physical motion and sensor feedback replace the learned simulation
interface, while the existing low-level controller is retained.
EIDA shows that this is possible when pose evolution and policy-facing velocity
feedback are fitted to target-system execution data and incorporated into a
lightweight simulator. Physical Unitree Go2 trials provide direct evidence of
transfer, while evaluation on 100 BARN environments [10]
assesses navigation transfer across simulators. The main contributions of this work are
summarized as follows:

An execution-interface dynamics adaptation framework that learns
body-frame pose increments from execution data collected on the target system
and uses them to update simulator geometry during navigation policy training.

A separated representation of motion evolution and velocity feedback
observable to the policy, together with recent observations that capture
temporally dependent execution responses.

Validation across wheeled and legged platforms, demonstrating that
adapting execution responses relevant to navigation improves navigation
transfer while preserving efficient parallel policy training.

1. An execution-interface dynamics adaptation framework that learns
body-frame pose increments from execution data collected on the target system
and uses them to update simulator geometry during navigation policy training.

2. A separated representation of motion evolution and velocity feedback
observable to the policy, together with recent observations that capture
temporally dependent execution responses.

3. Validation across wheeled and legged platforms, demonstrating that
adapting execution responses relevant to navigation improves navigation
transfer while preserving efficient parallel policy training.

title: AFD-CAMLs: Agile Force-Distribution-Aware Planning and Control for Cable-Suspended Aerial Multi-Lifting Systems
authors: Antreas Kourris,Sihao Sun
abstract:
Multiple UAVs can cooperatively transport heavy payloads while controlling
their position and orientation. Trajectory-based methods offer high agility
while satisfying system constraints, but can produce uneven force distributions
when the tension-to-wrench allocation is redundant or ill-conditioned,
particularly under geometric mismatch and low-level tracking errors. We propose
a hybrid planning-and-control framework to address this problem. A global
planner generates payload trajectories and cable-force references by exploring
the allocation null space under a prescribed internal-force setting. These
references augment the cost of a centralized local planner, promoting feasible
force distributions while generating trajectories for all UAVs. An admittance
filter then compares the planned forces with onboard cable-tension estimates
and adjusts the kinematic references to improve force tracking in degenerate or
near-degenerate configurations. Simulations and experiments involving four to
ten UAVs demonstrate more balanced tension distributions during both hovering
and demanding agile maneuvers, without compromising agility or payload-tracking
performance.
introduction:
Teams of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can cooperatively transport payloads
beyond the capacity of a single vehicle
[1, 2].
Adding UAVs increases lifting capacity but can make the cable-force distribution
non-unique. Accurate payload-pose tracking therefore does not ensure that the
load is shared safely and evenly among the vehicles. This distinction is
especially important for cable-suspended systems: the net force and moment on
the payload determine its motion, whereas internal-force components can change
the individual cable tensions without changing that net wrench. Excessive
tension can saturate or destabilize a vehicle, while insufficient tension can
cause cable slackness and invalidate the assumed system dynamics.

Existing methods can broadly be divided into position- and force-based
approaches. Quasi-static position-based methods determine UAV configurations
from payload poses, cable geometry, and static equilibrium
[1, 3]. These
methods are effective for slow motion but neglect dynamic coupling and do not
guarantee feasible cable tensions. Force-based methods compute the required
payload wrench from a dynamic model and allocate it among the cables
[4, 5, 6], allowing
secondary objectives such as tension or internal-force regulation
[7]. Most retain a cascaded wrench-allocation and
inner-loop structure whose time-scale separation limits agile operation. Their
force commands also depend on nominal payload and cable parameters. The
resulting distribution is therefore sensitive to uncertainty in payload mass
and inertia, attachment locations, and cable lengths
[5, 8].

Recent work introduced a trajectory-based approach that replaces the
conventional cascaded force controller with a centralized whole-body nonlinear
model predictive control (NMPC) planner and onboard trajectory-tracking
controllers [9, 8]. The planner predicts the coupled
load-cable dynamics and generates dynamically feasible trajectories for all
UAVs while enforcing thrust, cable-tautness, collision-avoidance, and
obstacle-avoidance constraints. Agility is improved because the onboard
controllers track complete kinematic references rather than realizing
instantaneous force commands through separate control layers. This formulation
also allows the planner to anticipate coupled payload and cable motion over a
finite horizon instead of allocating a wrench independently at each instant.

For four or more UAVs, however, multiple cable-force distributions can produce
the same payload wrench. The planner generates kinematic trajectories from a
nominal geometric model, and the low-level controllers do not directly enforce
the corresponding tensions. Attachment-point and cable-length errors, combined
with trajectory-tracking errors, can therefore shift the physical system toward
a different force equilibrium. The payload may still track accurately while
some UAVs become overloaded and other cables approach slackness. Improving
payload-pose tracking alone cannot correct this internal-force component because
it does not affect the resultant payload wrench. The problem becomes most
pronounced when the tension-to-wrench allocation matrix is degenerate or nearly
degenerate, because small geometric or tracking errors can then produce large
changes in the individual tensions. A practical solution must therefore select
a feasible distribution during planning and regulate its realization without
sacrificing the agility of the trajectory-based architecture.

This work extends the trajectory-based framework [8] with
explicit planning and feedback regulation of the cable-force distribution. An
internal-force-aware global planner explores the null space of the payload
wrench-allocation matrix to generate feasible cable-force and direction
references. These references are incorporated into the centralized NMPC cost so
that the locally planned trajectories account for the desired force
distribution. Because the cable forces are still realized indirectly through
vehicle motion, an admittance filter compares each planned tension with an
onboard estimate and converts the error into position, velocity, and
acceleration corrections. The resulting hybrid motion–force architecture
combines predictive whole-body planning with local force feedback.

The three main contributions are:

an internal-force-aware global planner that preserves the required
payload wrench while generating tension-feasible cable-force and direction
references through null-space optimization;

a force-reference-aware NMPC formulation and an admittance filter that
uses onboard tension estimates to regulate the realized force distribution
through local kinematic corrections; and

simulation studies with four to ten UAVs and real-world experiments with four UAVs (Figure 1) that
demonstrate improved force distribution under geometric and inertial-model
mismatch while preserving agile payload tracking.

title: Recova: Agent-Guided Failure Recovery for Autonomous Robotic Manipulation
authors: Isabella Liu,An-Chieh Cheng,Johan Bjorck,Zhiding Yu,Hongxu Yin,Jan Kautz,Linxi Fan,Yuke Zhu,Sifei Liu
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Manipulation failures can leave scenes in states from which a task policy
cannot recover. Learning corrective behaviors requires scalable failure
exploration and physical grounding. We present Recova, an agent-guided
framework that jointly develops task execution and recovery in a reconstructed
digital twin, then verifies and refines both through real-world experience.
In the twin, the agent diagnoses failures, tests corrective programs, and
collects successful task and recovery rollouts for separate policies. During
deployment, it monitors progress, invokes a learned or programmatic recovery,
verifies scene restoration, and resumes execution. When no suitable recovery
is available, a human demonstration resolves the failure and enters the
learning loop, allowing the system to expand its recovery capabilities.
Physical rollouts and human demonstrations are routed to the corresponding
policy for DAgger training. Across six LIBERO-Pro settings and four
MolmoSpaces categories, Recova achieves 78.8% and 64.9% mean success,
compared with 71.7% and 38.0% for the strongest baselines. With parallel
collection across four real-robot workstations, DAgger fine-tuning raises mean
success from 23.8% to 77.5%, and recovery skills further raise it to
87.5%. Over four collection rounds on one task, observed human intervention falls
from 87.5% to 0%. Together, these results show how agent-guided recovery
turns failures into reusable capabilities, improving robustness while
progressively reducing human intervention.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse
manipulation tasks from language instructions
(6; 26; 48), from folding laundry
and assembling boxes to cleaning unfamiliar homes
(4; 3). However, even a small mistake can halt an
otherwise capable policy. A tipped cup must be set upright before pouring can
continue; a pencil caught across a box rim must be moved before the lid can
close. In both cases, the robot must restore a workable scene before resuming
the task.

Most VLA training data, however, contain successful trajectories from
standard initial states and provide little guidance for restoring a failed
scene. Failures create a long tail of unusual configurations, and correcting
them may require undoing a previous action, repositioning an object, or
temporarily moving away from the nominal task goal. Consequently, policies
may struggle when objects appear in unfamiliar arrangements
(70) or when asked to continue after a failed attempt
(39). Simply retrying the task policy often leaves the
underlying obstruction unresolved. Robots therefore need a complementary
recovery capability that can expand as new failure modes arise.

Learning such recovery behaviors directly on hardware is costly, as exploring
failures requires frequent resets and risks damaging objects
(58; 29). Reconstructed digital twins provide a
safer and more scalable setting for reproducing failures and testing
corrections (58), while physical experience remains
essential for verifying and refining them under real contacts and
observations. Effective recovery therefore requires a loop that discovers
behaviors in simulation, validates them on the robot, and feeds physical
experience back into learning.

Language-model agents are natural candidates to coordinate this loop. Recent
models combine multimodal understanding with the ability to use tools,
execute code, and revise solutions from feedback
(2; 51). Prior robotics systems show
that agents can interpret failures and develop reusable programs
(40; 31; 41). The central challenge is to
connect these abilities into a complete recovery process: diagnose a failure,
select or develop a correction, verify that it worked, retain successful
solutions, and use the resulting data to improve the appropriate policy. The
agent must also decide whether new experience should become a reusable
program, a task-policy demonstration, or a recovery-policy demonstration.
When no suitable recovery is available, human demonstrations enter the loop
to resolve the failure and expand future recovery capabilities
(35).

We present Recova (Fig. 1), an agent-guided framework that
develops task execution and scene recovery in a reconstructed digital twin,
then continually improves both through real-world experience. In the twin,
the agent explores task execution, diagnoses failures, and develops corrective
behaviors. Successful task and recovery rollouts initialize separate task and
recovery policies, while programs that compose perception and motion
primitives capture reusable recovery strategies. Keeping these data pathways
separate allows the task and recovery policies to specialize in their
distinct roles.

During real-world deployment, the agent monitors task progress, invokes an
applicable learned or programmatic recovery, verifies that the scene is
workable again, and resumes execution. When no suitable recovery succeeds, it
requests human assistance. Successful task rollouts and human task
demonstrations improve the task policy, while human recovery demonstrations
improve the recovery policy. A parallel collection harness runs this loop
across four robot workstations, allowing task and recovery experience to
accumulate concurrently. Newly encountered failure modes also guide the
development of additional skills. Human intervention therefore resolves the
current failure while helping the robot recover more autonomously in the
future.

Our contributions are:

An agent-guided real-to-sim-to-real framework for jointly developing
task execution and failure recovery. It uses a reconstructed digital twin
to safely discover corrective behaviors, then verifies and refines them
through physical robot experience.

A parallel deployment-and-learning loop that coordinates task and
recovery policies, reusable recovery programs, outcome verification, and
human demonstrations. Across four concurrently operating robot
workstations, collected experience improves mean task success by 53.7
percentage points to 77.5%. On one task, the observed human-intervention
rate falls from 87.5% in the first collection round to 0% in the fourth.

A comprehensive evaluation on two simulation benchmarks and four
real-robot tasks. Recova exceeds the strongest baseline in our
comparison by 7.1 percentage points on LIBERO-Pro and 26.9 points on
MolmoSpaces. Recovery skills provide a further 10-point gain on the
real-robot tasks, reaching 87.5% mean success.

1. An agent-guided real-to-sim-to-real framework for jointly developing
task execution and failure recovery. It uses a reconstructed digital twin
to safely discover corrective behaviors, then verifies and refines them
through physical robot experience.

2. A parallel deployment-and-learning loop that coordinates task and
recovery policies, reusable recovery programs, outcome verification, and
human demonstrations. Across four concurrently operating robot
workstations, collected experience improves mean task success by 53.7
percentage points to 77.5%. On one task, the observed human-intervention
rate falls from 87.5% in the first collection round to 0% in the fourth.

3. A comprehensive evaluation on two simulation benchmarks and four
real-robot tasks. Recova exceeds the strongest baseline in our
comparison by 7.1 percentage points on LIBERO-Pro and 26.9 points on
MolmoSpaces. Recovery skills provide a further 10-point gain on the
real-robot tasks, reaching 87.5% mean success.
