title: Experience-Based Feasibility-Aware Generative Adversarial Imitation from Observation under Embodiment Mismatch
authors: Yoshiki Takebayashi,Giovanni Perantoni,Hikaru Sasaki,Matteo Saveriano,Takamitsu Matsubara
abstract:
With the increasing use of robot-free demonstration interfaces that provide state trajectories without action labels, imitation from observation has become a promising approach for learning robot behaviors from human demonstrations. However, due to differences in embodiment and dynamics between humans and robots, demonstrated human motions may not be feasible for the robot, potentially degrading policy performance. In this study, we propose Experience-Based Feasibility-Aware Generative Adversarial Imitation from Observation (EF-GAIfO), which estimates the feasibility of state-only demonstrations from the robot’s own experience rather than relying on explicit dynamics models or large prior exploration datasets. A key feature of EF-GAIfO is that the notion of feasibility evolves with policy learning: as the policy improves and the robot experiences a broader range of state transitions, the feasible region is progressively expanded, allowing additional demonstrations to be incorporated into learning.
This enables feasibility-aware imitation that adapts to the current stage of policy learning, rather than relying on a pre-designed feasibility criterion.
We validate the effectiveness of EF-GAIfO on a locomotion task in simulation and on a real quadruped robot performing a object-reaching-and-grasping task.
introduction:
In recent years, imitation learning approaches using human demonstrations collected through robot-free demonstration interfaces have attracted increasing attention.
Several approaches have been proposed, ranging from purely video-based ones [1] to those based on external infrastructures [2, 3], and those based on self-contained onboard tracking [4, 5].
Such interfaces allow users to provide demonstrations through their own hand movements without directly teleoperating a robot.
However, demonstrations collected through such interfaces typically consist of state trajectories without corresponding robot action labels.
Imitation from Observation (IfO) [6, 7], which learns policies from state-only demonstrations, is therefore a suitable framework for utilizing such data.

However, due to an embodiment mismatch between humans and robots, demonstrated state transitions collected via robot-free demonstration interfaces are not necessarily feasible for the robot.
Such demonstrations may contain state transitions that cannot be reproduced under the robot’s embodiment.
If these demonstrations are directly used for IfO, the learned policy may be influenced by robot-infeasible motions.
Consequently, the learned policy may be encouraged to reproduce robot-infeasible motions, potentially resulting in falls or degraded task performance.

To reduce the influence of infeasible demonstrations,
model-based approaches evaluate whether demonstrated motions are feasible for the robot using a robot dynamics model [8, 9].
These methods predict the feasibility of demonstrated motions using known or learned robot dynamics models.
However, whole-body dynamics are strongly coupled, and contact interactions and balance constraints must also be considered.
Therefore, constructing an accurate dynamics model is not straightforward.

These limitations motivate a different approach to feasibility estimation: rather than explicitly modeling, what the robot can do, we infer feasibility from what it has actually experienced (Fig. 1).
During policy learning, the robot continuously generates state transitions that are physically realizable under its embodiment, providing direct evidence of feasible motion.
We therefore use this experience distribution as an embodiment-specific reference: demonstration transitions well supported by the robot’s experience are likely to be feasible, without requiring an explicit dynamics model.

In this study, we propose Experience-based Feasibility-aware Generative Adversarial Imitation from Observation (EF-GAIfO).
EF-GAIfO estimates the feasibility of state-only demonstration transitions using experience data collected during GAIfO-based policy learning and reduces the influence of demonstrations with low estimated feasibility.
For feasibility estimation, we train a state-transition reconstruction model using the robot’s experience data and evaluate demonstration transitions based on their reconstruction error.
The estimated feasibility is incorporated into the discriminator objective as a weight, allowing the policy to preferentially imitate demonstration transitions that are supported by the robot’s experience.
We evaluate the proposed method through experiments in a point-mass environment and a quadruped robot environment.

title: Extreme Length Generalization in a Compact Recurrent Architecture for One-Shot Exploration
authors: Izen Thornton,Aaron Shey,William Su
abstract:
Autonomous robots on one-shot missions run over horizons far longer than the
trajectories seen during training, under a fixed onboard compute budget. We
present FRANK, a 507K-parameter recurrent
architecture that combines tau-gated recurrent modules, content-addressable
memory, and a feedforward reflex pathway. We evaluate it against recurrent,
state-space, and reduced modular baselines at matched parameter count on four
algorithmic sequence tasks, trained at length 5–20 and evaluated out to two
million tokens. At 100,000×100{,}000\times the maximum training length, 6 of 10
FRANK seeds retain exactly 100.0% accuracy, while none of the 50 baseline
configurations does, five architectures at ten seeds each with none left
incomplete (Fisher exact, two-sided p=4.2×10−6p=4.2\times 10^{-6}). Targeted
lesions across the four tasks yield four distinct component-reliance profiles,
consistent with task-dependent allocation across the recurrent, memory, and
reflex pathways. Separately, a FRANK policy trained in simulation
drives a physical ground vehicle to commanded waypoints through obstacles
without teleoperation.
introduction:
Deep ocean and deep space exploration share a constraint terrestrial robotics
rarely faces: the system has to work the first time, far past the conditions
anyone rehearsed. A controller reliable for the length of a test campaign that
quietly degrades beyond it is the failure a one-shot mission cannot detect in
time.

This is a length generalization problem, and the standard tools fail it in
different ways. Transformers with learned absolute positional embeddings cannot
represent positions past their training range, and relative schemes built for
extrapolation do not rescue the task we study: an ALiBi [7] probe
collapses to chance by 100×\times. Attention’s O⁡(L2)O(L^{2}) cost is a harder
limit: at two million tokens the score matrix alone would hold roughly
4×10124\times 10^{12} entries. Recurrent models run at any length but drift:
gated recurrent unit (GRU) [9] baselines match our model at 10×\times
and land at 10–30% at 100,000×\times; Mamba [8], a selective
state-space model, is at chance by 100×\times on every seed.

Prior work reports early results for FRANK [1] and a
single-seed lesion analysis [2]; the ten-seed re-run with
swept learning rates, the statistical testing, and the hardware deployment
(Fig. 1) are new.

title: MASkillBlender: Decentralized Whole-Body Coordination for Multi-Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Skill Blending
authors: Yifan Hu,Luhang Hong,Mingkang Long,Danning Wang,Chengfeng Jia,Rong Su,Junjie Fu,Guanghui Wen
abstract: Coordinated multi-humanoid loco-manipulation is promising yet challenging due to high-dimensional whole-body control, decentralized decision making, and scalability. While recent reinforcement learning methods have improved single-humanoid whole-body control, extending them to the multi-humanoid setting remains nontrivial and often requires substantial reward engineering or task-specific design. We propose MASkillBlender, a general multi-agent reinforcement learning framework to achieve decentralized multi-humanoid whole-body coordination. By learning a shared decentralized high-level policy over reusable pre-trained single-humanoid skills, MASkillBlender enables coordinated behaviors using only task-level rewards, without requiring task-specific motion references. To improve learning efficiency, we further introduce a permutation-based data augmentation strategy for homogeneous multi-humanoid systems, and theoretically show that the permuted samples preserve the policy-gradient direction of the original samples under the homogeneous Markov game formulation. We evaluate MASkillBlender on multiple multi-humanoid coordination tasks across two humanoid embodiments. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently achieves strong task performance and enables coordinated behaviors across different tasks and humanoid embodiments.
introduction:
Humanoid robots have substantial potential to replace or assist humans in completing daily tasks across diverse environments due to their human-like morphology [15]. With advancements in reinforcement learning (RL) and robot hardware, the loco-manipulation capabilities of humanoids have been significantly enhanced [17]. Nevertheless, many real-world tasks require multiple humanoids to coordinate their actions [50]. Compared with single-humanoid control, multi-humanoid settings introduce additional challenges due to complex inter-agent dependencies. Developing general learning methods for coordinated multi-humanoid control therefore represents an important step toward scalable and capable humanoid teams.

Recent studies have demonstrated increasingly sophisticated multi-humanoid whole-body interactions, showing the potential of learning-based approaches for coordinated humanoid control [10]. However, existing methods typically rely on human motion references to guide policy learning through motion imitation or tracking objectives. While such motion priors provide effective guidance for acquiring natural whole-body behaviors, they also introduce additional data and supervision requirements, and the resulting motion-based objectives may compete with task rewards during optimization, potentially constraining the policy from discovering coordination strategies that are most effective for the task [34]. Beyond the reliance on motion supervision, incorporating observations of other humanoids into each agent’s policy has been widely adopted to facilitate coordination. While such inter-agent information can improve learning and coordination performance, it may hinder scalability to larger teams and complicate robust real-world deployment.

For single-humanoid loco-manipulation, skill-based learning has emerged as an effective paradigm that does not rely on task-specific motion references [38, 25]. By blending pre-trained primitive skills into the control policy, humanoids can reuse existing motor capabilities and reduce the burden of low-level control learning during downstream task training. However, extending this paradigm to multi-humanoid control is not straightforward, since skills pre-trained for individual humanoids do not encode the inter-agent coordination required by downstream tasks. Learning how to compose these skills across agents under coupled task dynamics therefore remains challenging.

In this work, we propose MASkillBlender, a general skill-based multi-agent RL (MARL) framework for decentralized coordination in homogeneous multi-humanoid systems. Under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), a shared decentralized high-level policy learns to coordinate the composition of reusable pre-trained primitive skills across humanoids using local observations. The primitive skills remain fixed during downstream training, allowing the policy to focus on high-level skill composition and inter-agent coordination using only task-level rewards. To improve learning efficiency, we introduce a permutation-based data augmentation strategy that exploits the permutation symmetry of homogeneous multi-humanoid systems. To evaluate the proposed framework, we build three representative multi-humanoid coordination tasks spanning cooperative object manipulation and coordinated locomotion across two distinct humanoid embodiments, using only task-level rewards and limited local observations. To summarize, the main contributions of this work are as follows:

We propose MASkillBlender, a general skill-based MARL framework that learns decentralized multi-humanoid coordination over reusable pre-trained single-humanoid skills using only task-level rewards, without requiring task-specific motion references.

We propose MASkillBlender, a general skill-based MARL framework that learns decentralized multi-humanoid coordination over reusable pre-trained single-humanoid skills using only task-level rewards, without requiring task-specific motion references.

We incorporate a permutation-based data augmentation strategy into MASkillBlender and theoretically show that the augmented samples preserve the policy-gradient direction of the original samples.

We evaluate the proposed MARL framework on diverse multi-humanoid coordination tasks across different embodiments, and extensive simulation results show that the learned policies produce versatile coordinated behaviors and effectively handle all tasks in a fully decentralized manner.

1. We propose MASkillBlender, a general skill-based MARL framework that learns decentralized multi-humanoid coordination over reusable pre-trained single-humanoid skills using only task-level rewards, without requiring task-specific motion references.

2. We incorporate a permutation-based data augmentation strategy into MASkillBlender and theoretically show that the augmented samples preserve the policy-gradient direction of the original samples.

3. We evaluate the proposed MARL framework on diverse multi-humanoid coordination tasks across different embodiments, and extensive simulation results show that the learned policies produce versatile coordinated behaviors and effectively handle all tasks in a fully decentralized manner.

title: OrbitTAMP: Grounding Language Models for Task and Motion Planning in Spacecraft Rendezvous
authors: Yuji Takubo,Daniele Gammelli,Marco Pavone,Simone D'Amico
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract:
Spacecraft rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) are currently planned through an expertise-intensive process in which engineers translate high-level operational intent into safe, dynamically feasible trajectories, creating a bottleneck to scalable operations.
Large language model (LLM)-based agents could offer an intuitive interface for this process, although their outputs are not inherently grounded in orbital dynamics, operational constraints, or the structure of admissible spacecraft maneuvers.
To exploit their semantic reasoning while ensuring the generated plan’s physical validity, this paper presents a hierarchical framework for spacecraft task-and-motion planning (TAMP) that grounds LLM reasoning in a graph of reusable behaviors and domain-specific planning modules.
Within this framework, a pretrained LLM maps a natural-language command to a partial mission specification. The associated planners then resolve unspecified decisions within the admissible operational space.
Finally, trajectory optimization converts the completed mission specification into a dynamically feasible trajectory.
Numerical experiments demonstrate that this architecture substantially improves intent recovery over direct LLM generation, achieving 98% exact recovery of partial mission specifications across all evaluated splits when backed by frontier LLMs.
Additional test-time-compute experiments show that, for a compact 9B model, verifier-guided revision increases exact recovery from 75% to 88%, while broader behavior-plan search independently improves selection among admissible trajectory realizations.
Overall, these results establish a scalable and auditable foundation for language-driven agentic planning of spacecraft RPO.
introduction:
The proliferation of distributed space systems, such as swarms and constellations, is increasing the need for scalable spacecraft operations.
Rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO), in particular, require complex maneuver sequences for inspection, repair, refueling, and other servicing tasks.
Traditionally, teams of operators and mission designers translate high-level mission intent or concepts of operations (CONOPS) into explicit trajectory specifications using their knowledge of astrodynamics, mission constraints, and available guidance modes.
This dependence on specialized expertise limits the scalability of future spacecraft operations.

Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to establish natural language as an intuitive and broadly accessible interface between high-level mission intent and executable spacecraft trajectories.
Specifically, recent advances in agentic LLM frameworks have demonstrated that foundation models (FMs) can interpret high-level instructions, decompose objectives into multistep plans, invoke external tools, and coordinate reasoning with action across interactive decision-making, autonomous scientific experimentation, and embodied operations [1, 2, 3].
For spacecraft RPO, however, semantic interpretation alone is insufficient. Language-model outputs must be grounded in spacecraft-specific behavior structures, operational constraints, and orbital dynamics before they can support safe execution. The central challenge is therefore not merely to translate language into a quantitative configuration, but to embed LLM reasoning within a planning architecture that converts incomplete intent into admissible and physically realizable spacecraft motion.

Consider the command:
“approach the target slowly from the −V-V-bar, circumnavigate it for two orbits, and then depart to a 50​m50\,\mathrm{m} along-track separation.”
To a human operator, this command conveys a clear maneuver intent through an ordered composition of familiar spacecraft behaviors: approach, circumnavigate, and depart.
Such reusable behaviors provide abstractions for organizing complex motion, similar in function to skills [3] or meta-actions [4] in broader robotic systems.
As a trajectory-planning specification, however, the command remains incomplete.
It dictates several explicit requirements, including the two-orbit circumnavigation and final separation, while leaving other decisions such as phase durations, intermediate waypoints, and trajectory constraints unspecified.
This distinction is central to spacecraft trajectory planning: conventional task and trajectory planners typically operate on formally defined actions, objectives, and constraints, whereas natural-language mission commands generally specify only a subset of this information, and the unstated remainder is where mission-design expertise must be applied.
Grounding such a command therefore requires identifying the stated intent, resolving unspecified decisions within the admissible spacecraft operational space, and constructing a dynamically feasible and safe trajectory.

To address this problem, this paper introduces a hierarchical framework for grounding LLM reasoning for spacecraft task-and-motion planning (TAMP), illustrated in Fig. 1.
Extending the preliminary concepts of structural decomposition for spacecraft behavior planning [5, 6, 7], the framework organizes the planning process into three stages: semantic grounding, completion of unspecified mission decisions, and physical trajectory verification.
A pretrained LLM first maps the natural-language command to a partial mission specification that preserves the operator’s stated intent while explicitly representing unspecified information.
A graph of reusable spacecraft behaviors, together with domain-specific planning modules, then completes the behavior sequence, timing, and waypoint decisions within the admissible operational space.
Finally, trajectory optimization instantiates the resulting candidates as state-control trajectories and ensures their dynamical feasibility and safety.
This hierarchical architecture grounds LLM reasoning at each stage while enabling multistage planning, computational tool use, and intermediate verification.

The central contribution of this paper is a hierarchical planning formulation in which operator underspecification is preserved and systematically completed, realized as an agentic architecture that scaffolds pretrained, off-the-shelf LLMs with structured, spacecraft-specific planning and verification modules.
Because every stage completes the same partial specification, stated intent is preserved by construction rather than by prompt compliance and remains checkable throughout, while unstated decisions are resolved by the behavior graph and planning modules under orbital dynamics and safety constraints rather than left to the LLM.
This design is motivated by both the scarcity of domain-specific training data for space applications [8] and the need for transparent, verifiable, and explicitly constrained decision-making in safety-critical spacecraft operations.
The resulting architecture provides an auditable human–spacecraft interface and supports scalable language-driven planning for future distributed space systems.
Specifically, the contributions of this work are as follows:

A spacecraft RPO planning representation comprising a graph of reusable behaviors and a structured mission configuration that preserves partial operator specifications and supports hierarchical completion of behavior, timing, and waypoint decisions.

An LLM-backed TAMP formulation that uses these representations to decouple intent parsing from trajectory realization, grounding semantic decisions in the admissible behavior structure and resolving unstated decisions within operational constraints and spacecraft dynamics.

A stage-wise and end-to-end evaluation over 300 procedurally generated commands and multiple LLM backends and a deterministic parsing baseline that quantifies the effects of the grounding scaffold, model capability, and targeted test-time computation through verifier-guided revision and behavior-plan search.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
Sec. II compares the proposed framework with spacecraft planning, language grounding, and robotic TAMP.
Sec. III defines the common mission representation, behavior graph, and systematic completion process.
Sec. IV describes the on-orbit inspection case study and its specific implementations.
Sec. V reports the module-level and end-to-end evaluation results.
Finally, Sec. VI concludes the paper and discusses future work.

1. A spacecraft RPO planning representation comprising a graph of reusable behaviors and a structured mission configuration that preserves partial operator specifications and supports hierarchical completion of behavior, timing, and waypoint decisions.

2. An LLM-backed TAMP formulation that uses these representations to decouple intent parsing from trajectory realization, grounding semantic decisions in the admissible behavior structure and resolving unstated decisions within operational constraints and spacecraft dynamics.

3. A stage-wise and end-to-end evaluation over 300 procedurally generated commands and multiple LLM backends and a deterministic parsing baseline that quantifies the effects of the grounding scaffold, model capability, and targeted test-time computation through verifier-guided revision and behavior-plan search.

title: WBAG: A Whole-Body and Attached-Geometry Safety Framework for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation
authors: Samuel Zhen,Siwon Jo,Yanze Zhang,Wenhao Luo
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated impressive capabilities in generalizable robotic manipulation, but their deployment in the real world remains challenging due to potential collisions involving different parts of the robot, manipulated objects, and the surrounding environment. Existing inference-time VLA safety frameworks typically rely on simplified end-effector-centered representations that do not explicitly model the full articulated robot and attached-object geometry. In this paper, we present WBAG, a safety framework that models the robot’s whole-body and grasp-dependent attached geometry. WBAG constructs a grasp-conditioned safe set that adapts the protected geometry as objects are grasped, then converts this evolving geometry into differentiable CBF constraints that minimally modify the VLA’s native six-dimensional operational-space action for collision avoidance across robot, scene, and attached geometry. On the SafeLIBERO benchmark, a variant of LIBERO augmented with obstacles for safety evaluation, WBAG achieves the best overall safety and safe task success among the evaluated methods under a scene-level safety evaluator that monitors all eligible non-task objects, reaching 97.38% aggregate Scene Safety and 59.38% Safe Success.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language
instructions directly to robot actions across diverse manipulation tasks
[1], but their task-level generalization does not provide an explicit
geometric safety model to consistently safeguard robot motions. In cluttered environments, a VLA action may move the
end effector toward the target while causing an upstream link, wrist, gripper,
or manipulated object to collide. The relevant collision geometry spans the
articulated robot and changes when the robot grasps an object. Recent benchmark
evaluations further show that task completion alone can obscure physical safety
violations during manipulation [2, 3].

Control-theoretic safety methods, particularly control barrier functions (CBFs),
provide a principled mechanism for enforcing collision avoidance during robotic
control [4]. CBFs constrain control inputs to maintain forward invariance of a prescribed
safe set, but their effectiveness depends on how that set is represented. For
geometric collision avoidance, the safety function must capture separation
between the protected robot geometry and surrounding obstacles. The geometric
representation therefore determines which collision modes can be enforced.

Recent work on safety-critical control with VLA-based policies [5, 6, 7, 8, 9] spans both training-time and inference-time interventions.
SafeVLA [5] incorporates safety constraints during policy optimization through
constrained reinforcement learning. At inference time, AEGIS [6]
combines perception-derived geometric information with CBF constraints to filter
a pretrained VLA, while KNOWS [7] combines VLA-based target
identification with online obstacle tracking. Other methods enforce safety directly within flow-matching action generation.
Recent work in [8] apply predictive
trajectory-level barrier constraints through minimum-norm corrections during
iterative denoising, while [9] modify the
flow-matching dynamics using an aggregate CBF over the generated action chunk.
However, existing
inference-time safety frameworks
typically enforce collision avoidance using simplified end-effector-centered
geometry [6, 7, 8]. Such end-effector-centered representations do
not explicitly model the full articulated robot or the rigid geometry of an
attached object: the end effector may remain
separated while an upstream link, wrist, or attached geometry collides with an
obstacle.

Geometric methods such as Bernstein-polynomial signed distance fields (BP-SDFs) [10] provide smooth, differentiable representations of object geometry, enabling efficient distance queries and gradients that are well suited for optimization-based control. For articulated robots, BP-SDFs can represent individual links, whose poses are determined by forward kinematics as a function of robot configuration. Recent work [11] employs BP-SDFs to construct geometry-aware CBFs from the minimum distance between robot and obstacle geometries and derive corresponding safety constraints on the robot control input. Applying such geometric safety constraints to VLA manipulation requires connecting perception, manipulation state, and the policy’s native action interface. In our setting, scene and target geometry are reconstructed from RGB-D observations rather than assumed known, while the protected geometry changes when the target becomes rigidly attached after grasping. At the same time, the resulting link- and object-level clearances are functions of robot configuration, whereas the frozen VLA produces six-dimensional operational-space actions. These factors must therefore be coupled so that perception-derived, grasp-conditioned geometric constraints can be enforced directly on the VLA action without retraining the VLA or modifying the operational-space controller.

In this paper, we introduce WBAG, a whole-body and attached-geometry safety framework for pretrained VLA policies. WBAG reconstructs scene and target geometry from RGB-D observations and constructs a grasp-conditioned safe set: before grasping, it protects the articulated robot; after grasping, the protected set expands to include the rigidly attached object. We represent robot, scene, and attached geometry with differentiable BP-SDFs and enforce the resulting CBF constraints directly on the VLA’s native six-dimensional operational-space action. WBAG minimally modifies the policy output while accounting for collisions involving the whole robot and attached geometry, without retraining the underlying VLA or modifying the operational-space controller. We evaluate WBAG on SafeLIBERO using a scene-level safety evaluator that monitors all eligible non-task scene objects. WBAG achieves the highest aggregate Scene Safety and Safe Success among the evaluated configurations, reaching 97.38%97.38\% and 59.38%59.38\%, respectively.
Our main contributions are summarized as the following:

We formulate a grasp-conditioned geometric CBF over articulated robot links and dynamically attached geometry, with the protected set adapting across pre- and post-grasp manipulation.

We develop WBAG, a novel perception-to-control safety framework that reconstructs scene and target geometry from visual observations, maintains grasp-conditioned protected geometry, and enforces the resulting constraints directly on the VLA’s native operational-space action without retraining the VLA or modifying the operational-space controller used to execute its actions.

We conduct a controlled SafeLIBERO evaluation with scene-level safety measurement that isolates the effects of scene coverage, whole-body protection, and attached-geometry modeling on safe VLA manipulation.

1. We formulate a grasp-conditioned geometric CBF over articulated robot links and dynamically attached geometry, with the protected set adapting across pre- and post-grasp manipulation.

2. We develop WBAG, a novel perception-to-control safety framework that reconstructs scene and target geometry from visual observations, maintains grasp-conditioned protected geometry, and enforces the resulting constraints directly on the VLA’s native operational-space action without retraining the VLA or modifying the operational-space controller used to execute its actions.

3. We conduct a controlled SafeLIBERO evaluation with scene-level safety measurement that isolates the effects of scene coverage, whole-body protection, and attached-geometry modeling on safe VLA manipulation.

title: quARtet Marker: A 3D-Printable Multi-Tag Fiducial for Robust Near-Frontal Pose Estimation
authors: Araki Wakiuchi,Hikaru Sasaki,Takamitsu Matsubara
abstract: Robotic manipulation of labware is difficult when transparent or reflective objects must be identified and localized. Coded planar fiducials are a practical retrofit: easy to print, they leave the marked face flat and graspable. Yet a single planar tag is least reliable in near-frontal views, where perspective cues fade. Non-planar geometries restore those cues but intrude on the flat face that a parallel-jaw gripper must contact. Our idea is to tilt multiple tags within one compact footprint, so that each tag is seen at a non-frontal angle even when the marker faces the camera. We propose the quARtet marker, a 3D-printable fiducial embodying this idea: all detected corners of its four tilted AprilTags enter one Perspective-n-Point solve, and a shared configuration defines the fabricated geometry and the detector model. Because tilting consumes flat area, its three layouts trade pose-estimation consistency against graspability. In robot-referenced, same-setup fixed-camera experiments, all three layouts reduced the mean frontal orientation error from 2.18​°2.18\tcdegree for a single planar tag to 0.240.24–0.47​°0.47\tcdegree and the root-mean-square position error from 1.501.50 to 0.170.17–0.200.20 mm. A robot-mounted-camera pose-hold test confirmed this separation under closed-loop visual feedback. In swing-down trials under identical conditions, the two layouts with flat contact strips retained the object with about 22 mm of in-grasp slip, whereas the layout without flat strips slipped by roughly 100100 mm. For the tested conditions, the results support a rule: the layout without flat strips when pose-estimation consistency dominates, a layout with flat strips when the marked face must remain graspable.
introduction:
Laboratory automation can raise experimental throughput and keep experiments running for days with little human intervention Burger et al. (2020); Szymanski et al. (2023), and it can spare people contact with hazardous materials Burger et al. (2020), but it also places robots in visually difficult workspaces: transparent vessels challenge appearance and depth sensing Sajjan et al. (2020); Fang et al. (2022), reflective or weakly textured tools provide few stable visual features, and visually identical containers may hold different materials. To manipulate such labware, a robot must know both which object is present and its six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) pose: its position and orientation. Manually taught positions and pre-calibrated placements can sidestep part of this perception problem, but the setup and re-teaching effort they demand works against the plug-and-play integration sought when existing laboratories are automated Wolf et al. (2023). Printed coded fiducials, reference markers that a camera can both identify and localize, are therefore an attractive retrofit. Printed code tags already label chemical containers in laboratories Shukran et al. (2017), marker tracking has been used to automate sensor registration in robot workspaces Gong et al. (2019), and an ordinary camera decodes object identity and estimates pose from the same observation Romero-Ramirez et al. (2018); Wan et al. (2017); Rekimoto and Ayatsuka (2000). The markers are also inexpensive to print and to replace after contamination. Figure 1 illustrates this application context and the four practical demands considered in this work (the marker proposed to meet them is introduced in Section 3, Fig. 2). It is not a depiction of the validation experiments.

The remaining problem is the physical and geometric design of the marker itself. A single square tag estimates orientation from the perspective distortion of its outline. Near a frontal view that distortion becomes weak: a tag tilted slightly toward the camera projects to nearly the same image as one tilted equally away, so pixel-level image errors translate into large orientation changes Tanaka et al. (2012); Tanaka et al. (2014), and the reported pose can flip between these two near-mirror solutions Schweighofer and Pinz (2006); Tanaka et al. (2014). This near-frontal viewpoint matters in practice because a robot-mounted camera often approaches a target approximately along the marker normal. It is also the view in which a planar tag is easiest to detect and decode, because its image is largest and least foreshortened, so the pose is least reliable exactly where detection is most reliable. Adding more coplanar tags does not remove the ambiguity, because the enlarged array is still a single plane seen head-on, and enlarging a planar board is unattractive for small labware. Non-coplanar, multi-face marker geometries are an effective remedy Mateos (2020); García-Ruiz et al. (2023), as discussed further in Section 2. However, they raise structure above the marked face, and that face may be the only one available to a parallel-jaw gripper. Improving pose estimation through geometry can therefore cost exactly the flat surface that grasping requires.

A laboratory fiducial must therefore do more than estimate pose accurately: it must remain compatible with manipulation. When the marked face doubles as the gripper’s contact face, pose-estimation performance and graspability have to be designed together, alongside coded identification and low-cost fabrication paired with a detector model that matches the printed geometry. These are the four linked demands of Fig. 1(c)–(f). The problem addressed in this paper is thus to find a marker geometry that improves near-frontal pose estimation while preserving flat regions that a gripper can contact.

Our idea is to tilt multiple tags within one compact footprint. Even when the marker as a whole is viewed frontally, each tag is then observed at a non-frontal angle and supplies the perspective cues that a single planar tag loses near that view. At the same time, how the tags are tilted determines which flat regions of the face survive, so the tilt pattern itself becomes a design parameter that balances pose estimation against graspability.

Based on this insight, we propose the quARtet marker, a family of compact 3D-printable multi-tag fiducials. Four AprilTags are tilted within one square footprint, and all reliably detected corners are combined in a single Perspective-n-Point (PnP) solve, which recovers the marker pose from the correspondences between known 3D points and their 2D image projections Lepetit et al. (2009) and is computed with OpenCV Bradski (2000). Three layouts use the same detection principle but expose different flat regions for gripper contact, and a shared configuration drives both marker fabrication and reconstruction of the detector-side 3D corner coordinates, avoiding manual measurement of inter-tag geometry. The experiments compare the three layouts and a single-tag control in near-frontal pose estimation and in a physical grasp-retention test, making the pose-estimation–graspability trade-off of the layouts explicit.

Throughout this paper, pose estimation is the umbrella term for estimating both orientation and position. The experiments report these two error components separately. The terminology does not denote two different estimation tasks.

The main contributions are:

A compact, configuration-driven multi-tag marker system. Four tilted tags retain non-coplanar perspective cues within the footprint of one planar tag and are solved jointly. One parameter file defines both the editable computer-aided design (CAD) model and the detector geometry, and the toolchain and data are publicly available.

A controlled evaluation of the consistency–graspability trade-off. Fixed-camera measurements under a common robot-referenced protocol and an independently re-grasped swing-down test separate the benefits and costs of the three layouts (Section 3) relative to the single-tag control. The layout whose four tags lean outward from a raised center is the most consistent across the tested viewpoints, whereas the two layouts whose tags tilt about their base edges keep flat contact strips for the gripper.

A closed-loop characterization under visual feedback. A robot-mounted-camera pose-hold test with five runs per marker type shows that the near-frontal separation persists under visual feedback: every quARtet layout holds the target with a significantly smaller orientation error and step-to-step reorientation than the single-tag control.

Section 2 positions the work relative to geometric and detection-side alternatives. Section 3 describes the marker and shared-parameter pipeline. Section 4 evaluates pose estimation and graspability against two research questions. Sections 5 and 6 interpret the trade-off, limitations, and practical layout choice.

title: Online Planning for Sparse Ground Target Search from a High-Altitude UAV under Partial Observability
authors: Ashik E Rasul,Hyung-Jin Yoon
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) searching for ground targets from a high altitude face a unique challenge, particularly when the target is already within the field of view but effectively unobservable because of its small apparent scale. Standard object detectors often underperform in such scenarios because of resolution downscaling and limited context. In contrast, active object search frameworks address this challenge by directing the agent to a suitable pose to gather richer visual information. However, flight regulations in urban airspace often restrict such physical movements for UAVs. As an alternative active sensing approach, the UAV can leverage the pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) mechanism of the onboard camera to dynamically adjust its field of view and sequentially gather enhanced visual information from specific regions of interest. Once the candidate locations of the target are identified, it can deploy more expensive object detection schemes, such as an ensemble of multiple models, to get better reasoning at a fixed scale. In this work, we formulate the sequential exploration with PTZ operation as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), in which the agent maintains a belief state over the target’s true location. To solve the POMDP, we deploy partially observable Monte Carlo planning (POMCP), where we condition the sensing reliability on target object scale and deploy selective ensemble detection as an additional reasoning step.
introduction:
Humans are particularly good at searching for relevant information in a cluttered environment through a spatial attention mechanism [1, 2]. This capability allows us to detect small objects at a distance, even if they occupy a tiny area within our field of view (FOV). Emulating such adaptive perception capability is crucial for efficient object search and has been extensively studied in the computer vision community as human eye movement models [3, 4]. However, these models assume that the object of interest is always present in the input image, that the image already contains sufficient features of the target object, and that the sensor has a high detection probability with negligible noise in the operating range.

In a real-world object search scenario, most images collected by a mobile robot may not contain the target object, the target object may be occluded or may not reveal sufficient features, and the detector itself may be noisy. There has been significant advancement in object search in indoor environments by the robotics community, where these challenges are handled by physically moving the agent to a suitable pose to gather enhanced visual information [5, 6]. These works assume the observation uncertainty mostly arises from object occlusion or hidden features for the object’s relative pose, as the target object scale variation within the FOV is often negligible in indoor settings. For unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), searching for a sparse ground target from high altitude, such physical movement is not feasible due to flight regulations in urban airspace. Moreover, even if the target is visible within the FOV, it may be tiny, and the input image resolution may not be enough to reveal sufficient features. In this scenario, standard object detectors often struggle to produce reliable detections. Computer vision methods for tiny object detection also suffer in this case, as a higher-resolution version of the input image may not be available, and approaches such as slicing [7], that attempts to enhance the size of the target by exhaustive slicing of the whole image with overlaps, or coarse-to-fine [8] detection, that runs a coarse detector to find the candidate regions and runs a fine detector on the candidate regions for finding the target, leads to significant resolution downscaling that produces uncalibrated confidence scores and a number of false positive detections. Though the detection accuracy can be further enhanced with more expensive ensemble methods [9], which run inference with multiple models trained on a subset of data (bagging [10]) or with random initialization [11], they can still struggle under scale and resolution variation of the target image.

The UAV can leverage the pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) mechanism before capturing the images to selectively enhance the size, clarity, and position of the object of interest, while maintaining a fixed input resolution, as illustrated in Figure 1. However, such selective enhancement can be expensive, and any exhaustive exploration may be limited by on-board computational resources and time-sensitive mission objectives. Conventional autonomous PTZ camera control follows a preloaded policy, often learned offline, that assumes complete environmental observability and focuses primarily on target tracking rather than ensuring detection reliability [12, 13]. For the sparse target search scenario, these assumptions do not hold, as the UAV cannot access the full information about the environment simultaneously and can only receive noisy observations with variable uncertainty conditioned on the PTZ settings, environmental conditions, and the target’s relative pose. In other words, the environment is partially observable, and the UAV must maintain a belief state, which is an internal estimate of its surroundings, to effectively choose the next sequence of actions. At every time step, the UAV has to trade off between wide-scan exploration for quick area coverage to receive noisy observations and precise-scan exploration for slower area coverage to receive more reliable observations.

In this work, we formulate the sparse target search problem from a high altitude using camera PTZ functionality as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) [14]. In this setting, the control policy operates directly on the belief space to sequentially actuate the PTZ operation of the camera to optimize the long-term objective of finding the target with minimum steps. The belief gets updated as the UAV receives new observations. Unlike conventional approaches that assume complete knowledge of the environment (i.e., complete observability of the environment), assuming near-perfect sensors or fixed uncertainty across actions, we explicitly model the observation uncertainty conditioned on different object appearances within the FOV.
To solve the POMDP, we deploy Partially Observable Monte Carlo Planning (POMCP) [15]. To address the variation of the observation model in different deployment environments and UAV states, we formulate the detection reliability with a Beta-Bernoulli conjugate model that allows us to incorporate prior knowledge about the observation uncertainty as well as update the model iteratively as we gather more experiences from the deployment scenarios. Additionally, we selectively deploy an ensemble of DNNs at a fixed scale, conditioned on belief concentration, to improve prediction and enable successful target search.
Our proposed methodology is illustrated in Figure 2.

To evaluate our approach, we use a simulation environment [16] built in Unreal Engine that models realistic aerial scenarios, including cluttered urban landscapes, varying altitudes, camera attributes (Field of view, focal length, and aperture control), and dynamic lighting. This environment enables thorough testing of the proposed framework, allowing us to study the effect of uncertainty, limited observability, and PTZ camera control against the baselines. Our key contributions are:

We formulate the PTZ camera operation, by a high-altitude UAV searching for a sparse ground target, as a POMDP.

We formulate the PTZ camera operation, by a high-altitude UAV searching for a sparse ground target, as a POMDP.

We formulate the observation model uncertainty as a Beta-Bernoulli conjugate model, conditioned on the object appearance, with a prior assignment.

We deploy POMCP to solve the POMDP that sequentially selects the informative actions for environmental exploration. Within the POMCP implementation, we integrate our defined observation model and selectively deploy ensemble detection to enhance reasoning when belief concentration is already high.

Finally, we validate our method in a photo-realistic simulation environment to show the confident discovery of the targets with significantly fewer steps, with minimal dependency on camera resolution, compared to traditional tiny-object detection methods.

2. We formulate the observation model uncertainty as a Beta-Bernoulli conjugate model, conditioned on the object appearance, with a prior assignment.

3. We deploy POMCP to solve the POMDP that sequentially selects the informative actions for environmental exploration. Within the POMCP implementation, we integrate our defined observation model and selectively deploy ensemble detection to enhance reasoning when belief concentration is already high.

4. Finally, we validate our method in a photo-realistic simulation environment to show the confident discovery of the targets with significantly fewer steps, with minimal dependency on camera resolution, compared to traditional tiny-object detection methods.

title: Divide-and-Remember: Recursive Action-Relevant Memory for Long-Horizon VLA Policies
authors: Xuehui Yu,Eason Yu,Meiyi Wang,Haozhe Du,Stefano V. Albrecht,Harold Soh
abstract:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models struggle on history-dependent manipulation tasks, where the current observation alone does not determine the action, and the policy needs a memory of the history.
Existing memory methods decide what to remember by design, for example, keeping frames with large pixel changes, and show inconsistent gains across tasks.
We view what to remember as an optimisation problem. From the POMDP formulation of imitation learning, we show that the optimal memory maximises the conditional mutual information I⁡(at;mt∣ot)I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) between the action and the memory given the current observation.
Intuitively, this means preserving the action-relevant information in the history that is not already contained in the current observation. Based on our analysis, we propose Divide-and-Remember (D&R), a recursive memory method that learns a memory function mt=ℳ⁡(ht)m_{t}=\mathcal{M}(h_{t}) and scales to long contexts while staying compute-light.
It involves two strategies: (1) the selection over the full history is divided recursively into subproblems of top-KK selection over 2​K2K tokens, so that fixed-size, lightweight selectors learned end-to-end support an unbounded history;
(2) all recursion blocks share one selector, which captures the selection rule common to every block and keeps the method efficient.
On RoboMME, a benchmark of 1616 long-horizon manipulation tasks that require remembering when, where, what, and how to act, D&R achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate with consistent gains across all four suites under a budget of only 6464 tokens; real-robot experiments show the same gain.
Code, checkpoints and more results are at dnr-memory.github.io.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) policies are visuomotor policies trained by imitation learning, a.k.a. learning from demonstrations (LfD): a policy is learned from a dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} of demonstrations, each an observation–action sequence {(ot,at)}t=1T\{(o_{t},a_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T}. Powered by large-scale robotic datasets and pretrained vision–language models, VLAs have achieved remarkable progress in robotic manipulation.
However, many long-horizon tasks are partially observable, where the current observation oto_{t} alone cannot determine the correct action. In Figure 1(a), the robot must move a cube “in the same manner as before”, as shown in a video it has just watched; after either video it faces the same observation, and only the history tells it how to act.
When the task’s memory length, the shortest history the task requires, exceeds the policy’s context length (Definition 1), such ambiguity can only be resolved by the history ht={(ok,ak)}k<th_{t}=\{(o_{k},a_{k})\}_{k<t}. In this case, the policy needs memory, the ability to retain and reuse relevant information across time; we refer to this as the memory problem.

A growing body of research has integrated memory into VLAs, differing in what the memory encodes, from latent memory (Koo et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026) to perceptual memory (Yang et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026), and alleviates the memory problem to some extent. However, what information the memory should carry remains fragmented.
Latent memory learns a dense compression of the history hth_{t}, which tracks temporal facts well (e.g., a count of events) but aligns poorly with the pretrained token space of the VLA and loses spatial detail.
Perceptual memory keeps a subset of the history chosen by an inductive bias (e.g., the frames with the largest pixel change, or those picked by a VLM verifier); its verbatim snapshots preserve spatial facts (object locations and spatial relations) and object identity, but often miss some key robot behaviour, and the selection is not optimised for control.
This diversity reflects that existing work designs memory from task-specific (Yang et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026) perspectives, yielding inconsistent gains and a limited understanding of what the optimal formulation of memory is.

Starting from information theory and POMDPs, we cast the memory problem of a visuomotor policy as an optimisation problem: the optimal memory maximises the conditional mutual information I⁡(at;mt∣ot)I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) between the action ata_{t} and the memory mtm_{t} given the current observation oto_{t} (formal definition in Section 4); intuitively, it keeps the key facts that oto_{t} lacks but ata_{t} depends on, such as the grasp pose in Figure 1(b).
This objective gives a unified view of existing memories.
Perceptual heuristics keep the frames that differ most in pixels. This is a proxy for the conditional entropy H⁡(ok∣ot)H(o_{k}\mid o_{t}), i.e., how much a candidate frame oko_{k} differs from the current observation oto_{t}. It is only a loose upper bound on what the frame adds, I⁡(at;ok∣ot)≤H⁡(ok∣ot)I(a_{t};\,o_{k}\mid o_{t})\leq H(o_{k}\mid o_{t}), and spends the memory budget on information that does not help control, such as when the observation changes for reasons unrelated to the action (e.g., a lighting change).
Latent memory does optimise I⁡(at;mt∣ot)I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) through its variational lower bound; the action log-likelihood 𝔼𝒟​[log⁡πθ​(at∣ot,mt)]\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t},m_{t})] is maximised jointly over the policy weights θ\theta and the memory mtm_{t}, but it learns mtm_{t} in a new latent space and loses the spatial detail that the pretrained tokens of the VLA carry.
Thus, we ask: Can a memory be trained to maximise I⁡(at;mt∣ot)I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) directly, without heuristics, while staying in the pretrained token space of the VLA, so that it is optimised for control and still keeps the spatial details?

We answer this question with Divide-and-Remember (D&R), which optimises the memory against I⁡(at;mt∣ot)I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) in the pretrained token space of the VLA, so that choosing mtm_{t} becomes a discrete optimisation over the history tokens ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}. D&R is a recursive memory method, in which the full history is divided recursively into slices of 2​K2K tokens and a fixed-size, lightweight selector keeps KK tokens of each slice. The KK tokens kept from two neighbouring slices are merged into a new 2​K2K-token slice and selected again (see Figure 3), and the composition of these selections solves the memory selection over the full history. This design lets the history scale up while the learnable parameters stay light. The selector is trained end-to-end by the policy’s action loss, the variational lower bound of I⁡(at;mt∣ot)I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}).

We evaluate on RoboMME (Dai et al., 2026), a benchmark of 1616 long-horizon manipulation tasks that each require a different fact from the past. Under a memory budget of only 6464 tokens, D&R reaches a state-of-the-art average success rate of 38.6%38.6\%, against 32.2%32.2\% for the best latent memory and 17.9%17.9\% for the memoryless policy. D&R leads on every memory demand of the benchmark, whether the policy has to accumulate a count over repeated events, track an object after it is hidden, refer back to an earlier moment of the episode, or reproduce a demonstrated sequence.
We also evaluate D&R on a real robot over several long-run tasks, with a person intervening mid-task and under perception noise, where D&R achieved the highest success rate.

title: NarrativeFlow: Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Model Using Robot Velocity Fields
authors: Shota Kobayashi,Koki Seno,Daichi Yashima,Komei Sugiura
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Accepted at ACCV 2026
abstract:
We focus on language-conditioned flow-based manipulation, where robot flows (robot velocity fields) serve as embodiment-agnostic, motion-centric representations for leveraging data collected from multiple robot platforms.
This task is crucial because language-conditioned manipulation is essential for practical robotic systems, yet scaling robot foundation models remains limited by the labor-intensive collection of embodiment-specific data. Existing methods either coarsely approximate robot flows with sparse keypoint displacements, or cannot handle language-conditioned manipulation.
To address this limitation, we propose NarrativeFlow, which models robot flows as continuous velocity fields using a flow-matching formulation conditioned on language.
Accordingly, NarrativeFlow generates robot flows that are physically consistent with real-world manipulation.
To validate NarrativeFlow, we have conducted experiments on standard datasets for language-conditioned manipulation.
The experimental results show that NarrativeFlow outperforms representative baseline methods on standard evaluation metrics.
Furthermore, through real-world experiments, we show that NarrativeFlow achieves higher success rates than baseline methods across multiple manipulation tasks.
The project page is available at https://shota0520.github.io/NarrativeFlow-project-page/
introduction:
Labor shortages have increased demand for robotic systems that support workers and reduce physical burden in manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare.
To meet this demand, such systems must perform diverse tasks across a wide range of real-world environments, while following natural language instructions.
In this direction, recent work has explored robot foundation models, which are often pretrained on large-scale data collected from multiple robot platforms [4, 3, 33, 24].
This line of work indicates that the scale and diversity of training data are critical to model performance, yet training these models still requires labor-intensive collection of embodiment-specific data [4, 3, 33, 24].

In this study, we focus on language-conditioned flow-based manipulation.
In this task, a model generates a robot flow (robot velocity field) conditioned on an instruction, and then a robot performs object manipulation based on the robot flow.
Robot flows serve as embodiment-agnostic intermediate representations that bridge visual observations and robot actions.
Because such flows can be extracted from arbitrary robot videos, flow-based approaches can leverage large-scale data collected from multiple robot platforms rather than relying on costly embodiment-specific data collection.
However, this task remains challenging: indeed, a representative method, Im2Flow2Act [49], still underperforms a method using oracle robot flows by 21 percentage points in average success rate (see Table 4).

Many existing flow-based manipulation methods [13, 49, 2] do not formulate robot flows as dense velocity fields, but as displacements of sparse keypoints, even though robot manipulation is inherently a time-evolving physical process.
Specifically, these methods predict sparse keypoint coordinates and then derive robot flows from their displacements, yielding only a coarse approximation of continuous robot motion.
These formulations can be problematic because they assume that the displacements are deterministic, although such an assumption is rarely satisfied in practice.
By contrast, Flow as Flow [38] can model robot flows as dense velocity fields; however, it cannot handle language-conditioned settings.
Moreover, existing methods [13, 49, 2, 38] typically rely only on primary flow-generation objectives during training, which provide no explicit supervision for capturing task-relevant semantics.
As a result, such models can be misled by task-irrelevant visual details, such as background appearance and lighting.

To address these limitations, we propose NarrativeFlow, a language-conditioned robot flow generation method that formulates robot flows as probability velocity fields within a flow-matching framework.
By modeling velocity fields, NarrativeFlow generates robot flows that are more physically consistent with real-world manipulation.
Moreover, we introduce an auxiliary loss that aligns the model’s intermediate representations with task-relevant scene changes, enabling the model to capture task-relevant semantics.

Fig. 1 shows an overview of our approach.
We first train our model on cross-embodiment datasets.
At deployment, given an instruction and an initial image, the model generates a robot flow that represents the robot motion required for the specified task (e.g., picking up the can and placing it on the table).
Subsequently, the robot executes the manipulation based on the generated flow to complete the task.

The contributions of this study are as follows:

We propose NarrativeFlow, a language-conditioned robot flow generation method that formulates robot flows as probability velocity fields within a flow-matching framework, enabling high-quality robot flow generation.

We introduce the Narrative Delta loss as an auxiliary objective that aligns the model’s intermediate representations with task-relevant scene changes. We further introduce two subtask tokens to mitigate interference between this auxiliary objective and the primary flow-generation objective.

We show that NarrativeFlow outperforms baseline methods across standard datasets.

Through real-world experiments, we show that NarrativeFlow achieves higher success rates than baseline methods across multiple manipulation tasks.

title: ShowerFlex: Achieving Pseudo-Static Balancing in a Continuum Shower Hose
authors: Zhiyu Ren,Girish Krishnan
comment: . Accepted to ASME IDETC/CIE 2026, Mechanisms and Robotics Conference
abstract: With the global population rapidly aging, maintaining independence in Activities of Daily Living (ADLs)—particularly bathing or showering—has become a critical challenge. Older adults who sit while showering currently have limited options, often relying on rigid overhead showerheads or flexible hand-held hoses that require continuous gripping and precarious user maneuvers, increasing the risk of falls. To address this need, this paper introduces a highly articulated, pseudo-static balanced continuum mechanism designed specifically for accessible bathing assistance. The proposed mechanism features a modular continuum architecture composed of friction-locked ball-and-socket joints (loc-line), seamlessly integrated with a retractable spring-loaded reel for effective gravity compensation. This hybrid design achieves an intuitive “Push-and-Stay” interaction logic, maintaining an approximate static equilibrium with ergonomically low actuation force, without any external electronic power, while significantly minimizing the force needed for repositioning. Theoretically, we established a recursive forward kinematics framework to construct the geometric model of the structure, coupled with a comprehensive static equilibrium analysis to evaluate the system’s holding capacity across its 51-DOF structure. Numerical simulations utilizing Monte Carlo methods validate the system’s morphological adaptability and stability at various extreme positions within a standard bath space. Physical experiments further validate the prototype’s real-world performance, confirming its intrinsic static stability against gravity and ensuring that the actuation force remains well within the ergonomic capabilities of older adults. Ultimately, this research provides a low-cost, intrinsically safe showerhead design that reduces physical strain, restoring dignity and autonomy in personal hygiene.
introduction:
The global community is rapidly aging. According to the latest projections from the World Health Organization (2025), the global population of individuals aged 60 and over is expected to double, reaching 2.1 billion by 2050 [13] [6] [14]. Within this demographic shift, maintaining independence in “Activities of Daily Living” (ADLs), and in particular maintaining personal hygiene through routine showering or bathing stands as a critical determinant of healthy aging. Independent bathing is often the most important physiological threshold where functional decline becomes apparent [3] [2]. The inability to perform this intimate task not only poses physical health risks but also precipitates a severe decline in psychological well-being, often leading to a loss of dignity and a heightened sense of institutional dependency [7] [9].
For older adults who use wheelchairs or have trouble moving their legs, staying independent in the shower is difficult for two main reasons. First, moving from a wheelchair into the shower is physically demanding. To make this easier, homes often need structural changes, such as replacing traditional tubs with “walk-in” showers that have no curb or a very low entry point for a wheelchair to roll over. Second, for those who shower while sitting, ensuring that the shower reaches certain parts of the body like the back, head, and feet is often impossible  [8]. Reaching the water temperature and flow controls can also be a struggle. This paper focuses on that second challenge: making it easier for older adults to reach their body and operate shower controls comfortably while seated.

Despite these well-documented challenges, shower hardware has remained largely stagnant for decades. Traditional fixed showerheads are reliable, but their rigid design cannot adapt to the human body’s shape. This forces users into risky physical movements just to reach their back or feet  [8]. While adjustable showerheads from brands like Waterpik or Delta exist, they are designed for standing adults of different heights. They are ineffective for those who shower while seated, as the user typically sits three to four feet away from the water source. Handheld showerheads with flexible hoses are a common alternative, but they require the user to constantly hold and aim them. For frail older adults, this is a major safety risk: if one hand is busy holding a showerhead, they cannot use both hands to grip safety bars, significantly increasing the risk of a fall  [16].

To address these challenges, this paper presents “ShowerFlex: A friction and spring-balanced continuum hose with a showerhead at its distal end”. With ShowerFlex the showerhead can be positioned at any location and orientation within the bath space, and the hose holds its configuration without being continuously held or requiring external power supply. This allows for hands-free operation of the shower. Furthermore, our design allows the showerhead to be repositioned with little force, making critical areas such as the back and legs accessible to the shower. We refer to this hybrid strategy as pseudo-static balancing, a concept formally defined in Section 2.

Showerflex routes the hose through a Loc-Line® assembly, which is a series of hollow, friction‑locked ball‑and‑socket segments. One end of the Loc-Line connects to the water inlet, and the other attaches to a standard showerhead. A self‑locking retractable reel, anchored to a fixed support and connected to the showerhead, provides additional stability. The reel locks when stationary but allows smooth, user‑guided motion when slightly tensioned, while its internal springs help counteract the weight of the showerhead. Together, the Loc-Line and reel demonstrate the advantages of conventional static balancing, i.e. equilibrium at all configurations with minimal repositioning force.

The combination of friction locking and spring-loaded balancing is studied in this paper as a strategy to obtain the benefits of static balancing without actually requiring the forces to balance. To provide a theoretical basis for this behavior, we established a recursive forward kinematics model alongside a detailed static equilibrium analysis. These mathematical foundations enable numerical simulations, specifically using the Monte Carlo method to quantify the reachable workspace and verify the system’s stability for normal bathing tasks. Finally, we demonstrate the robustness by physical experimental validation, confirming the device’s intrinsic static stability and validating that the actuation force is well within the ergonomic capabilities of older adults.

title: A Survey on End-to-End Autonomous Driving Training from the Perspectives of Data, Strategy, and Platform
authors: Chengkai Xu,Yiming Cui,Jiaqi Liu,Yicheng Guo,Cheng Qin,Geyuan Zhang,Xinwei Dong,Shiyu Fang,Peng Hang,Jian Sun
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: accepted by IEEE transactions on intelligent transportation systems
abstract:
Autonomous driving is a cornerstone technology for the future of intelligent transportation, where end-to-end learning has emerged as a transformative paradigm that directly maps multimodal sensory inputs to driving actions through unified differentiable models. While offering advantages, the effectiveness of end-to-end autonomous driving (E2E-AD) is ultimately determined by the quality of its training ecosystem.
This paper provides a comprehensive review of training methods and ecosystem for E2E-AD. We introduce a Data-Strategy-Platform taxonomy that conceptualizes training as an interdependent system.
The data layer defines what can be learned, the strategy layer governs how learning aligns with driving objectives, and the platform layer supports scalability and continuous evolution. Within this framework, we survey recent advances across data-centric pipelines, learning paradigms, and training infrastructures, and analyze their interplay in shaping model performance, robustness, and deployability.
Finally, we reflect on current limitations and articulate a forward-looking vision that emphasizes a shift from data quantity to data value, from isolated optimization to foundation-driven generalization, and from static training to integrated training-testing loops, aiming toward robust, scalable, and trustworthy autonomous driving systems.
We maintain a continuously updated repository tracking cutting-edge literature and works at Our Project Page.
introduction:
Autonomous driving has emerged as a strategic frontier in intelligent transportation systems, offering prospects for safer mobility, higher traffic efficiency, and new paradigms of urban transport [1, 2].
Traditional research has largely followed a modular pipeline architecture, where perception, prediction, planning, and control are separated into distinct subsystems.
Although this decomposition facilitates interpretability and engineering controllability, modular systems are prone to error accumulation across interfaces and struggle to achieve global optimization in highly interactive and mixed traffic environments [3, 4].

In response, end-to-end autonomous driving (E2E-AD) has attracted significant research attention.
By mapping multimodal sensory inputs directly to driving actions through unified differentiable models, E2E-AD reduces system coupling and allows joint optimization of perception, decision-making, and control [5, 6, 7].
Such integration has demonstrated strong potential for handling complex interactions and long-horizon reasoning [8].
Moreover, recent progress in large-scale representation learning, generative models, and foundation models further expands the capabilities of E2E-AD, pushing the research frontier from concept demonstrations toward practical deployment.

Despite these structural advantages, E2E-AD still faces challenges in large-scale real-world application, and its development bottleneck lies not only in model design but also in the training process itself.
As models become larger and more capable [9], their effectiveness increasingly depends on whether the training ecosystem can provide: (i) data with sufficient coverage, quality, and governance to capture rare but safety-critical scenarios; (ii) strategies for optimization that can align multi-task objectives and stabilize long-horizon learning; and (iii) platforms with the computational scale and lifecycle management required for continuous model evolution. These three dimensions jointly define the performance boundary of E2E autonomous vehicles.

We clarify the positioning of this review against representative surveys in Table I. Existing studies provide valuable reviews of datasets [10, 11, 12], perception modules [13, 14], end-to-end architectures [8, 7], imitation learning [6], and foundation models [9, 15, 16]. In contrast, this survey focuses on the training ecosystem and examines how data, learning strategies, and platforms jointly determine training effectiveness.

The main contributions of this survey are as follows:

A Data-Strategy-Platform taxonomy is introduced, which frames E2E-AD training as a system-level challenge rather than an isolated algorithmic problem.

A comprehensive review of recent advances is conducted, encompassing data, paradigms, and infrastructures, with particular emphasis on both the current state of the art and the dynamic interplay among these three dimensions.

Beyond surveying existing work, a future vision for training E2E-AD is proposed, where the shift from data quantity to data value, from task-specific learners to universal foundation models, and from static offline training to continuous training-testing integration is highlighted.

The overall logical structure of the review is shown in Fig. 1. The Data Layer (Section III) establishes the learnable information boundary through scenario coverage and governance, which supports the Strategy Layer (Section IV), where paradigms ranging from imitation learning to world models are reviewed.
Finally, the Platform Layer (Section V) provides the computational foundation for training and validation. Section VI discusses the cross-layer evolution shown in Fig. 1.

1. A Data-Strategy-Platform taxonomy is introduced, which frames E2E-AD training as a system-level challenge rather than an isolated algorithmic problem.

2. A comprehensive review of recent advances is conducted, encompassing data, paradigms, and infrastructures, with particular emphasis on both the current state of the art and the dynamic interplay among these three dimensions.

3. Beyond surveying existing work, a future vision for training E2E-AD is proposed, where the shift from data quantity to data value, from task-specific learners to universal foundation models, and from static offline training to continuous training-testing integration is highlighted.
