title: eRLT: Efficient VLA Reinforcement Learning via Action-Relevant Token Routing
authors: Dehao Huang,Jianbang Liu,Jianpan Gao,Chao Tang,Zilang Cen,Zedong Dan,Jiaheng Wang,Tingguang Li,Yue Wang,Hong Zhang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models provide strong behavioral priors for robotic manipulation, yet efficiently adapting them to downstream tasks remains challenging. Recent work addresses this challenge by adapting frozen VLAs through online reinforcement learning (RL), whose sample efficiency depends on the quality of the state representation used by the actor and critic. Existing methods construct such representations either with VLA-independent visual encoders or through fixed compression of internal VLA representations. Neither design explicitly extracts the task-specific action-relevant VLA features most useful for downstream action refinement and action-value estimation, therefore limiting sample efficiency. To address this limitation, we introduce eRLT, which constructs an effective state representation by routing task-specific action-relevant information across both tokens and layers of the frozen VLA. Specifically, learned routing tokens dynamically aggregate visual-language features at multiple depths, while a lightweight layer router combines these summaries into a fixed-dimensional RL token. The routing module is initialized using expert demonstrations to capture features predictive of expert actions and then refined using critic feedback from online interactions for action-value estimation. Across seven LIBERO and RoboTwin tasks, eRLT improves mean normalized learning-curve AUC by up to 23.7%23.7\% over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments on USB connector insertion and motherboard ribbon-cable insertion further show AUC improvements of 108.9%108.9\% and 46.7%46.7\%, respectively, over the strongest baseline.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models inherit broad visual and semantic knowledge from internet-scale pretraining and learn generalist control from diverse robot data, enabling generalization across tasks and environments (Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2026). However, achieving high reliability on a specific downstream task often requires further adaptation. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is effective, but heavily relies on collecting additional high-quality task-specific demonstrations, whose coverage of states encountered during deployment is inherently limited. Online reinforcement learning (RL) provides a complementary approach by collecting experience from the policy’s own deployment distribution and learning from both successful and failed interactions (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026; Wagenmaker et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). In this work, we focus on lightweight online RL methods that keep the pretrained VLA frozen and adapt its behavior through a small actor-critic.

The success of lightweight online RL depends critically on the state representation supplied to the actor and critic. A VLA trained for generalist control encodes rich information about visual observations, language instructions, robot states, and actions. For task-specific adaptation, an effective state representation should retain the task-specific action-relevant information needed for action refinement and action-value estimation, including robot-object relations that determine appropriate corrections and task-progress cues that determine the expected return of those corrections. Such information is distributed across the VLA’s tokens and layers, and the most useful features vary across tasks. Existing methods construct the state representation either with visual encoders independent of the VLA (Wagenmaker et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025) or by compressing representations from a predetermined layer and token set (Kowshik et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). The former constructs the state representation outside the VLA and therefore cannot directly reuse its internal task-specific action-relevant features. The latter reuses VLA features, but restricts feature extraction to a predetermined layer and token set regardless of which features are most useful for the target task. Neither design explicitly extracts the task-specific action-relevant VLA features most useful for downstream action refinement and action-value estimation, limiting sample efficiency under constrained online interaction budgets.

To address this limitation, we introduce eRLT, which constructs an effective state representation by routing task-specific action-relevant information across the tokens and layers of the frozen VLA. At each selected VLM layer, learned routing tokens dynamically aggregate visual-language features, while a lightweight layer router combines these layer-wise summaries into a fixed-dimensional RL token. The routing module is firstly initialized by predicting expert action chunks from existing VLA SFT demonstrations, encouraging the RL token to retain information useful for action refinement. Then, during online RL stage, the critic’s Bellman objective further refines the routing module using online transitions, adapting the retained information for action-value estimation. The VLA remains frozen throughout both stages. By focusing the RL token on task-specific action-relevant VLA features, eRLT facilitates action refinement and action-value estimation, thereby supporting sample-efficient actor-critic learning from limited online interactions.

We evaluate eRLT on manipulation tasks from LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) and RoboTwin (Chen et al., 2025), as well as two real-world high-precision manipulation tasks: USB connector insertion and motherboard ribbon-cable insertion. Across the seven simulation tasks, eRLT improves mean normalized learning-curve AUC by 23.7%23.7\% relative to baselines with fixed VLA feature compression and by 7.1%7.1\% relative to baselines with VLA-independent state encoders. On the two real-world tasks, eRLT improves learning-curve AUC by 108.9%108.9\% and 46.7%46.7\%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline, and on USB connector insertion raises the final-window success rate from 50%50\% to 90%90\% under the same interaction budget. Ablations further validate the complementary roles of layer-wise routing, token-wise routing, task-specific action-relevant initialization, and online adaptation.

In summary, our contributions are three-fold:

We provide controlled evidence that the VLA layers and tokens most useful for online RL vary across downstream tasks.

We propose eRLT, which constructs an effective RL token by routing task-specific action-relevant information across VLA tokens and layers. The routing mechanism is initialized via expert action prediction and subsequently refined online using critic feedback.

We evaluate eRLT across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and two real-world precision high-precision manipulation tasks, demonstrating improved sample efficiency over existing state representations.

1. We provide controlled evidence that the VLA layers and tokens most useful for online RL vary across downstream tasks.

2. We propose eRLT, which constructs an effective RL token by routing task-specific action-relevant information across VLA tokens and layers. The routing mechanism is initialized via expert action prediction and subsequently refined online using critic feedback.

3. We evaluate eRLT across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and two real-world precision high-precision manipulation tasks, demonstrating improved sample efficiency over existing state representations.

title: Screw Attention: Rigid-Body Algebra Inside a Transformer
authors: Aly Magassouba
abstract: Learned manipulation policies rediscover from data the spatial relations that rigid-body mechanics supplies in closed form. This costs data, and it leaves the policies fragile to geometric changes in the scene. We present Screw Attention, a transformer layer in which the relation between two bodies is a spatial transform rather than a graph edge. Every token is a body with a pose. Each pair of tokens carries the relative pose and, for robot joints, the joint screw. Messages are transported along this relation into the receiver’s frame, while the attention scores see only frame-invariant quantities. By construction, the messages are equivariant to an independent change of frame at every token, and a single layer can express the velocity recursion of rigid-body mechanics. On simulated manipulation tasks, Screw Attention matches or outperforms controls of the same size, including graph, transformer and flat networks on LIBERO-Spatial. With 16,162 parameters it reaches 97.3% on LIBERO-Spatial from object poses (without images or language), above a flat network with 27×27\times more parameters. Under a change of per-link frame convention its success is unchanged, while every other learned network falls below 3%. Placed on an analytic controller as a gated residual, it raises insertion success by 17.3 points. It is unaffected by pose noise up to 10 mm and by joint offsets within the factory calibration of a Franka arm. These results suggest a criterion: geometry is decisive when the task requires relations between frames that no other part of the system supplies. Code and trained policies will be released.
introduction:
Learned policies have become one of the main approaches to robot manipulation,
using scale as their principal lever. For instance, vision-language-action models with billions of
parameters, trained on large corpora of demonstrations, now perform multi-step tasks from
raw images and natural language. However, recent robustness analyses expose a sharp weakness:
displacing the manipulated objects, or altering the robot’s initial configuration, degrades the
accuracy of such policies drastically [1, 2]. These failures are
not only of perception, but of representing spatial relationships.

Yet those relations are exactly what rigid-body mechanics supplies in closed form. The kinematic model specifies how motion at one joint propagates to distant links, how a force applied at the gripper is distributed across the actuators, and how the gripper pose relates to any commanded frame. These relations are available a priori, long before any data are collected. Classical controllers are built on this structure, which is why such controllers remain compact, predictable, and reliable within the regimes they are designed to cover. The limitations of this approach are equally well-defined: analytic methods cannot easily express contact, friction, deformation, uncertain payload properties, or any task whose objective is not a fixed set-point. In this respect, analytic methods and learned policies form two complementary paradigms. One is given the geometry but cannot represent what the model omits; the other can represent what the model omits but must rediscover the geometry.

Several lines of work have therefore reintroduced structure into learned policies, although each retains only part of it. Embodiment-aware policy
transformers [3, 4, 5] encode the robot’s
connectivity as an abstract graph, through per-limb descriptors or by biasing attention toward links that are neighbours in the
kinematic tree. Equivariant manipulation policies [6, 7, 8]
preserve the geometry of the scene, so that behaviour is consistent when the scene is
transformed, but they represent the robot only through its end-effector pose.
Kinematics-structured policies [9, 10] do carry the poses or transforms of
individual links, yet process them with learned matrices, discarding the very structure that made those poses worth carrying. In all cases, the relation between two bodies is either abstracted into a graph or reduced to coordinates that a learned map is free to reinterpret.

That relation is neither abstract nor arbitrary, and this observation underpins our approach. It is a physical relation with explicit content: the distance between two bodies, their relative orientation, and, when a joint is present, the axis of rotation or translation. Robotics provides a concise formalism for exactly these notions, the spatial or screw algebra of rigid-body
mechanics [11, 12, 13]. In this formalism such a relation is a single
object and composing two of them determines directly how motion of one body induces motion of another. A policy given these relations is therefore not required to learn kinematics from scratch, since the kinematic structure is already encoded in the relations themselves.

The question then becomes how to build an architecture that can make direct use of this kinematic
structure, rather than relearning it implicitly. To this end, we adopt a transformer [14] whose
tokens exchange screws (the velocities and forces of rigid-body mechanics) rather than only
feature vectors. As illustrated in Fig. 1, in our architecture, each input token is a body with a pose, which may be a robot link or an object in
the scene. Standard transformers relate tokens only through a learned compatibility between their features. In our approach, each pair of tokens also carries a given term that represents the physical relation between the two bodies, read from the kinematic model or, for objects, from perception. This addition enables two architectural shifts.

First, any message sent from one token to another is transformed into the receiving body’s own
frame. Indeed, quantities defined at different locations cannot be combined until they are expressed in
a common frame, so the message must be transformed before the receiving token can use it.
Second, the attention weights access the relation only through frame-invariant quantities (e.g.,
distances, joint types, adjacency), which enter as an attention bias. The distinction matters: a bias on the
scores is a reweighting a transformer can in principle learn unaided, whereas transporting a quantity
between coordinate frames is an operation it cannot express on its own. The physics therefore
enters where it adds genuine capability, on the messages.

Three properties follow from this construction. (i) The recursion that propagates velocities along the kinematic chain lies within what the layer can express, so the policy need not learn mechanics from data and can spend its capacity on the phenomena that mechanics omits. (ii) The geometry is
combined only through operations admitted by the spatial algebra, and these operations commute with changes of coordinate frame. As a result, the transported messages do not depend on how a frame is attached to a link, which is a modelling convention with no physical meaning. (iii) Because the readout emits the same command as an analytic controller, a joint torque or an end-effector twist, the layer can be used alone or on top of such a controller as a residual. Closing a gate recovers the controller exactly, so the balance between analytic and learned control is a choice made per task rather than fixed by the architecture.

In robotics, every link carries its own frame. The choice of where that frame is attached is a convention that varies across description formats [15] and sometimes even across descriptions of the same robot [16]. A policy whose behaviour depends on this convention can fail on a robot that is physically identical but described differently. Existing equivariant architectures [17, 8] are equivariant only to a single, global change of frame applied to the entire scene. By contrast, our layer is equivariant to an independent change of frame on every link, which is the freedom a robot description actually has.

With this foundation, our contributions are as follows.

An embodiment-aware attention layer grounded in rigid-body mechanics. Tokens are related through the physical relation between bodies rather than an abstract graph, and messages are transported into the receiver’s coordinate frame. As a result, the computation of how motion propagates along the robot can be expressed by the layer rather than learned from data (Section III-D). Moreover, the layer can be used on its own or as a residual on top of an analytic controller.

An embodiment-aware attention layer grounded in rigid-body mechanics. Tokens are related through the physical relation between bodies rather than an abstract graph, and messages are transported into the receiver’s coordinate frame. As a result, the computation of how motion propagates along the robot can be expressed by the layer rather than learned from data (Section III-D). Moreover, the layer can be used on its own or as a residual on top of an analytic controller.

An extensive empirical study across diverse tasks and a standard benchmark. We evaluate our architecture on three simulated manipulation tasks and on LIBERO-Spatial, comparing it against mechanism-matched controls. The structured policy outperforms graph, transformer and flat networks of the same size on LIBERO-Spatial, and even surpasses a flat network with 27×27\times more parameters. Under changes to the per-link frame convention, it is the only model whose success is unchanged, whereas all controls collapse to 0.0–2.3%. Used on top of an analytic controller on a contact-rich insertion task, it raises the success rate by 17.3 points. These results show that the structure contributes capability (Sections IV, V and IV-G).

A hypothesis for when the structure is decisive. Across the tasks studied, we identify a simple condition under which the geometry affects performance: the structure is decisive when the task requires reasoning over relations between coordinate frames that are not otherwise supplied by an analytic controller. When this condition is met, correct relations yield large gains over incorrect ones. When it is not, the correctness of the relations makes no measurable difference. This hypothesis is consistent with all results reported here (Section V, Appendix H).

title: TOAST: Stochastic Robot Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Keisuke Shirai,Tomohiro Motoda,Hanbit Oh,Ryoichi Nakajo,Roman Mykhailyshyn,Ryo Hanai,Shotaro Miwa,Yukiyasu Domae
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract: Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action models often represent continuous robot actions as discrete token sequences, enabling action prediction with standard next-token objectives. FAST has substantially improved this representation by compactly encoding action containing diverse temporal frequencies into relatively few tokens. However, while such compression reduces the number of action tokens required for autoregressive prediction, it does not necessarily improve the efficiency of policy learning from limited demonstrations. In particular, FAST typically assigns a single deterministic tokenization to each quantized action sequence, although multiple token sequences can represent and decode to the same robot motion. We investigate whether exploiting this representational redundancy can improve policy learning. In this paper, we propose TOkenization of Action Sequences with STochastic Sampling (TOAST), a stochastic action tokenization method that samples alternative tokenizations of the same quantized action sequence during policy training. This diversifies the discrete supervision while preserving the underlying robot action and requires no additional demonstrations. Experiments on LIBERO show that TOAST consistently improves over its deterministic counterpart, with the improvement increasing as training data decreases, achieving a 6.8 point gain in success rate when only 1/161/16 of training data is available. Across four real-robot manipulation tasks, TOAST further improves mean success rate by 15.815.8 points over the deterministic counterpart. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of stochastic action tokenization for autoregressive robot policy learning, particularly when training data are limited.
introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs), backed by the success of imitation learning [1], have been drawing attention as an approach for realizing general-purpose robot policies [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Autoregressive VLAs [2, 5, 10, 9] are policies that use a backbone multimodal large language model (MLLM) to predict action sequences as tokens via next-token prediction. Autoregressive VLAs offer advantages over flow matching-based ones [6, 7] of having a simpler architecture [11], leveraging MLLM’s pre-trained knowledge effectively [12], and realizing faster convergence [10]. In building autoregressive VLAs, the tokenizer determines what the policy has to predict, and recent work has explored efficient compression of action chunks in two ways: learned vector quantization, as in VQ-VLA [13], or training-free frequency-based compression, as in FAST [10], which applies byte pair encoding (BPE) [14] to the quantized coefficients of a discrete cosine transform. Both make prediction easier by shortening the token sequence.

However, the tokenization boundaries produced by frequency-based compression such as BPE are not necessarily physically meaningful for robot actions. Once the vocabulary contains tokens spanning multiple quantized action values, the same quantized action sequence can be represented by different token sequences, all of which decode to exactly the same motion. Deterministic tokenizers nevertheless select a single tokenization according to corpus-level frequency statistics, and the policy is trained under cross-entropy to reproduce only that sequence. A similar ambiguity has long been recognized in natural language processing, where stochastic tokenization [15, 16, 17] mitigates over-reliance on a single segmentation and has shown particular benefits when training data are limited. This issue can be especially important in robot learning, where demonstrations are costly to collect. When only limited training data are available, repeatedly supervising each action sequence with the same deterministic tokenization may encourage the policy to overfit to specific token patterns or segmentation boundaries that are not uniquely tied to the underlying motion.

To address this issue, we propose TOkenization of Action Sequences with STochastic Sampling (TOAST), the first stochastic action tokenization framework for autoregressive robot policy learning. As shown in Figure 1, TOAST samples multiple tokenizations of the same action sequence during training, exposing the policy to different discrete representations while preserving the underlying motion. Moreover, because multiple valid token sequences can be obtained from each demonstration without collecting additional robot trajectories, TOAST increases the diversity of supervision available from limited data. We therefore hypothesize that stochastic action tokenization becomes increasingly beneficial when fewer demonstrations are available. We instantiate this framework with a unigram tokenizer that enables probabilistic segmentation, together with dimension-major flattening for frequency-based action sequence compression.

We evaluate this hypothesis through both controlled simulation and real-world manipulation task experiments. The results show that stochastic tokenization consistently improves policy performance over its deterministic counterpart across training-set sizes, flattening orders, and vocabulary corpora. Notably, the relative benefit of stochastic tokenization is greater when fewer demonstrations are available, indicating improved data efficiency in policy learning. We further observe substantial gains on real-robot manipulation tasks, where collecting demonstrations is particularly expensive. These results show that stochastic action tokenization provides a simple and effective means of extracting more useful supervision from limited robot demonstrations.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We identify deterministic action tokenization as a source of over-reliance on a single discrete representation and formulate stochastic tokenization as a representation-level regularization effect for autoregressive VLAs.

We introduce TOAST, which samples equivalent tokenizations of the same motion during training, yielding more diverse supervision from each demonstration without additional robot data.

1. We identify deterministic action tokenization as a source of over-reliance on a single discrete representation and formulate stochastic tokenization as a representation-level regularization effect for autoregressive VLAs.

2. We introduce TOAST, which samples equivalent tokenizations of the same motion during training, yielding more diverse supervision from each demonstration without additional robot data.

title: Real-Time Human-Adaptive Task Allocation for Multi-Human Multi-Robot Supervision
authors: Seabin Lee,Sujeong Park,Nayoung Kim,Sungjin Park,Haechan Jung,Changjoo Nam
comment: . This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
abstract: We propose a human-factor-aware method of allocating robot supervision tasks to multiple human operators. In scenarios where multiple operators occasionally teleoperate multiple robots to help the robots overcome difficulties, the allocation of the supervisory control tasks to humans needs to consider the real-time cognitive states of individual operators. However, most existing methods assume fixed supervisory capacity per operator and overlook fluctuations in the human factors such as workload and fatigue. As a result, workload distribution can be unbalanced where some operators become overloaded while the others remain underused. Our method dynamically regulates supervisory capacity and allocates tasks in a way that maintains balanced mental workload, prevents overload, and improves overall team performance. The allocation method uses a greedy strategy that minimizes estimated operator workloads with task prioritization. Robots are assigned to operators by reflecting their current supervisory capacity where the required effort depends on the types of tasks. In the user study, the analysis across predefined time intervals shows that the proposed method consistently achieves higher performance and lower behavioral signs of fatigue compared to a baseline method that does not consider human factors. These results highlight adaptive capacity adjustment as an effective preventive mechanism for sustaining operator performance in long-duration, high-demand settings.
introduction:
The deployment of multi-robot systems in real-world environments continues to expand, aiming toward full autonomy. Multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) increases throughput and coordination by determining which robot performs which task [1]. Although MRTA followed by task and motion planning advances autonomy, current systems still require human supervisors to intervene when robots fail to deal with unexpected events and dynamic changes [2]. Human supervision remains essential because it pairs robotic precision with human judgment and can enhance safety and accuracy. This means that another task allocation is required between human operators and the dynamically emerging supervision tasks.

However, there are only a few studies on multi-human task allocation in the context of supervising multi-robot systems, and the existing ones typically assume fixed throughput of the human operators, overlooking variations in workload, fatigue, and task performance [3, 4, 5]. This assumption would no longer be valid if a small number of operators supervise many robots, as human cognitive resources are fundamentally limited [2]. During prolonged supervision, workloads tend to increase and performance can decline, requiring the human interface to adapt to the cognitive and physiological states of operators in human-in-the-loop settings [6]. In addition, operators may differ in skill and performance even for the same type of tasks. Therefore, an effective human-task allocation must not only satisfy mission requirements but also account for real-time human factors and technical capacity.

We propose Human-factor-Aware Multi-robot Allocation (HAMA), an adaptive method for multi-human multi-robot (MHMR) supervision that maintains robot task performance while considering human states. As illustrated in Fig. 1, HAMA estimates human factors such as workload and fatigue and updates the supervisory capacity of each operator (i.e., the maximum number of tasks that can be supervised) at predefined time intervals. We focus on two task types that require supervisory intervention: multi-robot deadlock resolution and docking at charging stations, where failures frequently occur in real-world scenarios. For missions with changing task priorities, HAMA supports reallocation to prioritize more urgent robots over earlier assignments. HAMA also accounts for differences in human factors between task types and across operators by using Area-Of-Interest (AOI) dwell time to estimate visual demand. Then robots requiring teleoperation are assigned to operators based on task priority, visual demand, and current capacity.

HAMA introduces dynamic supervisory capacity that adapts to human factors and mission performance, replacing fixed capacity limits used in prior systems. By integrating subjective reports, behavioral indicators, and physiological signals into a unified update rule, HAMA provides individualized operator capacities and enables real-time robot–operator reallocation as middleware. In user studies, HAMA improved team performance by about 10% and reduced blink counts by 16% compared to a fixed-capacity baseline, demonstrating that adaptive capacity can increase multi-robot throughput while mitigating fatigue in long-duration, high-demand settings.

title: UniTrackPLA: Unified Panorama-Language-Action Model for Instruction-Guided Navigation and Dynamic Person Tracking
authors: Pengfei Qi,Haoran Lin,Sizhuang Chen,Kai Luo,Sirui Zhang,Xinqi Liu,Fei Cheng,Wenrui Chen,Liming Yin,Kailun Yang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Image and Video Processing (eess.IV)
comment: The project page is atthis https URL
abstract: General-purpose embodied robots should support both navigation toward language-specified destinations and dynamic person tracking under arbitrary initial target azimuths. However, existing methods typically rely on forward-facing observations and address these tasks with separate policies, limiting omnidirectional perception and unified closed-loop control. We present UniTrackPLA, a unified panorama-language-action model for instruction-guided navigation and dynamic person tracking. Its Panoramic-Aware Encoding (PAE) preserves the temporal and azimuthal structure of perspective views projected from each panorama, enabling perspective-pretrained visual encoders to process omnidirectional observations. A shared vision-language backbone grounds instructions in the panoramic context and predicts continuous robot-centric waypoint chunks for both tasks. World-Action Consistency (WAC) further predicts action-conditioned future visual states and verifies waypoint prefixes online, allowing reliable actions to be reused while triggering replanning upon inconsistency. We also introduce OmniTrackNav-Bench, comprising 5,0005,000 simulated tracking trajectories, 10,00010,000 simulated VLN routes, and 9696 verified real-world routes, providing 919,978919,978 waypoint-supervision instances. UniTrackPLA improves overall tracking SR from 23.50%23.50\% to 35.00%35.00\% and Omni-VLN SR/SPL from 13.00%13.00\%/12.77%12.77\% to 19.75%19.75\%/19.29%19.29\%. Incorporating 7676 real-world routes further improves held-out EP@0.2m from 42.92%42.92\% to 92.08%92.08\%. Closed-loop experiments on a Go2-W robot demonstrate unified panoramic tracking and navigation across indoor and outdoor environments. The project page is at https://tw5775.github.io/UniTrackPLA.
introduction:
Embodied navigation enables robots to move through an environment according to visual observations and task instructions, constituting a fundamental capability for household assistance, human accompaniment, inspection, and mobile manipulation [1, 2, 3, 4]. Existing studies, however, have largely evolved along two separate paradigms. Vision-language navigation mainly focuses on reaching static semantic goals specified by language instructions [5, 6, 7, 8], whereas embodied visual tracking emphasizes continuously following dynamic targets whose positions evolve over time [9, 10, 11, 12, 13].
Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action prediction, improving instruction following and generalization in unseen environments [2, 5, 9, 14].
Nevertheless, static-goal navigation and dynamic person tracking are still commonly treated separately, with task-specific observations, action spaces, and policies.

We argue that these two tasks should instead be viewed as complementary instances of a broader embodied navigation problem. Instruction-guided navigation is primarily driven by relatively static semantic goals, while person tracking requires continuous adaptation to dynamically evolving physical targets. Despite this difference, both require the robot to ground task-relevant entities, reason about their spatial relationships, and continuously translate visual-language observations into motion decisions.
A more general embodied navigation system should therefore be able to bridge these two regimes within a shared perception-language-action paradigm. This raises a fundamental question: can a single policy support both instruction-guided navigation toward static goals and continuous tracking of dynamic persons under a unified observation and action interface?

Bridging static navigation and dynamic tracking requires a shared omnidirectional perceptual representation.
Panoramic perception provides a natural means of removing this heading dependence by exposing the surrounding scene within a single omnidirectional observation space [2, 5, 15].
Prior studies have explored panoramic RGB-D observations [16, 17], omnidirectional images [18], multiple perspective views [7], panoramic environment generation [19, 20], and latent panorama prediction [8] for static-goal search and vision-language navigation. Recent approaches further incorporate panoramic scene parsing [21], dynamic memory [22], and global-to-local reasoning [23, 24]. Nevertheless, existing panoramic systems mainly focus on static object search, route following, and scene reasoning, while dynamic target localization across arbitrary orientations and panorama boundaries remains insufficiently explored. More importantly, panoramic observations introduce a representation gap: most pretrained visual encoders are optimized for perspective images, whereas panoramic perception requires explicit reasoning over circular spatial structure and temporal evolution. Therefore, the key challenge is not merely to enlarge the field of view, but to retain the transferable representations of pretrained perspective-image encoders while recovering the spatial and temporal structure required for unified panoramic embodied navigation.

A unified policy must also handle the different temporal dynamics of static navigation and dynamic tracking. Continuous waypoint heads improve efficiency by predicting short-horizon action chunks [5, 9], but fixed-horizon execution may become unreliable as the visual world evolves: trajectories that remain valid in relatively stable navigation can quickly become stale when a tracked person changes direction, local traversability changes, or execution errors accumulate. Executing the full chunk risks propagating invalid actions, while using only the first waypoint sacrifices most of the predicted trajectory. The key challenge is therefore how long a predicted trajectory should remain trusted. Since pixel-level world models are costly for real-time control [25, 26], we instead employ lightweight action-conditioned latent future prediction to adaptively regulate the execution horizon.

To bridge static instruction-guided navigation and dynamic person tracking across both perception and execution, we propose UniTrackPLA, a unified Panorama-Language-Action framework. UniTrackPLA formulates both tasks under shared panoramic observations and a continuous waypoint action space. Panoramic-Aware Encoding (PAE) captures visual content, view azimuth, and temporal position while preserving compatibility with pretrained perspective-image encoders, and a shared multimodal policy predicts waypoint chunks for both navigation and tracking. We introduce World-Action Consistency (WAC), which predicts action-conditioned future states in latent space and adaptively determines whether to continue the current chunk or replan, enabling efficient yet responsive closed-loop control.

To support unified training and evaluation, we construct OmniTrackNav-Bench, comprising Omni-Tracking with 5,0005,000 dynamic-following trajectories and Omni-VLN with 10,00010,000 language-annotated panoramic navigation routes. Both tasks share the same panoramic observation and continuous waypoint representation, enabling unified multi-task learning within a single policy. We introduce a real-world
panoramic navigation dataset comprising 9696 routes.

Closed-loop experiments show that UniTrackPLA achieves a 35.00%35.00\% success rate on Omni-Tracking, compared with 23.50%23.50\% for our reproduced TrackVLA
baseline, and reaches 19.75%19.75\% SR and 19.29%19.29\% SPL on Omni-VLN, outperforming the baseline results of 13.00%13.00\% and 12.77%12.77\%. Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of PAE and WAC. With this dataset, EP@0.2m
on held-out real-world routes improves from 42.92%42.92\% to 92.08%92.08\%. Real-world deployment on a Go2-W robot with an Insta360 X4 further demonstrates both dynamic person tracking and instruction-guided navigation
using the same policy.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose UniTrackPLA, a panoramic VLA framework that bridges dynamic person following and vision-language navigation through shared panoramic perception, visual-language representations, and a continuous waypoint action space. Its PAE module jointly models panoramic azimuth and temporal context while reusing pretrained perspective-image encoders.

We introduce a lightweight World-Action Consistency module that unifies temporal action execution across static navigation and dynamic tracking. By predicting the latent future consequences of waypoint prefixes, WAC adaptively regulates the effective action horizon and dynamically determines whether to continue the current chunk or trigger replanning.

We construct the OmniTrackNav-Bench to support joint training and consistent evaluation across static navigation and dynamic tracking, comprising Omni-Tracking for arbitrary-orientation human following and Omni-VLN for dense panoramic language navigation. Extensive simulation experiments and real-robot deployments validate the effectiveness and generality of the overall framework.

title: Kinematic MeanFlow: One-Step Action Generation Policy for Robotic Foundation Models
authors: Jiawei Fan,Sifeng Wang,Yuqing Hou,Anbang Yao
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract:
In this paper, we study how to achieve one-step action generation in Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs), aiming to overcome the high inference latency of multi-step flow matching. MeanFlow provides a promising framework for this goal, yet its direct application leads to performance collapse.
We discover that this stems from two distinctive dynamics exhibited in the RFM velocity field: (1) the “local acceleration” exhibits stability early on, but surges sharply towards the end of the denoising process, and (2) the spread of its magnitudes across samples widens as denoising progresses.
To address these issues, we introduce Kinematic MeanFlow (K-MF), a novel one-step action policy tailored for RFMs.
Specifically, grounded in a kinematic identity, K-MF decouples the time derivative term in the MeanFlow formulation into two sub-interval terms separated by an intermediate point.
This decoupled formulation enables the two terms to capture early-stage and late-stage denoising dynamics, respectively,
while mitigating the error amplification across the process.
As a result, our K-MF empowers RFMs to achieve one-step action generation in both training from scratch and fine-tuning paradigms across diverse tasks, while outperforming multi-step flow matching in most settings.
In terms of inference efficiency, K-MF reduces action-head latency of GR00T-N1.6 by 67.5%–74.4% across L40 and Jetson Orin in eager and compiled modes, yielding end-to-end latency reductions of 30.3%–54.9%. Code will be available at https://github.com/IntelChina-AI/K-MF.
introduction:
Background. Robotic foundation models (RFMs) aim to establish a generalist robot manipulation policy
capable of real-time execution across diverse robotic embodiments.
Driven by this vision, the architecture of RFMs has continuously evolved.
The first evolution concerns the multimodal backbone. Early RFMs (Jang et al., 2021; Brohan et al., 2023) employ FiLM-conditioned convolutional neural networks to fuse the language instructions and visual observations.
Spurred by the remarkable generalization capabilities of large/vision language models (LLMs/VLMs) (Touvron et al., 2023a; Touvron et al., 2023b; Beyer et al., 2024), some studies (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024) leverage them as the core foundation for RFMs. Generally, such architectures integrate a pre-trained VLM11
1
            
            
            
          For brevity, we use “VLM” to represent architectures that either employ a pre-trained VLM or pair a pre-trained LLM with a vision encoder, as their training and inference pipelines in RFMs are conceptually identical. as the backbone to autoregressively generate discrete action tokens. However, this creates a severe inference burden for real-time control and thus drives the second major evolution in action generation policies.
Recent RFMs (Black et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026) adopt transformer-based flow matching policies. Specifically, flow matching establishes a velocity field mapping Gaussian noise to valid actions.
Using features obtained from a single VLM forward pass, the policy iteratively queries the transformer to predict instantaneous velocities across denoising timesteps, progressively transforming noise into multiple actions in parallel.
Even as recent architectures (Ye et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026) explore replacing VLM backbones with diffusion transformers (DiTs),
flow matching remains the prevalent choice for action generation in RFMs.

Motivation. Although this policy enables parallel action generation, its iterative forward passes required for denoising incur non-negligible inference overhead. Taking GR00T-N1.6 as an example, action head latency occupies about 40% of the end-to-end (E2E) inference time on desktop GPUs (e.g., NVIDIA L40) and up to 50% on robotic edge platforms (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson Orin).
In other words, the computational burden of the action head critically reduces the overall decision frequency of RFMs.
Therefore, reducing the number of denoising steps becomes a critical issue.
From a broader perspective, MeanFlow has recently emerged in image generation as a remarkably simple alternative to complex distillation or consistency constraints for one-step generation. Unlike flow matching that predicts instantaneous velocity 𝐯t\mathbf{v}_{t} at timestep tt, MeanFlow aims to learn the average velocity 𝐮t,r\mathbf{u}_{t,r}22
2
            
            
            
          Here, t,r∈[0,1]t,r\in[0,1], with 00 denoting clean data
and 11 denoting pure noise. We use 𝐮t,r\mathbf{u}_{t,r} as shorthand
for 𝐮⁡(𝐳t,r,t)\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{z}_{t},r,t), formally introduced in
Section 3. Throughout this paper, we adopt
the subscript order (t,r)(t,r) to reflect the denoising
direction from tt to rr, although the average velocity
is defined from rr to tt. between any two timesteps tt and rr.
Once trained, by directly predicting the average velocity across the endpoint timesteps, the model achieves one-step denoising in a single forward pass. In action generation, there have been a few efforts that built upon the MeanFlow formulation.
In imitation learning, MP1 (Sheng et al., 2026) couples 3D inputs with a dispersive loss on latent features to prevent representation collapse. Other studies improve MeanFlow in reinforcement learning (RL).
MVP (Zhan et al., 2026) introduces an instantaneous velocity constraint to stabilize RL training; MeanflowQL (Wang et al., 2026) reformulates MeanFlow into a residual mapping to enable joint optimization with Q-learning; DMPO (Zou et al., 2026) combines dispersive regularization with PPO fine-tuning for one-step policy learning. These efforts remain focused on specialist policies, where directly applying MeanFlow typically yields viable, albeit degraded, performance. In contrast, we empirically find that MeanFlow breaks down under the standard training recipe in generalist RFMs, motivating us to investigate the fundamental issues underlying this failure.

Observations and underlying issues. In principle, the ground-truth average velocity between tt and rr is defined as the time-averaged integral of instantaneous velocities.
To avoid the costly integration, MeanFlow reformulates the learning target to a form that evaluates locally at timestep tt: average velocity 𝐮t,r\mathbf{u}_{t,r} equals the combination of instantaneous velocity 𝐯t\mathbf{v}_{t} and the time derivative term dd​t​𝐮t,r\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,r} (see Eq. 3).
As 𝐯t\mathbf{v}_{t} remains constant for a given sample during training, the time derivative term primarily drives the optimization.
To investigate the challenges of adapting MeanFlow to RFMs, we compare the dynamics of “local acceleration” (Δ​𝐮/Δ​t\Delta\mathbf{u}/\Delta t) between image generation and action generation in RFMs across denoising timesteps. As shown in Figure 1(a), the local acceleration of image generation is stable throughout denoising with a narrow spread. In contrast, RFMs exhibit distinctive dynamics, characterized by two key observations with corresponding issues:

The local acceleration surges sharply in the late denoising stage (i.e., t<0.3t<0.3), ultimately reaching 76×76\times its initial value at t=1t=1. Issue 1: The time derivative term tends to incur substantial estimation errors if the model fails to infer the global trend from local observations33
3
                  
                  
                  
                Local acceleration reflects dd​t​𝐮t,r\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,r} (t−r<ϵt-r<\epsilon), whose temporal stability decides local-global consistency..

The spread of local acceleration magnitude widens as denoising proceeds (indicated by the expanding red shaded area). Our further analysis in Figure 5 reveals that the extent of this spread is strongly correlated with the task diversity of the RFM training data.
Issue 2: Minor estimation errors in the early denoising stage tend to be amplified as this spread widens.

Design insights and contributions. Our method builds on a fundamental kinematic identity: for any intermediate point c∈(r,t)c\in(r,t), the average velocity 𝐮t,r\mathbf{u}_{t,r} is exactly equal to the convex combination of the average velocities over the two sub-intervals 𝐮t,c\mathbf{u}_{t,c} and 𝐮c,r\mathbf{u}_{c,r}.
Leveraging this identity, we decouple the derivative dd​t​𝐮t,r\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,r} into two sub-interval terms, dd​t​𝐮t,c\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,c} and dd​c​𝐮c,r\frac{d}{dc}\mathbf{u}_{c,r}. This is primarily driven by two considerations: (1) for the first issue, the term dd​t​𝐮t,c\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,c} guarantees robust estimation in the early denoising stage, while dd​c​𝐮c,r\frac{d}{dc}\mathbf{u}_{c,r} focuses exclusively on corrections in the late denoising stage; (2) for the second issue, a second estimation at timestep cc serves as an anchor to reduce the impact of the widening spread and thereby mitigate error amplification throughout the denoising process.
Given this decomposition, we further investigate how to determine the intermediate point cc. We empirically find that a fixed midpoint clearly outperforms uniform random sampling, despite the latter covering a broader range of interval partitions. This suggests that the placement of the estimation anchor, rather than partition diversity, is critical.
We then introduce a learnable strategy that adaptively determines cc conditioned on tt and rr, yielding the best performance among the considered strategies.
Building on these components, we propose a simple but effective one-step action generation policy tailored for RFMs, termed Kinematic MeanFlow (K-MF). With K-MF, RFMs can generate actions in a single step, achieving comparable performance to the multi-step flow matching policy. This is validated by our systematic experiments across: (1) two training paradigms, including training from scratch and fine-tuning of pre-trained flow-matching RFMs; (2) different RFMs, including GR00T-N1.6 and SimVLA; (3) four datasets with varying training data scales, ranging from 658 to 87K trajectories; and (4) both Sim2Sim and Real2Sim evaluation settings.

title: Are Frontier VLM Agents Ready to Be Robot Generalists? An Empirical Study with the Embodied Agent Arena
authors: Haojian Huang,Pukun Zhao,Zexi Li,Yehang Zhang,Yangkai Wei,Wenqian Li,Han Yang,Kaiwen Zhou,Ying-Cong Chen,Yinchuan Li
comment: including appendices. Project page:this https URL
abstract: Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) combine scene estimation, interaction grounding, and executable actions. Understanding how these abilities support complete robotic tasks is central to evaluating their readiness as robot generalists. We introduce Embodied Agent Arena to examine where local competence supports, or falls short of, complete task success across Geometry, Spatial Reasoning, Affordance, Task Planning, and Manipulation. The arena contains 1,000 cases drawn from 32 established sources and GeoProbe, our new benchmark for geometric estimation on Blender renders and real-scene images. A minimal harness preserves source observations and operations while separating metric precision, functional grounding, and native goal completion. We evaluate seven VLMs, analyze Astra’s task-specific advantages, and compare richer-observation execution protocols and multi-round review. Across the arena, Astra’s advantage is strongest in precise estimation and usable-contact localization; completing coordinated, goal-directed actions remains the key gap to robot generalism.
introduction:
A robot generalist must turn scene understanding into actions that satisfy a complete goal. Estimating where an object lies, selecting a usable contact, and executing a grasp are useful abilities, yet none establishes that the object reaches its required destination. Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly address spatial relations (Ma et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2024) and action-relevant grounding (Wang et al., 2025a, Song et al., 2024). Learned visuomotor policies connect observations to robot actions (Kim et al., 2024, Black et al., 2024), while language-model controllers select skills or generate executable programs (Ahn et al., 2022, Liang et al., 2022). Frontier VLM agents now combine observation, programming, and feedback-driven decisions (Fu et al., 2026, Guo et al., 2026), making the relationship between local competence and complete execution a practical evaluation question.

Capability breadth and reliable completion require different evidence. An average score can hide whether errors concern metric scale, an object’s reference frame, or the final condition of a placement. Conversely, a terminal failure can conceal useful progress. Evaluating these outcomes separately reveals what a model can do and which additional requirements remain unsatisfied. Generalist readiness therefore calls for both cross-capability comparisons and task-level diagnoses.

We ask: Are frontier VLM agents ready to be robot generalists? Embodied Agent Arena evaluates the same models across Geometry, Spatial Reasoning, Affordance, Task Planning, and Manipulation (Figure 1). Its 1,000 cases combine 32 established sources with GeoProbe, our geometric-estimation benchmark. GeoProbe varies camera motion, object motion, and scale references to test which quantities remain accurately estimated as visual conditions change. A minimal harness preserves source observations and operations. Continuous errors, task-specific evidence, and terminal success reveal complementary aspects of agent capability.

Our comparisons locate the remaining gap in task requirements: Astra produces the closest paths yet often misses their endpoints, and its local manipulation strengths coexist with low household-goal completion. Under matched budgets and execution limits, richer visual observations reverse Astra’s CALVIN lead while producing gains on other tasks. A separate multi-round review study measures which answers improve after reinspection or specialist measurements. Our contributions are:

An evaluation perspective centered on task requirements. We distinguish local estimates and interaction evidence from complete goal satisfaction across five robotic capability domains.

A unified arena with a new geometric benchmark, GeoProbe. We combine 32 established sources with 168 GeoProbe cases, using controlled Blender scenes and real images to diagnose camera, motion, depth, and scale estimation.

A capability baseline for frontier VLM agents. We characterize seven agents across five robotic application domains within specified inference-time and execution budgets, with task-level comparisons and a deep dive into Astra’s strengths and failure modes.

1. An evaluation perspective centered on task requirements. We distinguish local estimates and interaction evidence from complete goal satisfaction across five robotic capability domains.

2. A unified arena with a new geometric benchmark, GeoProbe. We combine 32 established sources with 168 GeoProbe cases, using controlled Blender scenes and real images to diagnose camera, motion, depth, and scale estimation.

3. A capability baseline for frontier VLM agents. We characterize seven agents across five robotic application domains within specified inference-time and execution budgets, with task-level comparisons and a deep dive into Astra’s strengths and failure modes.

title: Reactive Humanoid Multi-Contact Using Learned Stability Models
authors: Stephen McCrory,Beomyeong Park,Nicholas Kitchel,Nehar Poddar,Robert Griffin
abstract: We present a planning and control approach to reactively use hand contacts to stabilize a humanoid in low stability scenarios, where only using feet contacts may result in a fall. Candidate contacts are sampled within the robot’s reachable workspace, and a preview is computed by rolling out the centroidal dynamics through pre-impact, impact and post-impact phases. Sampled points are scored based on the Center of Pressure (CoP) control authority at the post-impact phase. Central to our approach is a learned model of the robot’s CoP region during post-impact, which enables rapid evaluation of candidate contact points compared to traditional optimization-based methods. The presented planner has two stages: the first selects an optimal bracing region and the second computes an optimal bracing point within the region. Our simulation results demonstrate an average increase in impulse resilience of 89% over recovery without hand contacts and 17% over a naive planning strategy (closest reachable region). We validate our framework on hardware, performing push tests while standing and walking. The standing trials show an average 43% reduction in stabilization time compared to naive hand placement and the walking trials demonstrate a 18% reduction compared to baseline recovery (without hand contacts).
introduction:
As humanoid robots become capable of performing tasks in real-world scenarios, reliability becomes increasingly important. For this reason, push recovery has a rich history in legged robotics, with the broad goal of maximizing robustness [12, 24, 7, 16]. However, in spite of numerous successful strategies for bipedal push recovery, existing approaches are largely restricted to quasi-flat terrain and feet contacts. Making full use of the humanoid form-factor means utilizing upper body contacts to augment lower-body recovery techniques. Additionally, it requires models that go beyond quasi-flat terrain and handle arbitrary contact surfaces.

In this work, we propose a sample-based hand contact planner that reactively braces in low stability scenarios where the use of only foot contacts may result in a fall, such as the scenario in Fig. 1. Sampled contact points are previewed by rolling out the robot’s centroidal dynamics through pre-impact, impact and post-impact phases. The pre-impact and impact phases can be rolled out using conventional closed-form models such as the Linear Inverted Pendulum Model (LIPM) [12]. In contrast, the post-impact contact state cannot be modeled as a basic LIPM, but instead using optimization-based models that are compatible with arbitrary contact sets [3, 21]. Each roll-out is scored based on the Center of Pressure (CoP) control authority at the post-impact phase.

A central part of our approach is a set of neural networks that predict the feasible CoP placement at the post-impact rollout phase. We train these models using reference CoP data computed through conventional optimization-based techniques. These networks enable rapid evaluation of the robot’s post-impact state, with around 40×\times speed-up compared to optimization-based techniques. We apply these networks in a contact planner which performs two passes for each hand. The first pass selects the optimal bracing surface by scoring the closest reachable point on each candidate surface. The second pass samples within the optimal surface (if one exists) to compute the optimal bracing point.

Reactive contact planning for legged robots has been widely studied, with many successful hardware demonstrations. Reduced-order models such as the Linear Inverted Pendulum Model [12], the Angular Linear Inverted Pendulum [10] and Single Rigid Body Model [13] enable efficient previews of the robot’s centroidal dynamics. In turn, these models have been leveraged in heuristics for step placement, such as Raibert’s heuristic [25] and the Capture Point [24, 8]. Since these heuristics have closed-form linear representations, they have been applied in mixed-integer frameworks that select optimal contact surfaces online [1, 14, 29, 5]. Following this approach, Mason et al. [18] reactively plan hand contacts by first previewing a footstep sequence containing a slack variable for centroidal tracking. If this slack variable is sufficiently high, a solver activates which scores candidate hand contacts based on a recovery preview, given a heuristic maximum hand pushing force. Such applications of centroidal models have been successful, but have the caveat of requiring linear or quadratic functions to encode cost and constraints and often are applied only to quasi-flat terrains.

A related line of research addresses motion feasibility under arbitrary contact conditions given unilateral, friction and actuation constraints. Seminal work by Bretl et al. [3] posed this as a Linear Program, enabling efficient quasi-static stability assessment. This approach has been extended towards improving solve times [6], addressing dynamic stability [2] and modeling actuation constraints [21]. Marucci et al. apply a similar model to multi-contact planning on a piecewise affine map [17]. Other centroidal-based reactive recovery strategies have explored adapting gait frequency and posture to achieve high stability [15, 9].

There have also been machine-learning based approaches that aim to model stability and assess contact sequences. One approach, and the one taken in this work, is training a network to mimic an expensive optimization-based stability model [22]. Alternatively, Lin et al. use simulation data to train a set of networks to predict zero- and one-step capturability, given a robot’s state and environment [16]. These networks are applied in a graph-search that optimizes for predicted success in the presence of disturbances, such that the robot walks nearby potential bracing surfaces. This approach of using procedurally generated simulation environments has seen many applications in legged motion planning [4, 19]. Rouxel et al. use datasets from teleoperated hardware experiments to train a network to load/unload a humanoid’s hand based on predicted stability [26].

This work builds on the core concepts of reduced-order models to achieve reflexive response times, while maintaining accurate stability modeling under arbitrary contact conditions by applying learned stability models. Our work particularly builds on the MPC-style bracing planner by Mason et al. [18] and the concept of optimal region selection by Corbères et al. [5]. In building on these approaches, this work contains the following novel contributions.

A reactive (≤\leq10 ms) contact planner that models recovery for arbitrary (e.g. tilted or vertical) surfaces.

A reactive (≤\leq10 ms) contact planner that models recovery for arbitrary (e.g. tilted or vertical) surfaces.

A set of neural network models that predict the robot’s feasible CoP placement given arbitrary combinations of hand and feet contacts.

Simulation demonstrations of the planner’s capability to out-perform a naive heuristic through a comparison of the minimum unrejectable impulse.

Hardware demonstrations of the planner and controller’s capacity to use hand contacts to recover from high impulses.

1. A reactive (≤\leq10 ms) contact planner that models recovery for arbitrary (e.g. tilted or vertical) surfaces.

2. A set of neural network models that predict the robot’s feasible CoP placement given arbitrary combinations of hand and feet contacts.

3. Simulation demonstrations of the planner’s capability to out-perform a naive heuristic through a comparison of the minimum unrejectable impulse.

4. Hardware demonstrations of the planner and controller’s capacity to use hand contacts to recover from high impulses.

title: TRACE: Privacy-Preserving Next-Best-View Selection over Distributed 3D Gaussian-Splat Maps
authors: Amirhossein Mollaei Khass,Athanasios Cosse,Qiyu Sun,Nader Motee
abstract:
Share the light, not the map. We study next-best-view selection for a team of robots,
each of which builds its own 3D Gaussian Splatting map and keeps it private. A robot
picks the view with the largest expected information gain (EIG) about the splats along
its own path. This gain depends on the other maps. Their splats occlude its own and shine behind them,
so the gain has to be evaluated against the pooled map. No robot has this map. We show that the coupling passes through only two ray quantities, the transmittance
in front of a splat and the radiance behind it, and that both are sums over the hits of
the ray. Hence, they decompose across the robots and each robot sums them over depth bins in its own map, along the rays of a
candidate view, and sends the sums with their pose derivatives. The robot planning the
view turns them into its EIG and gradient on S​O​(3)SO(3). Transmittance and Radiance
Aggregates, Communicated for the EIG, give the protocol its name: TRACE. No robot shares its splats, and the message
size does not grow with a map. We prove that the reconstruction is exact unless a depth
bin behind a splat mixes hits of two robots, and we bound the error otherwise. Over 100
next-best-view decisions in Habitat-Sim, TRACE picks a heading within 15∘15^{\circ} of the
centralized one in 83.3%83.3\% of the cases, and its views reach 97.9%97.9\% of the
centralized EIG.
introduction:
A team of robots enters a building after an earthquake. Each robot maps what it sees and
plans where to look next, in order to reconstruct the part of the scene it must traverse
well enough to move through safely. The difficulty is that no robot sees everything it
needs from where it stands. The far side of a corner ahead of it is already behind a
second robot, and the top of a shelf it passes under was seen by a third that flew over
it. Such viewpoints are out of reach, yet they hold the geometry that keeps the first
robot safe. The value of a view is therefore a team
quantity [1, 2, 3]. A robot that scores its views on its
own map alone looks where the team has already looked, and still misses what it cannot
see. Coordinating these views is hard under limited bandwidth, energy and
computation [4, 5, 6].

We build these maps with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [7]. A 3DGS map is
a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives, and a view is rendered by projecting them onto
the image plane and compositing them front to back along each
ray [8, 9]. The render is differentiable in the parameters of the
map and in the pose of the camera. Next-best-view (NBV) methods exploit this property to
pick poses that reduce the uncertainty of the
map [10, 11, 12, 13]. The rendering Jacobian
gives the sensitivities that build a Fisher information objective, which is then optimized over the pose.

In a team of robots, this objective couples the maps at the level of the render. A
centralized method sends the observations or the local maps to a server, which builds
one 3DGS map and evaluates the team objective on
it [14, 15]. A distributed
method keeps them on board, and then no robot holds the whole scene. Along a shared ray,
the contribution of a primitive depends on the light that reaches it through the hits in
front of it, and on the radiance behind it. Both are set by the joint depth order of all
primitives on the ray, which no robot knows from its own map. A robot that renders only
its own map therefore biases the objective and its gradient.

We propose TRACE, a distributed NBV method that rebuilds these two quantities without
sharing observations or Gaussian parameters. Along the rays of a candidate view, each
robot reports the transmittance and radiance aggregates
communicated for the EIG, which is where the name comes from. These
aggregates are sums over depth bins. Hence, they carry what the other maps place along a
ray without revealing which splats placed it. Each robot then evaluates the pooled-map
gradient on its own and turns its camera, with no consensus over viewpoints.

Main contributions.
(i) We show that the EIG of a view, and its pose-gradient, depend on the maps of the
other robots only through two quantities on each ray, the transmittance in front of a
splat and the radiance behind it. (ii) We derive the pose-gradient of the masked EIG on
S​O​(3)SO(3) in closed form from the outputs of a standard rasterizer. (iii) We propose
TRACE, a protocol in which the robots exchange these two quantities in depth bins, with
their pose derivatives, and never their splats; the message size does not depend on the
number of splats. (iv) We prove that the EIG and its gradient are exact when no depth
bin behind a splat mixes hits of two robots, and we bound the error otherwise. (v) We
test TRACE in simulation against the centralized computation.

Related work.
NBV methods select camera poses that maximize information gain or improve coverage.
FisherRF [10] scores a view by the trace of a diagonal Fisher information
matrix, and COVER [13] builds an efficient coverage surrogate from an
approximation of it. GAVIS [11] models view-dependent uncertainty with an
anisotropic visibility field, and RT-GuIDE [16] uses the updates of the
Gaussian parameters as a cheap information proxy. Others add risk-aware
masks [17] or couple information gathering with safety-critical
control [18, 19]. Across a team, views are classically picked from
finite candidate sets by greedy submodular maximization on one shared
map [20]. All of these score a view on a map the planner can access.
Multi-agent neural mapping solves the other half of the problem, which is to build one
consistent model from distributed observations. Di-NeRF [1] trains a NeRF by
consensus and RAMEN [6] maps asynchronously. For 3DGS,
MAGiC-SLAM [5] merges local submaps by loop closures,
MAC-Ego3D [2] enforces geometric consistency by Gaussian consensus, and
CoMA-SLAM [14] works on Gaussian
surfels, while others cut communication with compact
submaps [4, 15]. All of these build one map of the whole scene.
Closest to our goal is distributed risk-averse NBV over 3DGS
maps [3], where each robot scores its views on its own map and
consensus reconciles the team. That work distributes the optimization, and the splats of the other robots never enter a local render. TRACE distributes the render instead. No global map is formed, and each robot evaluates the gain of the pooled map from what it receives along the rays of its own view.

title: Getting Out and Getting Back: World and Behavior Grounding in Real2Sim2Real Co-Training
authors: Samuel Liu,Youngsun Kim,Martin Matak,Gilwoo Lee
abstract: Simulation can expand scarce real demonstrations for co-training, yet how world fidelity and similarity to human behavior affect policy performance remains unclear. We distinguish world grounding, which aligns simulation with the real system, and behavior grounding, which aligns simulated trajectories with human motion. We build a real2sim2real pipeline that varies these axes independently to generate data for co-training. On a dynamic dexterous pick-and-sort task, fully grounded co-training raises success from 52% to 86%; averaged across configurations, world grounding improves success by 18 percentage points and behavior grounding by 10. Deployed policies behave like a mixture of real-derived and simulation-derived policies, imitating real demonstrations in covered states and relying on simulated behavior elsewhere, which we examine through latent-space analysis. Together, these results suggest complementary roles: world grounding lets policies use simulated experience beyond real-data coverage, while behavior grounding matters mainly when world grounding is imperfect. Grounded simulation remains beneficial when co-training foundation models.
introduction:
Human demonstrations, particularly teleoperation, are a primary source of data for robot learning [1, 28]. This is especially valuable for dexterous manipulation, where rewards are hard to design and high-dimensional space makes exploration difficult for reinforcement learning [18]. However, collecting diverse and high-quality demonstrations is costly [21, 16, 5, 15, 12], while variations across demonstrations can introduce inconsistency [16, 28].

Simulation offers a way to achieve both diversity and quality. From a small set of real demonstrations, simulation data can be generated at scale, with domain randomization adding diversity [23, 15] while success filtering preserves quality [15]. Such data have been shown to be especially valuable when co-trained alongside real data, even when real data is scarce [25, 14].

However, simulated and real data inevitably differ. To better understand the downstream effect of the sim2real gap, we separate the grounding of the simulation data into two axes: World Grounding and Behavior Grounding. The world gap lies in how the simulator’s rendering, physics, and robot control differ from the real system, while the behavior gap lies in how simulated trajectories differ from human demonstrations. Existing real2sim2real pipelines ground simulation in real environments and demonstrations through environment reconstruction, motion refinement, and demonstration adaptation [24, 8, 15]. Although these approaches improve policy performance, the individual and combined contributions of world fidelity and human-like behavior remain unclear.

We hypothesize that world grounding is the primary factor in co-trained policy performance since it determines whether actions learned in simulation have the same effect on the real robot. However, because world grounding is never perfect in practice, behavior grounding plays an important role in keeping simulated behavior close to real demonstrations, which the policy can fall back on.

We investigate the impact of world grounding and behavior grounding on policy performance on a dynamic dexterous pick-and-sort task with objects on a moving conveyor belt. We build a real2sim2real pipeline in which each axis can be independently set to grounded or ungrounded, letting us conduct a 2×2 factorial experiment. Policies for all four configurations are co-trained on 100 real demonstrations and 1,500 simulated episodes and evaluated over 50 real-world rollouts that include both nominal and shifted conditions.

Our main contributions are the following:

Independent grounding control. We introduce a pipeline that separates world and behavior grounding, enabling a controlled study of their individual and combined effect on dynamic dexterous manipulation.

Transition between real-derived and simulation-derived behavior. We observe that co-trained policies switch between the two within a rollout, adopting simulated behavior in states covered only by simulation, even when it differs substantially from human behavior.

Relevance to foundation models. We show that grounded simulation still benefits post-trained foundation models, extending these findings beyond policies trained from scratch.

1. Independent grounding control. We introduce a pipeline that separates world and behavior grounding, enabling a controlled study of their individual and combined effect on dynamic dexterous manipulation.

2. Transition between real-derived and simulation-derived behavior. We observe that co-trained policies switch between the two within a rollout, adopting simulated behavior in states covered only by simulation, even when it differs substantially from human behavior.

3. Relevance to foundation models. We show that grounded simulation still benefits post-trained foundation models, extending these findings beyond policies trained from scratch.
