title: ECoMEM: Explicit Concept Memory for Memory-Dependent Robot Control
authors: Yize Liu,Ke Wang,Mac Schwager,Yiqing Xu,Jiajun Wu
comment: Project website:this https URL
abstract:
A robot may lose sight of an object it must later retrieve, need to recall
what a person demonstrated earlier, or track which steps of a task it has
already completed. Current vision–language–action (VLA) policies often
fail once the information needed for action disappears from the current
observation, making memory critical for long-horizon robot behavior.
Existing approaches typically provide longer histories or learn implicit
memory from observation–action trajectories. But action supervision tells
a policy how to act, not what to remember: it does not specify
which past facts should persist or how they should change as new evidence
arrives. We therefore separate maintaining an evidence-grounded account of
the past from learning how to act on it. This insight motivates
Explicit Concept Memory (ECoMEM), which represents task-relevant
history with a reusable library of grounded concepts. An evidence-based
Writer selects and updates these records, while a learned Reader turns
them into memory tokens that directly condition the VLA. Across 16 RoboMME tasks, ECoMEM leads the evaluated robot policies on
15 tasks. On two new real-robot tasks, the same memory library either
transfers directly or requires only one new concept, achieving 86.1%86.1\%
success versus 8.6%8.6\% for a no-memory VLA. These results show that
explicit concepts provide a reusable and extensible memory interface for
robot control. Project website.
introduction:
A robot that acts over extended periods cannot treat every observation
as a fresh start. It may need to remember where an object was last seen
after it becomes occluded, which object a person interacted with earlier,
what parts of a task have already been completed, or the order in which
previous events occurred. In each case, the information needed for the
next action is no longer available in the current observation. Yet the
relevant past is often much smaller than the full interaction history:
what matters is a compact set of task-relevant facts about entities,
states, events, and progress.

Vision–language–action (VLA) policies increasingly incorporate history
through extended context, recurrent representations, learned memory
banks, and test-time adaptation (Torne et al., 2025; Koo et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026).
These mechanisms can preserve rich perceptual history, but they leave an
important question implicit: what from that history should become
memory? Action supervision specifies what the robot should do, but not
which past facts should be retained, when a belief should be revised, or
when two observations correspond to the same event. When memory is
learned only through the control objective, the policy may instead rely
on shortcuts in current observations, previous actions, or
trajectory-specific correlations (de Haan et al., 2019; Wen et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025). Successful action prediction therefore does not by
itself establish that the task-relevant history has been represented
reliably.

Making memory explicit helps, but does not remove the problem of memory
construction. Keyframe memories preserve visual evidence
 (Yang et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2025), leaving the policy to recover the
relevant facts from stored images. VLM-based approaches summarize
histories (Sridhar et al., 2026; Anwar et al., 2025), but place entity tracking,
state estimation, and temporal interpretation inside long-video
reasoning, where spatial and temporal errors remain challenging
 (Qi et al., 2025; Seth et al., 2025). Textual world states
 (Yoneda et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023) and scene graphs
 (Gu et al., 2024; Rana et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025) provide more structured
representations, but a robotic memory must additionally decide how
observations become persistent facts: what should survive occlusion,
what should be revised, what constitutes a completed event, and how
repeated evidence should be reconciled.

Our key idea is to separate maintaining an evidence-grounded
account of the past from learning how to act on it. Rather than
asking the policy to infer memory implicitly from history, we represent
task-relevant history as explicit facts about entities, states,
completed events, progress, and temporal order. These facts are updated
only when supported by visual and robot-state evidence, while the policy
learns how they should influence action. This separation also keeps task
requirements distinct from observations: the instruction specifies what
should be achieved, while memory records what has actually happened.

We instantiate this principle in Explicit Concept Memory
(ECoMEM), an explicit memory channel for VLA policies
(Figure 2). First, a shared concept library provides reusable
memory primitives spanning entity and spatial grounding, state and
relations, events and progress, and temporal and procedural structure.
Second, an evidence-based Writer selects the concepts required by
the instruction, grounds them to task entities, and maintains their
records over time, while a learned Reader maps the resulting
structured memory into latent tokens. Third, these memory tokens directly
condition the VLA alongside visual and language inputs. Recognition and
memory writing remain fixed during policy training, so evidence determines
what is remembered, while action supervision learns how that
memory should be used.

Across the 16 memory-dependent tasks of RoboMME (Dai et al., 2026),
ECoMEM achieves the highest average success among the evaluated robot
policies and leads on 15 of 16 tasks. Controlled experiments show that
spatial grounding, event and progress information, temporal structure,
task-conditioned selection, and language grounding each contribute to
effective memory construction. More importantly, the same abstraction
transfers to new physical-robot tasks: CupSwitch reuses the
existing library without adding a new recognizer, while
ScoopPour requires only one new event concept composed with the
existing memory machinery. Across shared real-robot conditions, ECoMEM succeeds in 68/7968/79 trials (86.1%86.1\%), compared with 5/585/58 (8.6%8.6\%)
for the no-memory π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline. These results suggest that
explicit, compositional concepts can serve not merely as task-specific
memory annotations, but as a reusable and extensible interface between
a robot’s accumulated experience and learned control.

title: DITTO-X: Forward and Reverse Teleoperation for Dexterous Manipulation and Human Intervention
authors: Zhanpeng He,Joaquin Palacios,Zhangyu Wang,Chenhao Li,Katelyn Lee,Matei Ciocarlie,C. Karen Liu,Jiajun Wu
abstract:
Teleoperated demonstrations are a primary source of data for robot manipulation, and teleoperated interventions are a primary mechanism for correcting policies at deployment. Yet most teleoperation systems close the loop through vision alone and are built around parallel-jaw grippers, limiting both what the robot can execute and what the operator can express through it.
This is most damaging in shared autonomy, where the operator sees the scene only through occluded cameras and must take over a dexterous hand mid-task, often with an object already grasped.
We present DITTO-X, a hand-agnostic dexterous teleoperation interface that renders joint-level force and fingertip contact events from sensing already on the robot hand, and drives three commercial dexterous hands (Sharpa, Wuji, and Inspire) without per-hand redesign. Because the exoskeleton is actuated, DITTO-X also supports reverse teleoperation, in which the robot back-drives the operator’s fingers into its own configuration before control is transferred, so the human enters the loop already matched to the state they inherit. Our results show that DITTO-X improves demonstration quality and throughput over a commercial hand-tracking glove, both in regular data collection and in human intervention during policy deployment for contact-rich manipulation tasks.
introduction:
Teleoperation plays a fundamental role in modern robotics, letting humans directly supervise, guide, and demonstrate complex manipulation tasks [1, 2]. In robot learning, teleoperated demonstrations remain a critical complement to scripted motion, human video, and handheld collection devices [3, 4], capturing the precise, contact-rich interactions that passive or ungrounded approaches struggle to reproduce. At deployment time, shared autonomy and human-in-the-loop frameworks rely on teleoperation to let operators intervene at uncertain or safety-critical moments [5, 6, 7], and the interventions they produce can be used to improve the policy.

Despite their widespread use, most teleoperation systems are poorly matched to dexterous manipulation. They are built around parallel-jaw grippers, which bound the natural movement an operator can demonstrate in the first place, and they close the loop through vision alone. Humans do not manipulate this way; we regulate contact forces, detect incipient slip, and reshape a grasp from cues we feel rather than see. Without those cues, the operator is blind to contact, and demonstrations are rendered slow and conservative. The limitation is therefore not only what the robot can execute, but also what the human can express through it.

This limitation becomes a failure mode in shared autonomy. When collecting demonstrations from scratch, the operator can both position themselves to see the scene and restart a failed attempt at little cost. Intervening on a running policy affords neither. Perception is restricted to onboard cameras, under which self-occlusion by the arm and hand is often unavoidable, especially at critical contact moments. The operator also inherits the robot’s state mid-task, so the kinematic mismatch between the human hand and the robot hand must be resolved at that exact moment. During tool use or in-hand manipulation, a non-smooth transition at takeover is enough to drop or break the object, resulting in unrecoverable failures.

We present DITTO-X, a dexterous interface for transparent teleoperation that works across different robotic hands for both regular data collection and human intervention. Improving the design of DITTO [8], which requires strict 1-to-1 kinematics between leader and follower and instruments only two fingers, DITTO-X is a hand-agnostic framework and currently drives three commercial, five-finger dexterous hands (Sharpa Wave, Wuji 2, and Inspire RH56DFX) without per-hand redesign. It closes the feedback loop at two levels: sustained joint-level force via motors on the exoskeleton and discrete fingertip contact events via haptics from sensing already available on the robot hand. This allows the operator to feel both when contact is made and how hard the robotic hand is squeezing, restoring cues that vision-only interfaces lack.

Our actuated exoskeleton can also be used to improve human intervention through a novel operating mode we call “reverse teleoperation”: while an operator is supervising an autonomous policy deployment, the exoskeleton can actively drive the operator’s fingers to match the robot’s current configuration. This allows for a seamless transition of control once the operator takes over and gives them a kinesthetic sense of the policy actions.

Our user study and policy learning results show that DITTO-X improves both the throughput and the quality of data collected for contact-rich policy training. With reverse teleoperation, operators intervene on a running policy fluently, without dropping objects already in hand, yielding better data for subsequent policy improvement.
We summarize our contributions as follows:

We present a dexterous teleoperation framework, equipped with force and haptic feedback, with support for three commercial robotic hands, spanning 6 to 22 actuated DoF, without hand-specific redesign.

We introduce reverse teleoperation, in which the actuated exoskeleton back-drives the operator’s hand to match the robot’s configuration, so that intervention on a running policy begins from a matched state rather than a discontinuous handoff.

We open-source the full system, including hardware design, forward and reverse teleoperation, and policy training and fine-tuning details. We also release all 1.8k episodes of contact-rich manipulation data from three embodiments, spanning teleoperated demonstrations, human interventions, and autonomous policy rollouts.

1. We present a dexterous teleoperation framework, equipped with force and haptic feedback, with support for three commercial robotic hands, spanning 6 to 22 actuated DoF, without hand-specific redesign.

2. We introduce reverse teleoperation, in which the actuated exoskeleton back-drives the operator’s hand to match the robot’s configuration, so that intervention on a running policy begins from a matched state rather than a discontinuous handoff.

3. We open-source the full system, including hardware design, forward and reverse teleoperation, and policy training and fine-tuning details. We also release all 1.8k episodes of contact-rich manipulation data from three embodiments, spanning teleoperated demonstrations, human interventions, and autonomous policy rollouts.

title: Measuring Asset and Scene Reconstruction Effects in Real-to-Sim Robot Evaluation
authors: Sanya Verma,Luca Cilio,Velissarios Christodoulou
abstract: Simulated evaluation is increasingly used alongside real-world evaluation of robot policies because it is cheaper and easier to repeat; however, its value depends on how closely its outcomes track the real robot’s. We test whether our reconstruction pipeline, combining metrically scaled object geometry, authored physical parameters and scene reconstruction, reduces disagreement between simulated and real robot scores relative to a default open-source recipe. We constructed two simulated versions of one bimanual robot cell: an authored reconstruction, using object geometry at estimated metric scale, projected textures, authored physics and our own scene splat; and a baseline, referred to as the default reconstruction, using the open-source recipe of a generative single-image mesh, engine-default physics and a Gaussian-splat scene. Both reconstructions use the same object photographs and scene video. Two policies ran five tasks each, giving ten task-policy pairs, which we call cells; each cell was run twenty times in each reconstruction with all other settings held fixed. Both reconstructions were scored against the same real trials, graded by a third-party evaluator. Pearson correlation between the ten simulated and real cell means is r = 0.90 for the authored reconstruction and 0.51 for the default. Mean score error is 6.97 percentage points for the authored reconstruction and 17.54 for the default, a reduction of 10.56 percentage points. These results show that improving the quality of the environment reconstruction through higher visual fidelity, authored physics and metric scale makes the simulation more faithful to the real world and narrows the sim-to-real gap. We release the harness, the per-trial scores, every reported run’s configuration, and the assets and scenes of both reconstructions.
introduction:
Evaluating a robot policy on hardware is costly and labour-intensive, and because real rollouts can be stochastic and hard to control systematically, a result is difficult to repeat exactly [1, 2]. One alternative to hardware is a digital twin: a simulated copy of the real robot cell in which the same policy runs the same tasks. SIMPLER [1] reported a strong correlation between simulated and real performance for the policies and tasks it studied. PolaRiS [2] and SimFoundry [3] build the twin from a short video scan of the robot cell and report Pearson correlations (r) of 0.90 and 0.91 respectively between simulated and real scores.

The remaining disagreement between real and simulated scores is attributed to two sources, both identified by SIMPLER [1]. The first is the visual gap: rendered images differ from real camera images. The second is the control gap: the simulated arm responds differently to the same command. Later work varies factors within these two categories. PolaRiS [2] compares four rendering conditions of the same scene, from Gaussian splatting to fully untextured, and measures the change in r and mean maximum rank violation (MMRV). Wang et al. [4] vary vision, language, layout and behaviour across nine tasks and five policies. How the manipulated objects themselves are reconstructed is not among the sources these studies vary.

In these pipelines, object physics is not investigated as a source of disagreement between real and simulated scores: it is left at engine defaults or estimated by a model without validation against measurement. PolaRiS builds object geometry with open-source TRELLIS [9] from several segmented views of each object, then sets “standard physics parameters for contact dynamics using default values from IsaacSim” and notes that “object mass parameters can be estimated by the users” [2, Section 4.1]; object physics is left at engine defaults. SimFoundry [3], like our pipeline, authors mass and friction per object, but reports only how well its complete output agrees with real, so the effect of that step is not measured.

Prior results suggest that the effect of authored physics is not negligible. Phys2Real [5] shows that better estimates of an object’s centre of mass raise real task success, although it measures success, not agreement between simulated and real evaluation. The nearest evidence on agreement between real and simulated evaluation is Wang et al. [4], who find that agreement is governed by simulator fidelity instead of purely object-level mismatch; their test varies which object is present, not how well a fixed object is built. The only measurement of asset fidelity against agreement is on deformable objects: Zhang et al. [6] replace PhysTwin’s [8] optimised per-spring stiffness with a single global value and MMRV on a rope-routing task rises from 0.174 to 0.248. No study that we are aware of measures how the fidelity of a fixed set of rigid objects changes agreement between simulated and real evaluation (Section 2). We therefore build one cell twice: an authored reconstruction, with our pipeline, which reconstructs geometry from one photograph, estimates metric scale from a ChArUco calibration board and authors physics per object, and a default reconstruction, a PolaRiS-inspired recipe, TRELLIS at its single-image setting with engine-default physics (Section 3).

We test whether the authored reconstruction narrows the sim-to-real gap in robot performance relative to the default reconstruction. Both reconstructions are run with the same policies and tasks and scored against the same real trials (Figure 2). The reconstructions differ on three axes. Object geometry and texture: reconstructed and projected from a single photograph of the object, scaled from a printed ChArUco calibration board of known size (authored), against a generative single-image mesh scaled by eye (default). Object physics: mass, friction and restitution authored per object, against engine defaults. Scene: our reconstruction splat pipeline, against a PolaRiS-inspired Gaussian-splat recipe, both from the same handheld video. Every other part of the run (robot model, controller, camera, placement and step budget) is identical between the reconstructions (Section 3).

Our main finding is that a reconstruction with metrically scaled geometry, authored physics and our own scene reconstruction taken together narrows the sim-to-real gap relative to the default recipe used in the literature: score error is 10.56 percentage points lower and progress disagreement 8.32 percentage points lower across five tasks and two policies, both with 95% intervals that exclude zero. The other two agreement measures, correlation and failure-stage disagreement, do not separate the two reconstructions with ten cells. We release the harness, the four agreement measures and the real reference of 200 paired trials, five tasks by two policies, run and graded by a third-party evaluator [11], and the assets and scenes of both reconstructions, so the comparison can be repeated on other cells and pipelines.

title: CF-JEPA: Improving Robustness of JEPA World Models via Controllability Factorization
authors: Morgan Byrd,Robert Wright,Sehoon Ha
comment: Website:this https URL
abstract: Controlling an agent with vision requires being able to separate useful information from irrelevant background information. JEPA-style latent world models seem like a natural approach for this, as they do not perform pixel-level reconstruction; however, they are still sensitive to these distractor signals and experience latent collapse. In this work, we introduce Controllability Factorized JEPA (CF-JEPA), a JEPA-style world model which splits the latent space into controllable and uncontrollable subspaces. This factorization allows us to capture all the distractor information into the uncontrollable region, while we use the control-relevant latent information for our task. With this, we show comparable performance across 2D and 3D control tasks under nominal conditions and improved performance under distracted conditions, where CF-JEPA is the only model that does not experience latent collapse. We also validate our model under distracted conditions for a simulated robot task, highlighting the practical application of such a scheme.
introduction:
Humans are capable of performing tasks using visual control, regardless of what sort of background visual distractor information or noise might be present. Random objects moving into the visual field can be easily ignored and do not interfere with task progress or break our understanding of the world. Robots deployed in diverse environments should likewise accomplish their tasks despite such visual distractors. Thus, a reasonable expectation of a generative world model might be to have a similar invariant nature to these kinds of external visual stimuli.

However, typical world models [1, 2] struggle under these conditions as they rely on pixel-level reconstruction to learn their representations, and reconstructing such random content is difficult and wasteful. There have been attempts to handle this [3, 4, 5], but they often still rely on reconstructing the scene along with additional techniques or rely on assumptions that may not hold in realistic robotic scenarios.

Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) appear to be a natural way to handle this kind of distraction, as they remove the generative model built on pixel-level reconstruction and predict dynamics in latent space instead. However, we find that such JEPA world models [6] like LeWM are still very susceptible to task-irrelevant visual distractor signals, and the latent space collapses as a result. Incorporating an inverse dynamics loss as in Sensorimotor World Model (SMWM) [7] improves robustness, but it still uses the full latent rather than separating distractor elements from control.

Building on the JEPA framework, we propose CF-JEPA, a world model with additional latent structure for improved robustness under visual distractor signals. We incorporate controllability factorization, where we partition the latent space into a control-relevant, action-conditioned region and a control-irrelevant, action-free region. This explicit partition has a minimal to moderate impact on nominal performance and offers a strong benefit in the presence of visual distractors, where CF-JEPA is the only tested model that does not collapse.

We evaluate CF-JEPA against LeWM and SMWM on four visual control tasks and a simulated robot task. With two visual distractors, LeWM collapses on all tasks, and SMWM collapses on Reacher, where its success rate drops to 0.10 while CF-JEPA retains 0.48. As the number of distractors grows, SMWM degrades rapidly, and its success rate on PushT and TwoRoom falls from 0.86 and 0.98 respectively to 0.27 and 0.46 as it collapses, while CF-JEPA maintains 0.57 and 0.82 respectively. We further hypothesize that the benefit of controllability factorization is most evident when the action space requires perceiving the state of the agent, and we confirm this on the simulated robot task. Finally, a diagnostic decoder on Reacher shows that the controllable latent of CF-JEPA preserves the agent, whereas the baseline latents lose the agent.

Our key contributions are the following:

CF-JEPA, a simple world model architecture that improves robustness to irrelevant visual distractors via controllability factorization, where we separate the irrelevant, uncontrollable environment features from the relevant, controllable features in our latent space.

title: Toward Humanoid Robots in Construction: A Teleoperation Feasibility Study
authors: Parastoo Ali Pour,David R. Martin,Chang Min Hur,Bo Zhang,Tommy Zhou,Brandon Thomas Lichter,Shane Stanfield,Pramod Khargonekar,Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque
comment: Accepted at IROS 2026 Workshop on Future of Construction
abstract: We present a teleoperation system that enables a single operator to perform construction tasks on a Unitree G1 humanoid, combining extended reality (XR) based upper body control with pedal-based locomotion to enable simultaneous manipulation and locomotion. Motivated by persistent labor shortages, hazardous working conditions, and challenges in humanoid autonomy, we investigate teleoperation as a practical near-term approach for reducing physical strain on workers while generating high quality demonstration data. We evaluate the system on two representative construction tasks drawn from O*NET occupational database, and report task success and completion time relative to a manual baseline. The system achieved 100% success on tool transport and 80% success on surface painting, with teleoperation requiring substantially more time compared to manual execution.

title: TacDyn-WAM: Learning Implicit Tactile Dynamics in a Heterogeneous Visuo-Tactile World Action Model
authors: Enyi Wang,Mingxin Wang,Quan Shi,Hetian Guo,Hongyu Wang,Xi Wang,Bin Qian,Yupeng Zheng,Wenxuan Song,Houde Liu,Yong Xu,Cheng Chi,Wenchao Ding,Yilun Chen,Yan Wang
abstract:
World action models improve robotic manipulation by conditioning actions on predicted futures, yet existing tactile variants largely inherit video-generation pipelines that reconstruct future tactile observations through iterative denoising.
Such prediction can become unreliable under deployment drift: small changes in contact position or force may substantially alter tactile pixels even when the underlying contact evolution remains predictable.
We introduce TacDyn-WAM, a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model that predicts implicit tactile dynamics rather than reconstructing future tactile observations.
It learns TacRep, a dynamics-aware tactile target space trained through masked spatio-temporal prediction on tactile clips and regularized by relational structure distillation.
A visual expert and an Implicit Tactile Dynamics Expert predict future visual and tactile representations in separate target spaces while interacting through joint attention; the tactile expert predicts future representations and their changes at multiple horizons in a single forward pass, and a read-only tactile memory supplies the current tactile state.
On UniVTAC, TacDyn-WAM achieves an average success rate of 81.5% using only the provided demonstrations, reaching state-of-the-art-level performance and remaining competitive with models pretrained on large-scale visuo-tactile trajectories.
Ablations confirm the benefits of both tactile pathways and TacRep over pixel-reconstruction and static alternatives.
On five real-robot tasks, TacDyn-WAM reaches 71.0% average success, and modest-scale pretraining raises it to 85.0%, further validating our method.
Project page.
introduction:
World models forecast how observations evolve, while world action models use this foresight for policy learning, allowing actions to depend on predicted futures rather than current observations alone (Cai et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026c; Ye et al., 2026a).
Yet in existing world action models, this foresight comes primarily from vision.
In contact-rich or precision manipulation tasks, such as insertion and alignment under occlusion, cameras cannot fully resolve contact states, local geometry, or interaction forces.
Early efforts incorporated tactile sensing into VLA models, giving rise to vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) models that encode tactile observations alongside vision and language (Huang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a; Bi et al., 2026b; Cheng et al., 2026).
By understanding the current tactile state, they improve contact-rich manipulation over vision-only policies.
However, they do not predict how this state will evolve, leaving policies reactive to tactile feedback.
Recent tactile world action models close this gap by predicting future tactile observations as part of the world model (NeoteAI Team et al., 2026a; Lou et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026b; Wu et al., 2026).
These models have achieved promising results, with some further benefiting from large-scale visuo-tactile pretraining.
Despite this progress, a core design question remains: what should tactile world models predict?

Most existing methods simply reuse video-generation pipelines: the same VAE encodes camera and tactile frames, while video backbones iteratively denoise future tactile latents.
This slows inference and ties prediction to pixel reconstruction, which is poorly suited to tactile observations.
Expert demonstrations cover only tactile images near correct contacts, whereas closed-loop errors may cause policies to drift from them.
This drift may leave camera views nearly unchanged, yet even slight changes in contact position or force can substantially alter tactile images, pushing them farther from the demonstration distribution.
Despite these pixel-level changes, contact evolution—whether an imprint deepens, slides, or rotates—often remains predictable.
We therefore argue for implicit tactile dynamics modeling: predicting contact evolution in a dynamics-aware representation space rather than reconstructing future tactile observations.

Latent prediction is a step toward this goal, but not every latent space is equally suited to forecasting tactile evolution.
N0N_{0}-VTLA (NeoteAI Team et al., 2026b) predicts the net tactile change at a single horizon in the feature space of a frozen DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2023).
However, DINOv2 is trained on static natural images and is not explicitly optimized to capture frame-to-frame tactile evolution; recent tactile representation learning also shows the limitations of single-frame encoders in modeling such dynamics (Feng et al., 2026).
In contrast, V-JEPA 2.1 (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026) learns representations by predicting masked spatio-temporal features in videos, encouraging its encoder to capture predictable motion rather than exact pixel details.
Building on this objective, we learn a target space from tactile video clips that captures temporal change, while preserving spatial structure to support robust prediction under tactile distribution shifts.
Moreover, because a single net change can hide intermediate contact events when a squeeze or slip returns to a similar final state, we predict both future representations and their changes from the present at multiple horizons.
This captures contact evolution rather than only its endpoint.

In this paper, we present TacDyn-WAM, a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model whose two world-model experts use separate parameters and target spaces.
The visual expert predicts future visual latents, while the Implicit Tactile Dynamics Expert (ITDE) predicts tactile evolution in the TacRep space.
Joint attention couples their predictions at every layer and allows the Action Expert to use both.
The ITDE requires only a single forward pass without iterative denoising.
A separate Tactile Understanding Memory provides direct access to the current tactile state, while staged training progressively integrates the tactile modules with the pretrained experts.

On UniVTAC (Chen et al., 2026), TacDyn-WAM achieves state-of-the-art-level performance using only the provided demonstrations.
It is competitive with the two strongest models on this benchmark, N0N_{0}-VTLA and N0N_{0}-TWAM, both of which rely on large-scale visuo-tactile pretraining.
Notably, N0N_{0}-TWAM follows the video-generation recipe and has roughly twice the parameters of TacDyn-WAM.
Ablations show the benefits of both tactile pathways and TacRep’s advantage over pixel-reconstruction and static alternatives.
On five real-robot tasks, TacDyn-WAM trained on per-task demonstrations alone reaches 71.0% average success, 16 points above the tactile policy FTP-1, and modest-scale pretraining on about 6,000 real visuo-tactile trajectories raises it to 85.0%.

In summary, this work makes the following contributions:

We propose TacDyn-WAM, a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model that jointly predicts future visual latents and tactile evolution in distinct target spaces, while a read-only Tactile Understanding Memory provides the current tactile state.

We introduce TacRep, a dynamics-aware representation space for implicit tactile dynamics prediction, enabling one-pass multi-horizon prediction without pixel reconstruction or iterative denoising.

TacDyn-WAM achieves state-of-the-art-level performance on UniVTAC using only the provided demonstrations, and ablations validate the design.
On a real robot, it outperforms vision-only and tactile baselines and benefits further from modest-scale tactile pretraining.

1. We propose TacDyn-WAM, a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model that jointly predicts future visual latents and tactile evolution in distinct target spaces, while a read-only Tactile Understanding Memory provides the current tactile state.

2. We introduce TacRep, a dynamics-aware representation space for implicit tactile dynamics prediction, enabling one-pass multi-horizon prediction without pixel reconstruction or iterative denoising.

3. TacDyn-WAM achieves state-of-the-art-level performance on UniVTAC using only the provided demonstrations, and ablations validate the design.
On a real robot, it outperforms vision-only and tactile baselines and benefits further from modest-scale tactile pretraining.

title: When Reasoning Helps Action: Monitoring and Steering Chain-of-Thought in Vision-Language-Action Policies
authors: Sathwik Karnik,Joseph JR. Lee,Aryaman Gupta,Somil Bansal
abstract:
Reasoning-enabled VLA policies expose chain-of-thought (CoT) traces that appear to explain and guide their actions, creating a potential interface for runtime safety through reasoning monitoring and correction. In this work, we define and operationalize two evaluation axes for assessing when this interface can improve embodied behavior: correctability, which measures whether unreliable reasoning can be detected and improved during generation, and actionability, which measures whether reasoning corrections produce behaviorally meaningful changes in the intended direction.
To enable correctability, we introduce Token-level Reward for Utility-Steered Chain-of-Thought (trust), an offline-trained value model that predicts eventual reasoning correctness from partial prefixes and uses these estimates to monitor and selectively steer reasoning generation in frozen VLA policies.
On the Alpamayo 1.5 driving VLA, trust monitors correctness with 88.9% accuracy and improves reasoning correctness from 75.9% to 90.0%. On a baseline-defined challenging subset in AlpaSim, trust reduces collision rate by 30.4% and maximum trajectory error by 11.5% relative to the unsteered policy, outperforming a compute-matched Best-of-4 baseline.
On the DeepThinkVLA manipulation VLA, trust improves the correctness of grasp-state claims from 69.3% to 90.2% and action-choice claims from 68.8% to 85.9%, yet closed-loop task performance on LIBERO-Plus remains largely unchanged. Empirical analysis reveals intent-consistent behavioral effects in Alpamayo 1.5 but limited effects in DeepThinkVLA, helping interpret these different task-level outcomes.
Together, our results show that gains in reasoning correctness do not automatically imply gains in embodied performance, motivating evaluation of correctability and actionability when using CoT as a runtime safety interface. Our project page is available at https://s-karnik.github.io/trust-reasoning-project-page/.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models [brohan2023rt] have become a dominant paradigm for robot policies, mapping visual observations and natural-language instructions directly to action sequences. Recent reasoning-enabled VLA models further incorporate the chain-of-thought (CoT) capabilities of multimodal large language models (LLMs) [yin2024survey], generating textual scene interpretations, intentions, and high-level plans before predicting actions. Such explicit reasoning has been shown to improve long-horizon manipulation [zhao2025cot] and robustness in driving [wang2025alpamayo]. It also offers an appealing interface for runtime safety: if the model’s reasoning becomes inconsistent with the observation or task, we may be able to detect and correct that reasoning before unsafe actions are executed.

In this work, we define and operationalize two evaluation axes for assessing when CoT can serve as a runtime safety interface for embodied policies.
Correctability assesses whether unreliable reasoning can be detected and steered during generation. Actionability assesses whether corrections to action-relevant reasoning produce meaningful behavioral changes in the intended direction. These axes distinguish the ability to improve reasoning from the policy’s ability to act on those improvements. This distinction is critical because a policy’s reasoning may become accurate while its actions remain insensitive to the corrected trace.

Fig. 1 illustrates the actionability of correcting the reasoning.
In the Alpamayo 1.5 [wang2025alpamayo] driving example, the policy focuses on a green straight-through signal while approaching a yellow left-turn arrow. Substituting reasoning that identifies the arrow and calls for stopping changes the predicted trajectory, causing the vehicle to decelerate toward a stop and reducing the minimum average displacement error (ADE) from 8.83 m to 2.02 m over six samples.
Here, the reasoning correction is actionable: it produces the intended behavioral effect.
In the DeepThinkVLA [yin2025deepthinkvla] manipulation example, the policy incorrectly claims that an object has been grasped. Correcting this claim, however, produces little change in the generated action chunk.
Here, the reasoning can be corrected, but the correction is not actionable in the tested setting.
These examples suggest that reasoning corrections may not always translate into corresponding changes in action, motivating a systematic investigation of their behavioral consequences in VLA policies.

To enable correctability during generation, we introduce Token-level Reward for
Utility-Steered Chain-of-Thought (trust), an
offline-trained value model that predicts, from the visual observation and a partial reasoning prefix, whether the completed reasoning trace will be correct. As a runtime monitor, trust flags prefixes predicted to lead to incorrect reasoning. As an inference-time steering mechanism, trust applies gated value-augmented sampling (VAS) [han2024value] to flagged prefixes, reweighting the policy’s next-token distribution toward higher-valued continuations. The value model uses only observations and reasoning tokens, requires no access to the VLA policy’s weights or hidden states, and leaves the policy frozen during monitoring and steering.

We evaluate trust on Alpamayo 1.5 for driving and DeepThinkVLA for manipulation. In both domains, trust improves reasoning correctness, demonstrating correctability.
In AlpaSim [alpasim_2025], this reasoning improvement translates into better trajectory and safety metrics on a baseline-defined challenging subset, outperforming a compute-matched Best-of-4 baseline.
On LIBERO-Plus [fei2025libero], however, DeepThinkVLA’s reasoning improves while task performance remains largely unchanged. Through reasoning-substitution and intent-level analyses,
we show that these analyses help interpret the contrasting task-level outcomes: Alpamayo 1.5 exhibits intent-consistent behavioral changes under corrected reasoning, whereas DeepThinkVLA is less responsive to the tested reasoning corrections.

To summarize, our main contributions are: (1) we define and operationalize two evaluation axes for using CoT as a runtime safety interface in embodied policies;
(2) we introduce trust, an offline-trained value model that predicts eventual reasoning correctness from partial prefixes and enables token-level monitoring and selective inference-time steering in frozen VLA policies; and (3) we provide closed-loop evaluations and reasoning-substitution analyses showing that improved reasoning correctness can improve behavior when corrections are actionable, but may leave task performance unchanged when the policy is weakly responsive to corrected reasoning.

title: Token-World: World Modeling in Vision-Language Model Token Space for Robot Manipulation
authors: Chuyao Fu,Xiaowei Chi,Yuhan Rui,Yu-kai Wang,Zezhong Qian,Xiaojie Zhang,Yunfan Lou,Kevin Zhang,Kuangzhi Ge,Chak Wing Mak,Zhiyang Chen,Athena Zhuoming Zhong,Hongyang Chen,Haoran Li,Yike Guo,Sirui Han,Shanghang Zhang
comment: Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
abstract: A common approach to world-model simulation for vision-language-action (VLA) systems is to predict future RGB observations and then re-encode them into policy inputs, introducing an indirect interface between simulation and downstream policy execution. We instead investigate whether world dynamics can be modeled in a compact, policy-oriented state derived from VLM visual tokens. A key challenge is that raw VLM visual tokens are high-dimensional, making efficient and accurate autoregressive dynamics modeling challenging. To address this, we introduce Token-World, an action-conditioned world model that compresses VLM features into a compact token state, learns future dynamics in this reduced space, and maps predicted states back to the original policy-facing representation for downstream use. Across manipulation benchmarks, Token-World improves open-loop feature fidelity and policy-action consistency over recent world-model simulators, with slower degradation over long rollout horizons. In closed-loop evaluation, its simulated policy performance correlates more strongly with reference policy performance than Ctrl-World (r=0.794r=0.794 vs. 0.5830.583), while requiring lower simulation latency. Ablations further show that compact-representation design and dimensionality substantially affect future-state prediction. Code will be available at https://chuyaofu.github.io/Token-World/.
introduction:
World models [1] offer a promising route toward scalable embodied learning by serving as learned simulators of action-conditioned environment dynamics [2, 3, 4, 5]. Instead of executing every behavior in the physical world, an agent can roll out future observations inside the model, which is especially valuable in robotics where real-world interaction is costly and slow[5]. Recent work has therefore explored world models as simulators from several perspectives: using predicted futures to evaluate policies [6, 7], synthesizing additional interaction data for policy learning[8, 9], and performing reinforcement learning through imagined rollouts[10, 11, 12].

As world models are increasingly used as learned simulators, they are often paired with VLA policies that map visual observations and language instructions to actions [13, 14, 15, 16]. However, existing pipelines often use an indirect simulation interface, where future RGB observations are first predicted by the world model, then re-encoded into VLA visual tokens before being consumed by the VLA policy [6, 8, 10, 11, 12]. As world models move toward scalable simulators for VLA agents, this indirect interface becomes a critical bottleneck: the simulator predicts human-viewable pixels, whereas the downstream policy ultimately consumes policy-facing visual tokens.This mismatch is not merely computational: RGB reconstruction encourages the simulator to allocate capacity to visual details that may be irrelevant to the policy, while token-space rollout directly targets the representation used for downstream action generation.

A representation-aligned alternative is to simulate the future directly in the VLM visual-token space consumed by the policy. Such an interface avoids repeatedly reconstructing RGB observations and re-encoding them into policy inputs during imagined rollouts. However, policy-facing VLM tokens are high-dimensional representations optimized primarily for perception and action rather than generative dynamics modeling [14, 15, 16]. Directly predicting their temporal evolution therefore imposes both a substantial modeling burden and considerable computational cost.

In this work, we introduce Token-World, an autoregressive action-conditioned world-model simulator that rolls out in compact policy-aligned VLM token space. Its dynamics model is a flow-matching DiT, without relying on pretrained video-generation models. To make high-dimensional policy-facing VLM features tractable for dynamics learning, Token-World compresses the feature dimension into a compact semantic token state. Future states are predicted in this compact space and mapped back to the original VLM visual-token space only when consumed by the downstream policy, avoiding intermediate RGB generation throughout the rollout.

Across manipulation benchmarks, Token-World improves open-loop feature fidelity and policy-action consistency over recent world-model simulators, while degrading more slowly over long rollout horizons.
In closed-loop evaluation, its simulated success rates track reference policy performance more closely than Ctrl-World (r=0.794r=0.794 vs. 0.5830.583), while providing higher simulation efficiency.
Controlled ablations further show that both the design and dimensionality of the compact VLM representation substantially affect future-state prediction.
In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We study direct VLM visual-token simulation as an alternative to RGB-based world-model pipelines, enabling the simulator to operate on the representation interface consumed by downstream VLA policies.

We present Token-World, an autoregressive action-conditioned world-model simulator that uses a flow-matching DiT to model dynamics in a compact VLM visual-token space, without relying on pretrained video-generation models.

We validate Token-World through open-loop prediction, closed-loop policy evaluation, and representation ablations, showing improved long-horizon feature and policy-action fidelity, more reliable policy success estimation, lower simulation cost, and the importance of compact-representation design for dynamics prediction.

1. We study direct VLM visual-token simulation as an alternative to RGB-based world-model pipelines, enabling the simulator to operate on the representation interface consumed by downstream VLA policies.

2. We present Token-World, an autoregressive action-conditioned world-model simulator that uses a flow-matching DiT to model dynamics in a compact VLM visual-token space, without relying on pretrained video-generation models.

3. We validate Token-World through open-loop prediction, closed-loop policy evaluation, and representation ablations, showing improved long-horizon feature and policy-action fidelity, more reliable policy success estimation, lower simulation cost, and the importance of compact-representation design for dynamics prediction.

title: Does Continual Imitation Learning Remain Grounded? A Language-Perturbed Benchmark for Robotic Task Retention
authors: Siddeshwar Raghavan,Ziqin Yuan,Fengqing Zhu,Byung-Cheol Min
abstract: Continual imitation learning evaluates whether a robot can learn new knowledge without forgetting previously learned skills. However, retaining task performance does not ensure the behavior remains grounded in language because policies may rely on scene cues, object associations, or memorized task structure. We introduce a benchmark protocol to study how language-guided behavior changes as robotic policies learn successive tasks. We construct meaning-preserving and meaning-changing instruction variants for the Goal, Spatial, Object, and Long suites of LIBERO. Policy experiments focus on LIBERO-Goal, evaluating Original and Paraphrase instructions after each continual-learning stage. We compare representative continual imitation learning methods under their original assumptions while separating task competence from language sensitivity. The proposed diagnostics complement standard learning and forgetting metrics by measuring semantic robustness, goal adaptation, and language sensitivity. Results show that strong continual-learning performance does not always translate to reliable language grounding, and our diagnostics help determine whether retained skills remain correctly guided by their instructions. Additional materials are available at https://sites.google.com/view/stillgrounded.
introduction:
Robot policies conditioned on language must acquire new behaviors while retaining previously learned skills. Continual imitation learning studies this challenge through streams of incoming manipulation tasks. Benchmarks such as LIBERO [1] characterize acquisition and retention using task success, forward transfer, negative backward transfer, area under the continual performance curve, and final success rate. However, these metrics do not establish whether retained behavior remains appropriately guided by language.

This distinction matters because a policy may select behaviors using scene layout, object associations, or memorized task routing rather than the instruction itself. Figure 1 illustrates why task retention alone does not establish language grounding. Success under a paraphrase does not necessarily indicate language use, since the policy may behave identically while ignoring the instruction. Likewise, a behavioral change does not guarantee completion of the modified goal, which may also be infeasible in the current scene. We therefore test whether equivalent instructions preserve behavior, valid goal changes induce the appropriate response, and policies respond appropriately when no valid goal can be executed.

Recent robustness benchmarks such as LIBERO PRO [2] and LIBERO-Plus [3] show that strong task performance does not always mean that a policy is using language reliably. A robot may still succeed by relying on scene layout, object associations, or other shortcuts. In continual learning, this raises an additional question: as new tasks are learned, does the connection between language and behavior remain stable?

We study this by evaluating saved continual learning checkpoints with fixed changes to the instruction. We consider four cases, the original instruction, a paraphrase with the same meaning, a minimal semantic change that requests a different goal, and a collision that makes the request incompatible with the current scene. These cases let us test whether a policy preserves behavior when meaning stays the same, changes behavior when the requested goal changes, and responds sensibly when no valid goal can be executed. Not every instruction change can be evaluated in the same way. Paraphrases can be compared against the original task goal, while valid minimal contrasts can be evaluated against the modified goal. For incompatible requests, there may be no correct success target, so we instead examine behavioral responses such as whether the policy continues toward a known goal, initiates motion, or changes its action distribution. This avoids treating every instruction change as a simple success-or-failure test.

Our analysis is performed after training using policies saved at successive continual-learning stages. This allows us to study how language robustness changes over time without modifying the training process itself. We also report whether each method uses task identity or explicit routing, since strong retention through task-specific modules is different from behavior selected through language alone.

Although our experiments use LIBERO dataset, the protocol decouples instruction construction and evaluation from benchmark-specific scene and goal definitions, making it possible to extend the same analysis to other continual robot-learning settings and benchmarks.

We summarize our contributions below:

We introduce a temporal evaluation protocol for studying how language guided behavior changes across successive continual learning checkpoints.

We use goal-based metrics when an instruction defines a valid goal, and behavioral diagnostics when it does not.

We establish protocol coverage across all four LIBERO suites and evaluate policies on LIBERO-Goal, comparing representative continual imitation learning methods without modifying their algorithmic design.

title: Same Scene, Different Task: Skill Alignment for Compositional Generalization in VLAs
authors: Taegeun Yang,Youngju Na,Yoonki Cho,Sung-Eui Yoon
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models often struggle to generalize to skill combinations absent from their fine-tuning demonstrations, even when every constituent skill has been demonstrated.
We focus on a vision shortcut as one failure mode: during fine-tuning, visual observations can serve as a proxy for the instruction, so a policy may execute a demonstrated combination associated with similar observations rather than the instructed combination.
This motivates training with counterfactual pairs formed by holding a demonstration observation fixed while changing the instruction to specify an undemonstrated combination.
These pairs, however, lack corresponding demonstrated action targets.
Crucially, the currently required skill has already been demonstrated, but actions from those executions cannot serve as direct targets because the same skill can require different actions across observations.
We propose CRAFT, which transfers supervision from demonstrated executions of the required skill to counterfactual pairs using skill representations that can be reused across executions of the same skill.
Across three VLA models and two simulation benchmarks, CRAFT improves success on undemonstrated combinations while maintaining high success on demonstrated ones; it also improves compositional generalization on a real robot.
Project Website.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025).
Adapting these models to a target robot embodiment, sensor configuration, or environment often involves fine-tuning on robot demonstrations collected in that setting (Kim et al., 2025).
Because collecting demonstrations that cover every task of interest is costly, scalable adaptation requires generalization beyond the demonstrated tasks.
Prior work has studied how adapted VLAs retain capabilities from pretraining (Yadav et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026), generalize across objects and visual conditions (Dey et al., 2025), and remain robust to language variation (Grover et al., 2025).
In this work, we study a complementary form of generalization: whether a VLA can recombine skills demonstrated during adaptation into combinations absent from those demonstrations.

Many robotic tasks can be viewed as compositions of skills, such as picking an object and then placing it at a target location (Ahn et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2025).
We define a skill as an operation paired with the entity specified for that operation, such as picking a red cube or placing an object on a blue plate.
For example, demonstrations of “pick the yellow cube and place it on the yellow plate” and “pick the green cube and place it on the green plate” contain all the constituent skills needed for “pick the yellow cube and place it on the green plate,” even though that combination is absent from the demonstrations (Figure 1).
As the number of possible entities grows, collecting demonstrations for every skill combination becomes increasingly costly.
This motivates a compositional generalization setting in which all required skills appear in the fine-tuning demonstrations, but their combination does not.
Yet even when every constituent skill is demonstrated, we observe that fine-tuned VLAs often perform well on demonstrated combinations but struggle with new combinations (Appendix A.1).

To address this gap, we focus on one failure mode: a vision shortcut, in which fine-tuned VLAs use visual observations as a proxy for the instruction (Xu et al., 2025; Lian et al., 2026).
Under such a shortcut, a policy may execute a demonstrated combination associated with similar observations even when instructed to perform a new one (Figure 1).
To mitigate this shortcut, we form counterfactual pairs during fine-tuning by keeping a demonstration observation fixed while changing the instruction to specify a combination absent from the demonstrations.
The resulting pair, however, has no corresponding demonstrated action target.
Crucially, the skill currently required under the changed instruction has already been demonstrated.
Nonetheless, actions from those demonstrations cannot generally serve as direct targets for the counterfactual pair, because the same skill can require different actions across observations.
Thus, the key challenge is to transfer supervision from demonstrated executions of the required skill to the counterfactual pair while accounting for how the required action varies across observations.

We propose CRAFT (Counterfactual Skill-Representation Alignment for Fine-Tuning), which addresses this challenge by learning skill representations that can be reused across executions of the same skill while allowing action prediction to vary with the observation.
CRAFT introduces a skill representation that reflects the currently required skill and a state representation derived from the visual observation; together, they condition action prediction.
For each counterfactual pair, CRAFT selects a demonstrated execution of the required skill.
It combines the pair’s skill representation with that execution’s state representation and supervises the prediction with that execution’s action target.
This supervision trains the counterfactual pair’s skill representation to reflect the required skill in action prediction.
Thus, CRAFT transfers supervision from demonstrated executions of the required skill to the counterfactual pair without requiring a demonstrated action target for that pair.

We evaluate CRAFT across π\pi-family (Black et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025) and GR00T (Bjorck et al., 2025) VLA models on two compositional benchmarks in simulation, with additional evaluation of π0.5\pi_{0.5} on a real robot.
CRAFT substantially improves success on undemonstrated skill combinations while maintaining high performance on demonstrated combinations.
Our contributions are as follows:

We propose CRAFT, a counterfactual supervision approach that uses existing demonstrations of constituent skills to train VLAs to execute skill combinations absent from the original demonstrations, without collecting demonstrations for those combinations.

We introduce two compositional benchmarks for two- and three-skill tasks, with demonstration datasets that cover every constituent skill but only a subset of skill combinations; we will release the datasets and simulation environments.

Across π\pi-family and GR00T VLA models, CRAFT improves success on skill combinations absent from the original demonstrations while maintaining high success on demonstrated combinations; we additionally validate CRAFT with π0.5\pi_{0.5} on a real robot.

1. We propose CRAFT, a counterfactual supervision approach that uses existing demonstrations of constituent skills to train VLAs to execute skill combinations absent from the original demonstrations, without collecting demonstrations for those combinations.

2. We introduce two compositional benchmarks for two- and three-skill tasks, with demonstration datasets that cover every constituent skill but only a subset of skill combinations; we will release the datasets and simulation environments.

3. Across π\pi-family and GR00T VLA models, CRAFT improves success on skill combinations absent from the original demonstrations while maintaining high success on demonstrated combinations; we additionally validate CRAFT with π0.5\pi_{0.5} on a real robot.

title: ScaffoldM3C: A Multimodal Sequential Monte Carlo Framework for Generative Stable Construction Planning
authors: Gadiel Sznaier Camps,Chengyang He,Guillaume Sartoretti,Eduardo Montijano,Mac Schwager
comment: This work has been submitted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Learning (T-RL) and is currently under review. Project Page:this https URL
abstract:
Autonomously constructing physically realizable 3D structures remains a significant challenge due to combinatorial action spaces, interchangeable components, equifinal assembly sequences, and strict stability requirements during construction. State-of-the-art methods fine-tune large language models for text-based generative construction. However, these approaches do not allow for Multimodal (text, image, sketch) conditioning, overlook the practical role of scaffolding for stabilizing intermediate structures, and suffer from slow inference speeds. Therefore, we formulate construction as a probabilistic next-block generation task with multiple potential assembly actions and multiple potential task conditioning modalities. Concurrently, we explicitly consider the utility of scaffolding by introducing an auxiliary scaffold block token.
We present Scaffold Multimodal Monte Carlo (ScaffoldM3C), a multimodal, lightweight, auto-regressive model for stable block-based construction, that proposes a set of next-step candidate blocks. Leveraging these candidates, we utilize Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to maintain a population of possible assembly sequences, allowing us to consider multiple, potentially different, assembly directions simultaneously. We train our multimodal architecture by extending the StableText2Brick dataset [1] to contain image conditioning prompts and scaffold-stabilized build sequences.
ScaffoldM3C is 4×4\times smaller than competing baselines, yielding a 5×5\times to 20×20\times speedup during inference, while achieving comparable construction quality to state-of-the-art methods and higher overall stability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and real-world robot assembly demonstrations.
introduction:
Automated construction requires sophisticated long-horizon spatial, temporal, and semantic reasoning. Unlike other object generation problems, construction depends on physical assembly feasibility. Subassemblies often require temporary support until completion, and multiple component choices or sequence orders can yield the same final structure. Valid plans must therefore select components, determine placements, and order steps to ensure every intermediate state remains physically realizable and unobstructed.

Existing approaches simplify this problem by imposing strong assumptions on representation [2], conditioning modality [3], or assembly processes [4]. Construction is typically formulated as a sequential decision-making over voxel spaces [5] or with restricted libraries [6] to improve tractability at the cost of geometric fidelity and modeling placement uncertainty. Rule-based planning [7], search [8], or post-processing [1] have been proposed to enforce physical validity post-generation. While resulting in improved stability, these strategies decouple generation from physical reasoning, requiring costly validity checks, rollbacks, or rigid constraints at inference [9].

Recent foundation-model approaches frame construction as autoregressive generation, adapting large language models for next-brick prediction from text prompts [1]. However, this paradigm suffers from three fundamental limitations. First, text-only conditioning prevents users from providing visual or geometric guidance. Second, a lack of explicit reasoning over temporary support forces a heavy reliance on costly physics-based “predict-evaluate-rollback” pipelines. Third, current autoregressive generation methods rely on single-hypothesis rollouts, which discount the possibility of multiple valid actions, thus often rejecting more feasible long-horizon plans in favor of immediate short-term alignment.
To address these challenges, we propose ScaffoldM3C, a scaffolding-aware Vision-Language-Construction (VLC) framework for stable block-based assembly. Our main contributions are:

(1) Probabilistic Multi-Hypothesis Assembly Formulation: We model assembly probabilistically by generating candidate block proposals with placement likelihoods, enabling Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) inference to maintain diverse, feasible build sequences. We augment this search mechanism with specialized auxiliary scaffolding blocks to resolve intermediate stability issues during generation.

(2) Lightweight Multimodal Task-Specific Architecture: We introduce a dual-stream Vision-Language-Construction (VLC) architecture with interwoven cross-attention that decouples conditioning (text and images) from assembly, as well as an extended multimodal scaffolded dataset.

Trained from scratch without relying on foundation models, ScaffoldM3C uses 4×4\times fewer parameters and achieves 5×5\times to 20×20\times faster inference while delivering comparable or superior overall structural stability.

title: Towards a General Humanoid Loco-Manipulation Model via Egocentric Whole-Body Human Data Pretraining
authors: Chongyang Xu,Zhao Wu,Jin Chen,Yiming Jiang,Jinhui Ye,Yuming Jiang,Shifeng Zhang,Ziliang Feng,Mu Xu,Yilun Chen,Li Lu,Steven C.H. Hoi
abstract:
Humanoid whole-body manipulation has advanced rapidly, enabling policies to coordinate locomotion, posture, bimanual interaction, and dexterous hand movements.
Meanwhile, egocentric human videos provide diverse examples of everyday interactions across objects and scenes, offering scalable supervision without robot operation.
However, existing supervision from these videos provides limited coverage of whole-body movement and coordination with hand–object interaction, while obtaining such supervision through humanoid teleoperation is also costly and difficult to scale.
We therefore explore how human experience can support scalable learning of humanoid loco-manipulation.
To support this study, we introduce HumanVerse-500, a 500-hour dataset of diverse human loco-manipulation behaviors in open-world environments, collected with a lightweight wearable system that synchronizes egocentric video with body and hand motion.
Building on this dataset, we develop λ0\lambda_{0}, a whole-body humanoid vision–language–action policy, through three-stage training that first learns interaction from diverse egocentric datasets, then coordinates body and hand motion using HumanVerse-500, and finally adapts the policy to downstream tasks and robot embodiments.
Across these stages, λ0\lambda_{0} learns a shared representation space for human experience transfer, while domain-specific interfaces handle differences between human and robot states and actions.
We evaluate λ0\lambda_{0} on SIMPLE and 4 real-world loco-manipulation tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance, and further analyze its scaling behavior, generalization, and training-stage contributions to understand how human data support downstream whole-body humanoid control.
We will release our code, models, and data to support further research.
introduction:
Humanoid whole-body manipulation has advanced rapidly, enabling robots to coordinate locomotion, posture, and dexterous manipulation within a unified policy (Jiang et al., 2026; Shi and others, 2026; Wei and others, 2026; Hu and others, 2026; Figure AI, 2026b; Figure AI, 2026a).
Learning these coordinated behaviors requires demonstrations that capture both whole-body movement and interaction with objects.
Such demonstrations can be collected through whole-body teleoperation, where human operators guide humanoids through coordinated movements and object interactions (Fu et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025; Luo and others, 2026; GEAR Team et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026).
Collecting diverse demonstrations this way requires substantial robot time and human effort, making it difficult to scale across tasks and environments (Shi and others, 2026; Punamiya and others, 2026).

Egocentric human videos offer a scalable alternative, capturing diverse everyday interactions without requiring robot operation (Grauman and others, 2022; Kareer et al., 2025; Hoque et al., 2026; Punamiya and others, 2026; Figure, 2026).
Recent methods recover wrist and hand trajectories from these videos, turning observed interactions into action supervision for robot learning (Li and others, 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026).
Pretraining on these action-labeled videos can improve downstream manipulation, supporting the use of human experience for scalable robot learning (Zheng and others, 2026; Punamiya and others, 2026).
However, wrist and hand trajectories alone do not fully capture the whole-body coordination required for humanoid loco-manipulation.
A humanoid must approach an object, adjust its posture to reach it, and maintain its grasp while carrying it elsewhere (Shi and others, 2026; Zhao et al., 2026).
Learning these behaviors requires supervision that preserves the temporal coordination between body movement and hand–object interaction.
We therefore ask how diverse human experience can provide scalable whole-body supervision for humanoid loco-manipulation.

To address this question, we introduce HumanVerse-500, a 500-hour dataset of human loco-manipulation collected across diverse activities in open-world environments.
We use a lightweight wearable system to capture egocentric video and body motion, then reconstruct hand motion from video to provide synchronized whole-body supervision.
Building on HumanVerse-500, we develop λ0\lambda_{0}, a whole-body humanoid vision–language–action policy that transfers human experience to robot control (Fig. 1).
We train the policy in three stages to learn interaction from diverse egocentric datasets, coordinate body and hand motion using HumanVerse-500, and adapt to downstream tasks and robot embodiments.
A shared representation space enables transfer across stages, while domain-specific interfaces handle differences between human and robot states and actions.

We evaluate λ0\lambda_{0} on SIMPLE and four real-world loco-manipulation tasks, improving success rates over the strongest evaluated baselines by 3.9 and 22.5 percentage points, respectively.
Across the evaluated data scales, more whole-body human data reduces validation loss and improves real-world task progress.
Ablations further identify whole-body mid-training as the larger contributor to real-world success among the two human-data stages, while human demonstrations improve progress on robot-unseen objects.
These results support scalable whole-body human data as a source of supervision for humanoid loco-manipulation.
Our contributions are summarised as follows:

We introduce HumanVerse-500, a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation with synchronized egocentric video, body motion, and hand motion.

We develop λ0\lambda_{0}, a whole-body humanoid vision–language–action policy that transfers human experience through three-stage training in a shared human–robot representation space.

We reveal a consistent scaling trend in whole-body human pretraining and demonstrate its benefits for downstream performance and generalization in humanoid loco-manipulation.

1. We introduce HumanVerse-500, a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation with synchronized egocentric video, body motion, and hand motion.

2. We develop λ0\lambda_{0}, a whole-body humanoid vision–language–action policy that transfers human experience through three-stage training in a shared human–robot representation space.

3. We reveal a consistent scaling trend in whole-body human pretraining and demonstrate its benefits for downstream performance and generalization in humanoid loco-manipulation.

title: Whole-Body Aerial Grasping and Lifting via Partial Visual Observations
authors: Jiaye Jin,Rui Jin,Xinhang Xu,Haotian Jin,Ruiyang Liu,Yi Wang,Jiayan Zhao,Kun Cao,Lihua Xie
abstract: Aerial grasp-and-lift tasks require whole-body coordination across approach, acquisition, and lifting under partial target observations. Early approach failures can limit exposure to later task stages during training, while changing visibility complicates alignment and closure timing during execution. We present a recurrent teacher–student framework that learns a single policy in simulation to jointly command flight, arm motion, and gripper closure without an explicit task-phase input. A privileged teacher learns through reinforcement learning with a critical-state curriculum that exposes acquisition and lifting states before connecting them to normal approach trajectories. Its behavior is distilled into a recurrent visual student that replaces privileged target states with dual-view point clouds and proprioception, integrating observation history for closed-loop control. A dedicated closure objective supervises closure timing from sustained model-defined readiness sequences. Training and primary evaluation use a simulated acquisition-and-payload model with condition-triggered latching, virtual attachment, and wrench-based payload loading for short-distance lifting. Across 8,996 completed simulation episodes under this model, the frozen student achieves full-task success rates of 99.97%, 97.14%, and 95.84% under nominal, physics/control-randomized, and additional camera-randomized conditions, respectively. The nominal latch-count-weighted mean of per-seed 90th-percentile alignment errors at acquisition is 8.12 mm.
introduction:
Uncrewed aerial manipulators (UAMs) extend UAV capabilities from observation [1, 2, 3] to physical interactions [4, 5, 6, 7].
Physical demonstrations show that onboard perception can support object retrieval [8]. Beyond reaching a suitable end-effector pose, the controller must coordinate relative motion, closure timing, and loaded flight. We study whole-body coordination and policy learning across approach, acquisition, and lifting using an environment-defined attachment and payload-wrench model.

The first challenge is coordinating the aerial base, arm, and gripper during acquisition and lifting. End-effector pose depends on vehicle motion and arm configuration; acquisition also constrains relative velocity, posture, and closure timing. Whole-body planning can enforce geometric and dynamic constraints [9], but the feedback policy must coordinate motion and closure as observations change. Improving alignment can alter relative motion or disturb the base. After acquisition, the controller must stabilize the vehicle while lifting the added load.

The second challenge is discovering and connecting behaviors across the task. Early approach failures can prevent reinforcement learning from reaching successful closure or loaded flight, even with dense approach rewards. Goal relabeling and demonstration-guided exploration improve sparse-reward manipulation learning [10, 11]; this aerial task also requires reaching and connecting critical interaction states. Near-acquisition and post-acquisition starts expose later behaviors, but normal approach trajectories may not reach them. Learning must therefore address both skill discovery and skill connection, turning experience at critical states into successful trajectories from normal task starts.

The third challenge is maintaining closed-loop control under partial target observations. Visual feedback enables repeated grasp corrections [12], but vehicle and arm motion change body- and wrist-camera viewpoints and occlusions. A single point cloud may omit information needed to assess alignment or time closure. A recurrent policy can integrate visible geometry, proprioception, and observation history to retain context for motion and closure decisions as visibility changes during acquisition and lifting.

We develop a recurrent teacher–student framework for whole-body acquisition and lifting without an explicit task-phase input. A privileged teacher learns through reinforcement learning with near-acquisition, bridge, and post-acquisition resets, then connects these behaviors to normal approach starts. Its policy jointly commands the aerial base, three-DOF arm, and gripper. We distill this behavior into a visual student using dual-view point clouds and proprioception. A shared geometric encoder and recurrent state integrate target geometry and observation history. Short-horizon labels from sustained, model-defined acquisition readiness supervise closure, while the student retains the teacher’s whole-body action interface.

Across 8,996 completed episodes under the acquisition-and-payload model, the frozen student achieves 99.97%, 97.14%, and 95.84% full-task success under nominal, physics/control-randomized, and additional camera-randomized conditions. The nominal weighted mean of per-seed 90th-percentile alignment errors at acquisition is 8.12 mm. Nominal full-task success is close to the privileged teacher’s under this model. Separate MuJoCo sim-to-sim trials assess three additional objects with virtual attachment or native contact. Physical-platform validation remains outside this study.

Our main contributions are:

A unified whole-body acquisition-and-lifting policy that jointly commands the aerial base, arm, and gripper without an explicit task-phase input.

A critical-state curriculum for skill discovery through near-acquisition, bridge, and post-acquisition resets, followed by skill connection from normal task starts.

Recurrent privileged-to-visual transfer with dual-view observations, memory, and closure supervision that retains the teacher’s whole-body action interface.

1. A unified whole-body acquisition-and-lifting policy that jointly commands the aerial base, arm, and gripper without an explicit task-phase input.

2. A critical-state curriculum for skill discovery through near-acquisition, bridge, and post-acquisition resets, followed by skill connection from normal task starts.

3. Recurrent privileged-to-visual transfer with dual-view observations, memory, and closure supervision that retains the teacher’s whole-body action interface.
