title: 3DROID: A Renderable 3D Gaussian Dataset with Measured Per-Scene Reliability
authors: Wonguen Cho,Junhoo Lee,Nojun Kwak
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Robot manipulation models primarily reason from 2D observations while acting in the 3D physical world.
To bridge this gap, recent work has augmented robot data with geometric priors such as depth, point clouds, and 3D trajectories, while renderable 3D Gaussian representations provide another promising form of 3D supervision.
However, 3DGS representation is designed mainly for photometric fidelity and may not preserve real-world metric scale, particularly when the supplied camera extrinsics are unreliable.
We study the effect of extrinsic reliability and pose conditioning on feed-forward 3DGS, and propose a calibration-aware pipeline that anchors reconstructed scenes to the robot’s metric workspace.
Our experiments show that pose conditioning improves novel-view fidelity, while its geometric benefit depends on the reliability of the injected extrinsics.
Using this pipeline, we present a renderable, metric-pose-anchored dataset with scene-level reliability information for robot manipulation research. Our dataset is available at

https://huggingface.co/datasets/wonguen/3DROID
introduction:
Robot manipulation is inherently geometric: grasping and placement require
reasoning about objects, free space, and motion in 3D. Explicit 3D
representations improve spatial reasoning over 2D observations [10, 16, 17, 21], motivating recent 3D annotations and renderable robot scenes
 [3, 13, 22].
Unlike point- or token-based annotations, renderable scenes provide a view-consistent appearance model from which observations and occlusions can be generated at new camera poses, enabling visual augmentation and simulation without additional data collection [22].
Such novel-view augmentation has also been shown to improve policy robustness
to unseen camera poses [13].

Constructing these representations at dataset scale favors feed-forward reconstruction.
Classical 3DGS optimizes each scene independently from its
available observations, making sparse robot views underconstrained and requiring repeated optimization over thousands of episodes
 [8].
Feed-forward variants instead amortize reconstruction
across training scenes: their learned priors support inference from limited views, while a single forward pass avoids repeated per-scene optimization  [7, 11, 18, 19].
This makes them a practical basis for constructing large-scale renderable robot datasets.

These advantages address sparsity and computational cost, but not physical reliability.
Both classical and feed-forward 3DGS are developed primarily for
photorealistic novel-view synthesis.
For manipulation, however, synthesized observations are useful only if they remain consistent with the metric workspace in which robot states and actions are defined [17].
A reconstruction may preserve appearance while silently moving surfaces or changing scene scale.
Moreover, camera calibrations in real-world robot datasets are not uniformly reliable,
so shipped poses cannot simply be treated as ground truth.
Whether the resulting scenes preserve metric scale therefore remains unclear,
and calibration must be validated independently of the reconstructor.

Prior work addresses parts of this problem from complementary directions.
Geometry-aware Gaussian methods introduce surface constraints, stereo cues, or 3D priors to improve geometric stability [5, 14, 13], while camera-refinement methods align visual observations with robot geometry [6].
Yet these model- and calibration-level solutions do not by themselves specify how reliability should be communicated when reconstructions are released as data.
This leaves a dataset-level question: how can calibration suitability and reconstruction reliability be measured and exposed for each scene?

In this paper, we therefore build 3DROID by reconstructing DROID [9] with pose-conditioned feed-forward 3DGS and
separating photometric fidelity from physical consistency.
Building on robot–depth alignment used for camera refinement [6], we validate calibration before reconstruction and separately assess geometric reliability afterward, together with measurement coverage.
This separates calibration suitability from reconstruction reliability.
We therefore release measured support rather than claim geometric ground truth or downstream policy gains.
Table 1 summarizes the scene-level assets added by 3DROID and the source modalities that remain in DROID.

Our contributions are threefold:

We release 3DROID, a DROID-derived dataset of renderable 3D Gaussian scenes with per-scene calibration and reconstruction-reliability metadata.

We empirically show that metric pose conditioning anchors reconstruction scale to the physical workspace and yields median per-scene PSNR gains of +0.73+0.73 to +2.73+2.73 dB at a fixed extrinsic source.

We repurpose robot–depth consistency as a coverage-aware reconstruction evaluation protocol that compares rendered 3DGS depth with classical stereo and kinematically localized robot geometry.

1. We release 3DROID, a DROID-derived dataset of renderable 3D Gaussian scenes with per-scene calibration and reconstruction-reliability metadata.

2. We empirically show that metric pose conditioning anchors reconstruction scale to the physical workspace and yields median per-scene PSNR gains of +0.73+0.73 to +2.73+2.73 dB at a fixed extrinsic source.

3. We repurpose robot–depth consistency as a coverage-aware reconstruction evaluation protocol that compares rendered 3DGS depth with classical stereo and kinematically localized robot geometry.

title: Managing Context and Communication in Distributed Agentic UAV Swarms
authors: Andrea Iannoli,Ivan Zyrianoff,Angelo Trotta,Lorenzo Gigli,Marco Di Felice
subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: . This paper has been accepted for presentation at the 24th IEEE Consumer Communications & Networking Conference 2027 (CCNC 2027)
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms increasingly rely on language-model agents to provide adaptive mission-level reasoning in uncertain environments. Fully distributed control, in which each UAV hosts an independent Small Language Model (SLM), removes reliance on a centralized coordinator but introduces an information-management problem: long-running interaction histories can degrade the reasoning context, while indiscriminate information dissemination increases communication and inference overhead. We address these challenges with a distributed UAV-agent architecture that enables continuous local SLM control through an event-driven reason–act–observe lifecycle. Runtime knowledge is represented as structured atomic notes and organized into core, local, and peer-specific memory. A deterministic interest-aware gossip engine selectively disseminates these notes according to recipient-specific semantic novelty and recency. We evaluate the architecture using ten UAVs in a simulated search-and-rescue mission. Our approach completes all experimental runs, whereas unrestricted flooding messages completes only 70–85%, and delegating forwarding decisions to the SLM prevents mission completion in every run. Compared with unrestricted flooding, our approach approximately halves inference-token consumption, reduces transmitted data, and achieves lower survivor-count error.
introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms combine rapid deployment, parallel sensing, and wide-area coverage, making them attractive for search-and-rescue, disaster recovery, environmental monitoring, and infrastructure inspection. These missions are executed in uncertain environments in which predefined plans may become inadequate as hazards, observations, connectivity, and resource availability change [1]. Agentic AI can complement conventional perception and flight-control components with goal interpretation, contextual reasoning, and adaptive planning, enabling UAVs to revise mission-level decisions when unexpected conditions arise [2].

Embedding such reasoning capabilities into continuous UAV swarm control, however, is challenging. Model decisions must be grounded in heterogeneous sensing and actuation interfaces, executed through a long-running closed loop, and constrained by safety requirements despite the non-determinism of language models [3]. To mitigate these difficulties, language-level reasoning in many existing systems remains centralized: a cloud, edge, or swarm-level agent maintains a global view and generates mission plans, while individual UAVs execute them through conventional controllers [4, 3]. Such architectures depend on reliable connectivity to an external coordinator and introduce communication and computational bottlenecks as observations and control decisions are continuously exchanged and the swarm state grows [2]. Assigning an independent agent to each UAV instead enables local decision making, distributes the reasoning workload, and removes a central point of failure. Although distributed LLM-based UAV designs are beginning to emerge [5], fully decentralized control introduces additional challenges: each agent reasons from partial observations, coordinates over bandwidth-constrained links, and operates under onboard memory, computation, energy, and latency constraints that favor smaller Small Language Models (SLMs) with more limited reasoning capabilities [2]. However, existing distributed agentic UAV architectures do not explicitly address how long-running local knowledge should be organized and selectively disseminated among resource-constrained agents.

Indeed, every action produces observations and execution feedback, while cooperation contributes a continuous stream of peer messages. As these records accumulate, replaying the complete transcript can bury mission-critical information among transient or redundant events. This degradation is commonly described as context rot, which refers to the model failing to use relevant information embedded in long inputs even before the context limit is reached [6]. In a UAV swarm, such degradation can directly affect mission safety and completion, e.g., an agent that overlooks a mandatory landing instruction may continue unsafe execution, potentially resulting in a collision, vehicle loss, or mission failure. Long-running control therefore requires a bounded and structured representation of accumulated knowledge that preserves mission-relevant information while separating it from transient history [7, 8]. Regarding information dissemination, indiscriminately flooding observations wastes bandwidth and fills peer contexts with redundant information. Delegating each per-message, per-neighbor forwarding decision to the SLM can also introduce substantial reasoning overhead, enlarge the context, and interfere with the UAV control lifecycle.

We therefore propose a fully distributed architecture in which every UAV hosts an independent SLM-based agent, a Context Manager, and an Interest-Aware Gossip Engine. Each UAV continuously reasons over mission information, locally accumulated knowledge, execution feedback, and asynchronously received peer information, enabling its subsequent actions to adapt without a centralized coordinator. Knowledge produced during this process is represented as atomic notes, which are self-contained, metadata-enriched semantic units derived from the interaction history [8]. The Context Manager organizes these notes into a fixed Core Memory containing mission information, a Local Note Queue, and a peer-specific Neighbor Note Queue. The queues are token-bounded to prevent uncontrolled context growth while preserving information relevant to subsequent reasoning.

For information dissemination, we draw on a fundamental property of effective gossip: information should be forwarded only when it is novel to the recipient. Unlike conventional gossip mechanisms that are agnostic to message content, our approach evaluates forwarding decisions directly from the semantic content of the information being exchanged. For each one-hop neighbor, newly generated or received notes are compared with the peer-specific history using semantic similarity and recency. A strong match with recent information indicates that the peer likely already possesses equivalent knowledge, whereas semantic dissimilarity indicates greater novelty. Fixed thresholds map this novelty estimate to suppression, compact forwarding, or full forwarding. These decisions are performed deterministically rather than through additional SLM invocations, providing low-overhead and transparent information dissemination.

The main contributions of this work are:

Distributed agent lifecycle: mission-agnostic lifecycle for local UAV control by independent SLM-based agents, without a centralized coordinator;

Context organization: A bounded memory organization that structures mission, local, and peer-specific knowledge as semantic notes for long-running SLM control;

Interest-Aware Gossip Engine: A deterministic recipient-specific dissemination policy that combines semantic novelty and recency to suppress, compact, or fully forward information.

We evaluate the architecture using ten UAVs in a search-and-rescue mission involving 5, 10, or 20 moving survivors, with the objective of correctly identifying the total number of individuals. The proposed policy completes all experimental runs, whereas the evaluated SLM-based baselines exhibit mission failures. Compared with the most successful SLM baseline, the proposed approach uses approximately half the inference tokens and reduces transmitted data from approximately 6–7 MB to below 0.5 MB per mission, while achieving a lower survivor-count error.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. 2 reviews related work; Sec. 3 presents architecture; Sec. 4 and Sec. 5 describe context management and interest-aware gossip, respectively; Sec. 6 reports the evaluation; and Sec. 7 concludes the paper.

1. Distributed agent lifecycle: mission-agnostic lifecycle for local UAV control by independent SLM-based agents, without a centralized coordinator;

2. Context organization: A bounded memory organization that structures mission, local, and peer-specific knowledge as semantic notes for long-running SLM control;

3. Interest-Aware Gossip Engine: A deterministic recipient-specific dissemination policy that combines semantic novelty and recency to suppress, compact, or fully forward information.

title: FedCKA: Representation-Guided Layer Personalization for Federated 3D Perception Across Driving Domains
authors: Jolle Verhoog,Ali Burak Ünal,Holger Caesar
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: . Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027
abstract:
Robust perception in intelligent vehicles demands 3D object detectors that remain dependable under domain shifts, such as changes in time of day, location, or weather. However, due to costly annotation and rare shifts, some environments lack sufficient data to train a standalone detector. Federated learning offers a privacy-preserving framework for collaborative model training, enabling clients to benefit from shared learning across diverse environments. Yet, this framework traditionally relies on a single global consensus model, which struggles to perform across heterogeneous local data distributions. Local conditions are better captured by adapting a subset of the model, but many personalization approaches rely on predefined layer partitions or fixed personalization ratios, thereby limiting adaptation to client-specific divergence.
To reduce this rigidity, we propose FedCKA, a Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA)-based strategy that dynamically handles the personalization-globalization trade-off. Specifically, FedCKA computes layer-wise feature similarities between local client models and the global consensus model during training. By converting layer-wise similarity scores into client-specific aggregation masks, FedCKA selectively shares representation-consistent layers.
Evaluation on a unified multi-domain benchmark based on nuScenes shows that FedCKA outperforms established federated baselines, including FedBN, FedRep, and FedSelect, improving average NDS by 7 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The findings offer both a comparative benchmark and a promising direction for robust federated 3D perception across shifts in location, weather, and illumination. Code is available at https://github.com/j-verhoog/FedCKA.
introduction:
3D Object Detection (3D-OD) is central to robotic perception in Intelligent Vehicles (IV), providing object poses and dimensions needed for planning and safe navigation.
However, domain shifts across vehicles, times of day, weather, and locations substantially degrade 3D detection performance [1] (see Fig. 1).
Because labeled data in niche or edge-case domains can be too scarce to support robust standalone training, a collaborative framework is desirable.
Yet, for IV applications, centrally collecting multimodal sensor data is constrained by privacy barriers and massive data volumes [2], while naive localized retraining remains computationally expensive [3].

These constraints motivate Federated Learning (FL), which enables privacy-preserving collaborative training for multi-domain adaptation without data centralization [4, 5, 6], by sharing only model updates. However, real-world deployment across heterogeneous data distributions introduces a central personalization-globalization trade-off: which model components should be globally shared versus locally personalized? Many personalization methods resolve this trade-off through static layer partitions or fixed personalization ratios, which may fail to capture client- and layer-wise representation divergence.
For multi-modal 3D-OD, this rigidity is particularly problematic because domain shifts can affect sensor backbones and fusion modules asymmetrically [7].

Despite this need, FL for multimodal 3D-OD remains underexplored. While prior federated detection and, more recently, federated 3D-OD studies exist, they do not systematically isolate location-, weather-, and illumination-induced client heterogeneity.
This limits insight into whether personalization helps under these structured client-level domain shifts.
While recent federated 3D detection approaches, including FedM2Former [9] and FedPillarNet [10], address client heterogeneity through personalized learning, they do not systematically isolate location-, weather-, and illumination-induced domains or compare representative FL personalization strategies within a unified 3D-OD benchmark.

To address this gap, we study how federated 3D-OD methods handle location-, weather-, and illumination-induced client heterogeneity, and whether representation consistency can determine which layers should be globally aggregated or locally personalized.
We isolate client-data heterogeneity by focusing on labeled, client-level domain adaptation across location, weather, and illumination, leaving system-level constraints such as client reliability and sensor-configuration variability to future work.
We make the following contributions:

Establish a unified multi-domain federated 3D object detection benchmark based on explicit location-, weather-, and illumination-induced client heterogeneity, enabling controlled evaluation under realistic domain shifts.

Establish a unified multi-domain federated 3D object detection benchmark based on explicit location-, weather-, and illumination-induced client heterogeneity, enabling controlled evaluation under realistic domain shifts.

Introduce FedCKA, a dynamic CKA-based layer masking strategy that uses layer-wise representation similarity to determine which model components should be globally aggregated versus locally personalized.

Demonstrate that FedCKA outperforms established federated baselines, including FedBN, FedRep, and FedSelect, improving average NDS by 7 percentage points over the strongest competitor by identifying domain-sensitive layers.

title: Supervise What Decides Success: Criterion-Aligned Auxiliary Losses for Latent World-Model Planning
authors: Takumi Hara,Kanata Suzuki
comment: . Under review
abstract: Latent world models plan by scoring candidate action sequences with distances in latent space. However, task success is judged by physical quantities, which we call the success-criterion quantities. In all four latent world models we examine, the end-effector position is encoded in the latent state with an error larger than the success criterion allows. Such a latent state cannot separate successful candidates from failing ones. We propose an auxiliary loss that uses success-criterion quantities as training targets, whereas existing latent world models take them only as inputs. During training, a linear head on the encoder and predictor outputs regresses the success-criterion quantities, and the regression error is added to the training loss. The head is discarded after training, so the model, its cost, and its inputs at test time are unchanged. This loss alone improves the success rate on PushT and cube by 3.5% and 3.4% (absolute), respectively, and both improvements are statistically significant. A success criterion thus specifies what a world model must retain in its latent state, and we show that it can serve directly as a training target.
introduction:
A world model predicts how actions change the world (Hafner et al., 2019; Hafner et al., 2020). A latent world model encodes the observation image into a low-dimensional latent state with an encoder and makes this prediction in latent space (Zhou et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026). Given a goal image of the scene the robot should reach, the planner selects the action sequence whose predicted latent state is closest to the latent state of the goal image. No pixels are reconstructed. The only quantity that ranks candidate action sequences is this latent distance.

Whether a trial succeeds is decided by the success criterion of each benchmark. A success criterion asks whether the positions of the hand and the objects lie within a tolerance of their values at the goal. Since the latent distance alone ranks the candidates, planning can succeed only if a candidate whose physical quantities used in the criterion, which we call the success-criterion quantities, lie within the tolerance is also the one with the smallest latent distance. Nothing in training asks for this condition. The training loss supervises only the next latent state; the success-criterion quantities appear nowhere in the loss. Indeed, in all four latent world models we examine, the hand position read out from the latent state by linear regression deviates from the true hand position by more than the tolerance of the success criterion. This deviation does not vanish with representation size or pretraining.

Prior work that uses physical quantities, including the success-criterion quantities, in training falls into two groups. DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025) and V-JEPA 2-AC (Assran et al., 2025) concatenate the proprioceptive state, such as the end-effector position, which we call the hand, to the input. Feeding a quantity as an input does not ask whether the latent state after the predictor retains it at the precision of the success criterion (Section 3.2). PhyLatent (Zeng et al., 2026) and PSG-JEPA (Yan et al., 2026) use physical quantities as training targets, but the designer chooses which quantities to supervise, and whether the targets correspond to the success criterion is never asked.

We propose an auxiliary loss that uses the success-criterion quantities as training targets. A linear head is applied to both the encoder output and the predictor output, and the error between its readout and the success-criterion quantities recorded in the demonstrations is added to the training loss (Figure 1). The head is discarded after training, so the model, its inputs, and the latent distance used for planning are identical to the baseline at test time, and the computation does not increase. What is supervised is fixed by the success criterion, not chosen by the designer.

The auxiliary loss, however, only drives down the readout error of the success-criterion quantities by one shared linear head from the encoder output and the predictor output. How much a difference in the success-criterion quantities between two candidates shows up as a difference in their latent distances enters the loss nowhere. A corrected readout therefore need not raise the planning success rate. Prior work reports cases where a proxy metric, such as video-prediction quality or linear-probe accuracy, improves while the success rate does not (Tian et al., 2023; Burns et al., 2024), and in our own experiments the frozen V-JEPA 2 shows a corrected readout together with a lower success rate. We therefore evaluate the auxiliary loss by the success rate, and use an ablation over which success-criterion quantities are supervised to determine in which trials the effect appears and which supervision avoids degradation.

Our contributions are threefold.

We propose an auxiliary loss that uses the success-criterion quantities as training targets. A linear head is applied to the encoder and predictor outputs only during training, so the model, its inputs, and the latent distance used for planning are unchanged at test time (Section 2).

On four manipulation tasks, a model supervised with the success-criterion quantities significantly improves the success rate over the baseline, and the improvement replicates on a world model with a frozen pretrained encoder (Section 3.2).

Through an ablation over which success-criterion quantities are supervised, we show that supervising all quantities in the criterion never significantly degrades the success rate on any task, for both a world model trained from scratch and one with a frozen pretrained encoder (Section 3.3).

A success criterion specifies what a world model must retain in its latent state. This work shows that the specification can be used directly as a training target, and delineates how far its effect reaches.

1. We propose an auxiliary loss that uses the success-criterion quantities as training targets. A linear head is applied to the encoder and predictor outputs only during training, so the model, its inputs, and the latent distance used for planning are unchanged at test time (Section 2).

2. On four manipulation tasks, a model supervised with the success-criterion quantities significantly improves the success rate over the baseline, and the improvement replicates on a world model with a frozen pretrained encoder (Section 3.2).

3. Through an ablation over which success-criterion quantities are supervised, we show that supervising all quantities in the criterion never significantly degrades the success rate on any task, for both a world model trained from scratch and one with a frozen pretrained encoder (Section 3.3).

title: PhysicsLENS: Diagnosing Physical Property Blindness in Video Generation Models
authors: Isaiah Milkey,Som Sagar,Aditya Taparia,Xinyuan Liu,Jiqing Wen,Ransalu Senanayake
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Reliable video world models could provide scalable predictive environments for robot learning, planning, and evaluation. However, generated robot videos can violate physical principles and complete tasks through physically implausible behavior, limiting their reliability for robot learning and planning.
Current video-generation benchmarks exclude physics that are inherently hidden by visuals (e.g., weight, viscosity, friction). Due to this, video models are evaluated on the fidelity of physics, not the underlying accuracy of physics.
We introduce PhysicsLENS, a dataset and benchmark for evaluating plausibility of physical properties grounded in robotics. PhysicsLENS uses matched scenario pairs that hold the same conditioning frame and task, while varying underlying physics in the scene description. Scenarios are curated from public robot video sources and annotated across seven physical domains: collision, gravity, momentum, friction, deformation, fluid, and causality. We evaluate across four video generation models, producing over 400 human-annotated labels.
Results show that plausible-looking videos often ignore the stated property (34 of 47), and that stating the property lowers plausibility only slightly and not significantly.
introduction:
Video generation models could provide scalable predictive environments for robot learning (Yang et al., 2024; NVIDIA, 2025a), planning (Du et al., 2023), and evaluation (Quevedo et al., 2025). By generating diverse interactions without repeatedly collecting real-world data, these models could expose robots to rare events, unfamiliar objects, and changing physical conditions (Jang et al., 2025). However, increasing the volume of generated data is useful only if the videos reliably represent the physical consequences of actions. A video may appear realistic and depict successful task completion while violating friction, momentum, object permanence, or other physical constraints. Such violations undermine the usefulness of generated videos as predictive environments, yet may go undetected by benchmarks focused on visual realism and task success. We therefore require a benchmark that evaluates whether generated interactions respect the physical properties and constraints that govern them.

Existing video-generation benchmarks capture this reliability only partially. Most benchmarks focus on visual quality, temporal consistency, or motion plausibility. These criteria can identify obvious artifacts, but cannot determine whether a model correctly grounds the physical properties specified in its conditioning input. Properties such as weight, friction, viscosity, and deformability may not be observable from a single image. Consequently, visually identical scenes can require different outcomes: a robot should interact differently with a heavy object than with a light one, or with a slippery surface than with a rough one. A model can therefore generate a plausible video while producing behavior that is physically incorrect for the stated condition.

We introduce PhysicsLENS, a benchmark for evaluating both physical plausibility and physical-property grounding in robot video generation. The dataset comprises of curated image–text prompts, more than 400 clips generated by four video generation models, and structured human annotations for every clip. We construct prompts from public robot videos, grouping scenarios into seven physical domains: collision, gravity, momentum, friction, deformation, fluid, and causality. In unobservable scenarios, the text specifies a physical property that cannot be inferred from that frame. Matched unobservable prompts keep the visual context and task fixed while varying the specified property, allowing us to test whether generated interactions reflect the corresponding physical consequences. Figure 1 summarizes the benchmark workflow.

The benchmark evaluates generated clips through two complementary tracks. In the human evaluation track, annotators rate physical plausibility and task completion, describe and categorize visible physical violations, and assess whether interactions in unobservable scenarios reflect the stated property. In the automated evaluation track, a four-stage hierarchical pipeline screens each clip, localizes potential violations, verifies them through targeted vision-language model questions, and reports supporting evidence. Across four video-generation models and 439 generated clips, the results show that a video’s apparent physical plausibility does not guarantee correct grounding in a hidden property. Our contributions are:

We introduce PhysicsLENS, a robotics-focused benchmark covering seven physical domains and distinguishing physical plausibility from physical-property grounding.

We construct matched scenarios that preserve visual context while varying text-specified physical conditions, including properties that cannot be inferred from appearance alone.

We present a multi-stage evaluation procedure and benchmark four video-generation models with more than 400 human judgments, finding that plausible-looking videos often ignore the stated property.

title: FutureWorlds: Learning Robotic World Models from Alternative Futures
authors: Hao Wu,Shengju Qian,Weiyan Wang,Fan Xu,Fan Zhang,Yuanpeng He,Qingsong Wen,Yuxuan Liang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: including references and appendix. Code:this https URL
abstract:
Robotic world models predict action-conditioned future scenes, providing a foundation for understanding action outcomes.
However, turning alternative predictions into useful learning signals remains challenging: similar candidates limit informative quality comparisons, while diverging trajectories require persistent maintenance of their individual histories.
We introduce FutureWorlds, a framework that unifies candidate construction, history maintenance, and learning from relative quality.
Built on a multimodal discrete autoregressive model, FutureWorlds uses diverse beam search during reinforcement learning to construct candidate futures that balance confidence and diversity.
Candidate-specific bounded memory preserves scene states and ensures that generation and policy scoring use matching histories.
We further propose MemSPO (Memory-Conditioned Search-Guided Policy Optimization), which converts video trajectory rewards into group-relative advantages to optimize the world model.
On RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa, FutureWorlds reduces LPIPS for 32-frame predictions by 14.78%, 20.84%, and 9.12%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline on each dataset.
Under fixed evaluation configurations, only 200 MemSPO updates further improve generation quality and support continued prediction beyond the training horizon.
Memory ablations, decoding sensitivity analysis, and optical-flow evaluation show that these gains extend beyond visual quality to more accurate motion prediction and more consistent object states.
Project page and code: https://github.com/Alexander-wu/FutureWorlds.
introduction:
Robotic world models predict how scenes evolve in response to actions, providing a foundation for action-outcome prediction (Finn et al., 2016), visual planning (Ebert et al., 2018; Hafner et al., 2019), behavior learning (Hafner et al., 2020), and policy evaluation (Yin et al., 2026; GigaWorld Team et al., 2026). Given the same observations, action sequence, and instruction, a model can propose multiple predictions of the future. These alternative futures represent different hypotheses about the scene’s evolution, with varying robot motions, object states, and prediction quality. Their differences offer a learning opportunity: by constructing useful alternatives and comparing their outcomes against recorded observations, a world model can learn from the predictions it generates.

Most autoregressive world models learn from recorded trajectories through supervised training. Their reliance on ground-truth histories during training differs from the self-generated histories available at inference, allowing errors to accumulate along a rollout (Ross et al., 2011; Bengio et al., 2015). Token-level likelihood also does not directly optimize complete generated sequences (Ranzato et al., 2016; Rennie et al., 2017). Figure 1 illustrates this challenge: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can leave predictions with insufficient robot motion or inaccurate poses. Reinforcement learning (RL) connects generated outputs to sequence-level rewards (Black et al., 2024). In world modeling, RLVR-World uses decoded prediction metrics (Wu et al., 2025a), while RLIR introduces inverse-dynamics rewards for action following (Ye et al., 2025). These advances enable learning from trajectory feedback, but the resulting learning signal also depends on which futures the model compares. More candidates alone do not guarantee useful comparative feedback. Effective post-training therefore requires informative candidate differences and history-consistent comparisons that turn alternative futures into reliable learning signals.

Learning from alternative futures requires coordinated candidate construction and history management. Candidate quality and diversity depend on the generation strategy (Holtzman et al., 2020): independent sampling does not explicitly coordinate these properties across candidates, while conventional beam search can concentrate on nearly identical sequences (Vijayakumar et al., 2018). A useful candidate set therefore needs to balance model confidence with distinct predictions. As these predictions unfold, each branch develops its own robot and object states. Retaining the corresponding history becomes especially important when prediction extends beyond the pretraining horizon, motivating bounded memory for sustained generation (Dai et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2026). Learning introduces a further requirement: policy scoring must condition on the same retained history that produces each candidate. These considerations connect three roles—constructing informative alternatives, maintaining their individual histories, and learning from their relative quality.

We introduce FutureWorlds, a framework that learns robotic world models by constructing, maintaining, and comparing alternative futures (Figure 2). We instantiate the framework with a multimodal discrete autoregressive model (van den Oord et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2024), whose token probabilities support candidate expansion and trajectory scoring under visual, action, and language conditioning. To construct alternatives, diverse beam search combines model likelihood with cross-candidate differences during RL training. To maintain their histories, candidate-specific memory retains scene and state anchors alongside rolling context, supporting longer predictions within a bounded memory budget. Search and memory operate together as each candidate evolves, and generation and policy scoring use matching histories. To compare and learn, MemSPO (Memory-Conditioned Search-Guided Policy Optimization) converts video trajectory rewards into group-relative advantages and updates the model through a search-guided surrogate based on GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and clipped policy optimization (Schulman et al., 2017). Candidate quality differences thus become feedback for improving the model that generates them.

Our evaluation covers RT-1 (Brohan et al., 2023), BridgeData V2 (Walke et al., 2023), and RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2026). On 32-frame predictions, FutureWorlds reduces LPIPS by 14.78%, 20.84%, and 9.12% relative to the strongest baseline on each dataset. Under fixed evaluation configurations, only 200 MemSPO updates improve generation and support prediction beyond the training horizon. Memory ablations, decoding sensitivity analysis, and motion evaluation further assess historical context, robustness, and dynamic consistency. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

Learning from Alternative Futures.
We introduce FutureWorlds, a framework that organizes model-generated futures into training experiences through coordinated candidate construction, history maintenance, and relative comparison.

Search-Guided, History-Consistent Learning.
We propose MemSPO, a GRPO-based post-training algorithm that combines diverse candidate search with candidate-specific memory and matches the histories used for generation and policy scoring.

Experimental Evaluation.
We evaluate generation quality and long-horizon prediction, analyze memory and decoding robustness, and assess motion consistency and inference resource requirements. LPIPS decreases by 9.12–20.84% versus the strongest baseline on each dataset.

title: The Effect of Gait Stability Based on Two Types of Impact Strategies for Two-Link Walking and Brachiating Robots
authors: Alan Estrada Flores,Nelson Rosa Jr
comment: submitted for review; code available atthis https URL
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
The two-link walking models of Garcia et al. (1998) and Goswami et al. (1998) and the
brachiating model of Gomes and Ruina (2005) have provided valuable insight into the
mechanics of limbed locomotion in the fields of biomechanics and robotics.
Figure 1 shows example motions of the model in Gomes and Ruina (2005).
In addition to contributions to human and robot gait analysis, these works show
that the underlying impulsive dynamics exhibit rich nonlinear phenomena.

For bipedal walking, these results include the existence of passive dynamic
walking gaits (i.e., unactuated periodic walking motions of the impulsive
dynamics), period-doubling bifurcations, strange attractors, and chaotic motion
Garcia et al. (1998); Goswami et al. (1998). A large body of work has since explored
variations of these canonical walking models with the addition of, e.g., springs
and dampers, limbs, and forcing functions (see Safartoobi et al. (2022) and
references therein). Common results include the existence of period-doubling (PD)
bifurcations and their associated route to chaos. The results for brachiation
are much more sparse, but a core result is the existence of unstable passive
dynamic gaits with zero energy loss across impacts and
energetically-conservative swing dynamics Gomes and Ruina (2005). These results have
been extended to show the existence of stable and unstable passive dynamic and
actuated gaits and observations of fold (FD) and Neimark-Sacker (NS) bifurcations
Rosa et al. (2012); Rosa and Lynch (2013).

Given past work, a gap that still persists is the lack of a unified bifurcation
analysis of two-link models and their set of walking and brachiating gaits
Rosa and Lynch (2013). Ultimately, both of these fields study the same equations of
motion, but results are only reported in isolation. Specifically, both fields
analyze the behavior of fixed points of a discrete step-to-step map. The map
represents the continuous swing motion of the robot as it pivots about its hand
or foot followed by an instantaneous plastic collision with an inclined surface.
Because of the bilateral symmetry of many two-link models, a periodic motion
(i.e., a gait) can be identified after just one step and a relabeling of
coordinates Garcia et al. (1998); Goswami et al. (1998); Safartoobi et al. (2022); Rosa et al. (2012); Rosa and Lynch (2013).
The periodicity of a fixed point is thus defined with respect to the number of
steps the robot takes. In other words, a gait that takes nn steps is a
period-nn fixed point.

Another understudied facet in both fields is the switching function of the
impulsive dynamics. In our numerical study, we explore a step-to-step map under
state-based switching (SBS) and time-based switching (TBS) strategies. In SBS, a collision occurs whenever the distance between the surface and the
end effector of the robot (serving as a foot for walking or hand for
brachiating) is zero. In the literature, SBS is the de facto choice with the
slope of the surface treated as a free parameter of the system. For TBS,
collisions occur after a pre-determined duration of time has elapsed. In this
case, switching time is the free parameter. TBS is a viable control option for
robots in vertical environments (e.g., Rosa et al. (2012); Mbewe and Boje (2025)) as contacts
can be made at any point in time on the surface.

As further motivation for this study, an interesting aspect of switching strategies is that both strategies produce the same set of period-one gaits. We omit a
formal proof as this is intuitively true. For every gait under SBS, we can
take a stopwatch to determine the switching time, and, for every gait under TBS,
we can record the slope at the switching time. Given this fact, we still
observe different long-term gait behaviors across impacts depending on the
switching strategy. This leads to our core contributions.

In this paper, we explore the impulsive dynamics common to single-joint,
two-link models of walking and brachiating gaits with respect to slope and
switching time. In particular, we expand on the observations made in
Rosa and Lynch (2013) with respect to how the stability of a gait and bifurcations
encountered within a family of gaits change under TBS and SBS of the impulsive
dynamics. Our contributions are

A numerical study of gait stability under two switching
strategies. We study the stability of gait families with respect to
time-based and state-based switching functions of the impulsive dynamics. When
there is a loss of stability in a gait family, we observe PD, NS, and FD bifurcations.

An exploration of the role of symmetry with gait families.
Two-link models with bilateral symmetry have period-one gait families that are
mirror images of each other about the switching time axis. We investigate the
evolution of unstable gaits in these families for one such model. In
particular, we find that near FD bifurcations, unstable gaits that start in one
gait family converge to stable gaits in the mirrored family of gaits under TBS.

Figure 2 provides a visual summary of these
contributions.

title: Closed-Loop Refinement and Execution for Learned Driving Planners
authors: Huaijin Hu,Shanting Wang,Zhongyu Mo,Andreas A. Malikopoulos
comment: . Submitted to the 2027 American Control Conference (ACC 2027)
abstract:
Learning-based driving planners are usually trained and evaluated in open loop
against logged trajectories. In closed loop, a trajectory with small
displacement error can still stall the vehicle, steer it into a conflict
with surrounding agents, or be executed with abrupt braking. We introduce Closed-Loop
Refinement and Execution (CLRE), a hierarchical receding-horizon control
framework designed to mitigate these failure modes while leaving the upstream
planner frozen and adding no new learned model. The upper layer treats the
nominal trajectory as a reference and solves a finite-horizon optimal control
problem that trades route progress against interaction with predicted agents.
Solving it from several initializations gives a candidate set, and a prediction-conditioned oriented-bounding-box (OBB) feasibility test retains
only candidates whose minimum predicted OBB clearance over the horizon meets a
threshold. The lower layer
executes the lowest-cost survivor, or a route-centerline backup when none
remains, through the tracking controller supplied with the planner, augmented
by a range-based speed bound and a saturated proportional braking law. In
closed-loop simulation on 126 Bench2Drive routes with VAD as the upstream
planner, CLRE raises the driving score from 43.41 to 56.42 and route completion
from 57.27 to 72.23, and reduces collision events from 70 to 53.
introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving has emerged as an alternative to
conventional modular pipelines by learning driving decisions directly
from sensor observations and scene representations. Methods such as
UniAD [1] and VAD [2] predict a
short-horizon ego trajectory that is subsequently converted into
vehicle commands by a downstream tracking controller. These planners
are commonly trained and evaluated in open loop against logged expert
trajectories. However, accurate open-loop trajectory prediction does
not necessarily imply reliable closed-loop execution.

In closed loop each executed action changes the next observation, so
planning errors accumulate. Open-loop and closed-loop performance can be
substantially misaligned [3], Li et
al. [4] showed that open-loop displacement metrics can
be largely explained by the ego status alone, and
NeuroNCAP [5] reported that planners with strong
open-loop performance still collide in interactive scenarios. Bench2Drive
makes the point sharper by testing end-to-end systems in closed-loop CARLA
scenarios, where collisions, stalling, and route incompletion all count
against the score [6]. In this work, we focus on three
practically important failure modes that arise when learned trajectories are
executed in closed loop: insufficient route progress or stalling, motion
toward predicted conflicts, and abrupt longitudinal intervention.

Several lines of work try to close this gap, and each handles part of it. One line adds learned machinery around the planner, by retraining it with a
kinematic refinement network [7],
a learned cost that picks among sampled candidate trajectories [8], or online adaptation through test-time training [9]. These methods improve closed-loop behavior, but they need extra training or a learned model at deployment. A second line uses the learned trajectory as a reference for explicit optimization. Examples include coupling learned prediction with a differentiable planner [10], tracking learned waypoints with model predictive control [11], or handling uncertain predictions with chance constraints [12]. Here, the interaction with nearby agents enters the optimization as objective terms that are traded off against other costs, or as chance constraints on uncertain predictions, and the resulting trajectory is not checked separately. So a trajectory with low total cost can still leave too little clearance. A third line checks a planned trajectory at runtime and replaces it or falls back when it fails a safety check, either for a learned plan [13] or for an optimized one [14, 15]. This screens the nominal plan but does not improve it. A stalled or overly cautious plan passes the check unchanged, and a rejected plan has no better plan to put in its place.

Supervising a nominal policy with a separate safety layer is well established
in control. Predictive safety filters, control barrier functions, and
reachability-based methods modify or override nominal inputs to maintain
prescribed safety
conditions [16, 17], and barrier
certificates [18] and safety-prioritized receding-horizon
control [19] have been applied to vehicle coordination.
These methods check safety against an explicit model of the environment. A learned driving
stack instead supplies its own predictions of surrounding agents, so any
runtime condition built on them inherits their limitations.

These gaps motivate our approach. We propose the Closed-Loop Refinement and
Execution (CLRE) framework, which keeps the upstream planner frozen and adds no
new learned model. Unlike waypoint-tracking MPC or runtime filters that operate
on a single nominal plan, CLRE first refines the plan to recover progress and
reduce predicted interactions, and then independently screens the resulting
candidates with a prediction-conditioned OBB feasibility test. The lower layer
executes the selected candidate with additional intervention when needed.

The main contributions of this paper are the following.

We propose CLRE, a training-free framework that improves the
closed-loop behavior of a frozen learned planner through trajectory
refinement, OBB feasibility testing, and execution-level intervention.

We develop a receding-horizon refinement method that balances
nominal-path tracking, route progress, and predicted-agent interaction,
followed by an OBB feasibility test that screens the resulting candidates
against predicted agent motion.

We introduce an execution layer with a forward-range speed bound,
backup policy, and saturated braking, and evaluate the complete framework
on Bench2Drive through ablation, sensitivity, and cross-planner studies.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows:
Section II formulates the receding-horizon refinement problem
and Section III constructs the objective, the OBB feasibility test,
and the execution layer. Section IV reports closed-loop
benchmark results. Finally, we draw concluding remarks in
Section V.

1. We propose CLRE, a training-free framework that improves the
closed-loop behavior of a frozen learned planner through trajectory
refinement, OBB feasibility testing, and execution-level intervention.

2. We develop a receding-horizon refinement method that balances
nominal-path tracking, route progress, and predicted-agent interaction,
followed by an OBB feasibility test that screens the resulting candidates
against predicted agent motion.

3. We introduce an execution layer with a forward-range speed bound,
backup policy, and saturated braking, and evaluate the complete framework
on Bench2Drive through ablation, sensitivity, and cross-planner studies.

title: In CEM, a World Model Is Also a Proposal Mechanism
authors: Oliver Obst,Frieder Stolzenburg
comment: including appendix
abstract:
The cross-entropy method (CEM) uses world-model scores to select action
sequences and fit the distribution sampled in its next iteration. A scoring
error can therefore change both the present decision and the candidates
considered later. We evaluate these two roles separately. Four types of
predictive model generate CEM traces, and every model rescores every saved
candidate pool. Executing the same candidates in the environment provides a reference
elite set and proposal update.
introduction:
A world model used for planning determines which actions receive further
consideration. In model-predictive control (MPC), the planner predicts the
outcomes of candidate action sequences, selects a sequence, and executes its
first action before replanning. The cross-entropy method (CEM) performs this
search by repeatedly sampling candidates and fitting a new sampling
distribution to those with the lowest predicted
cost [Bharadhwaj et al., 2020]. We call that distribution the proposal
and the retained candidates the elite set.

As an illustrative example, consider two candidate pools for the same physical state and cost objective.
Pool A contains a sequence with realised cost 1, but the scorer selects one
with realised cost 5. This is a selection error: a lower-cost sequence was
available. Pool B contains only sequences with realised cost 8 or higher. Its scorer orders
every candidate correctly and selects the cost-8 sequence. Earlier CEM
updates could have left the planner searching this second region. Correct
ordering within that pool still produces a higher-cost choice than the
misranked choice from pool A.

A fixed-pool comparison with environment executions can measure ranking
errors, elite membership, proposal-refit disagreement, and selection regret
among the available candidates. In the example, it can expose the error in
pool A and confirm the ordering in pool B. It cannot show which lower-cost
sequences another proposal would have sampled. Correct within-pool ordering
does not ensure that the pool contains low-cost actions.

Evaluation also depends on where the candidates came from. Logged rollouts
use a data-collection policy; actor-centred ranking tests perturb a reference
action sequence. These tests can measure prediction or ordering on their
chosen action distributions. CEM changes its own distribution after each
elite decision. We call this planner-induced query shift: model
scores change the optimiser’s future queries. The physical system need not
change.

Rank agreement measured along a CEM trace already captures how ordering
changes during search [Wang et al., 2026]. Our comparison adds
pools produced by other models’ update histories. Applying the same scorer
to those pools tests whether its disagreement depends on pool source;
applying different scorers to one pool compares their decisions on identical
actions. Realised candidate costs separately record which pools contain
lower-cost sequences.

Our comparison uses four predictors fitted over frozen Dreamer
contexts [Hafner et al., 2020]. A context is the backbone’s internal
representation of the observation history. Each predictor replaces the full
Dreamer dynamics during planning, so we call it a surrogate. It
predicts future contexts under a candidate action sequence. A fixed readout
maps those contexts to the task variables used in the planning cost. The
four surrogates share data, transition form, cost, and CEM settings; their
feature maps differ.

Each surrogate first runs its own CEM search. We save the candidate pool at
every iteration, execute its candidates from the same restored simulator
state, and then score that pool with every surrogate. This separates two
roles: the generator produced the pool through its earlier updates;
the scorer ranks the saved pool now. We call this a crossed design
because each of the four generators is paired with each of the four scorers,
giving all 16 combinations. A column follows one
scorer across pool sources. A row holds the pool fixed and compares scorers.
The matrix describes proposal disagreement associated with generators,
scorers, and their pairings. It does not assign causal effects to those
components.

The intervention tests a consequence that rescoring alone cannot establish.
At the first update, we fit one proposal from model-ranked elites and another
from environment-ranked elites in the same pool. Both branches then continue
with the original scorer and matched random samples. This one-update
splice changes how later candidates are generated through one earlier
decision. Its endpoint is the realised cost of the sequence selected after
the remaining CEM iterations. Figure 1 shows the audit
and intervention together.

title: Lang3DSeg: Annotation-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation with Point Transformers
authors: Cigdem Kokenoz,Amir Salarpour,Alkim Domeke,Christopher Salas,Pedram MohajerAnsari,Long Cheng,Mert D. Pesé,Bing Li
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)

abstract: Accurate 3D semantic perception is critical for safe autonomous navigation. However, supervised LiDAR segmentation remains tied to closed taxonomies and to the cost of point-wise manual annotation. Open-vocabulary methods avoid that cost by projecting the output of 2D vision-language models onto LiDAR and distilling it into a 3D network. These methods rely almost exclusively on voxel-based sparse convolutions, and point transformers have so far been limited to indoor environments, where 3D data is dense and bounded.
introduction:
Accurate 3D semantic perception underpins autonomous navigation safety in unstructured environments. Supervised point transformers reach high benchmark accuracy, but they depend on dense point-wise annotation and are bound to the closed taxonomy they were trained on. Both properties limit a robot that must operate around rare obstacles, unfamiliar vehicle types, or terrain the annotation schema never
anticipated to mark or label.

Open-vocabulary distillation offers a way out. A 2D vision-language model labels camera images, those labels are projected onto the LiDAR sweep, and a 3D network learns from the result without human annotation. What has not changed across this literature is the 3D backbone: most methods in the setting, from CLIP2Scene [1] through Better Call SAL [2], OV3D [3], and GGSD [4], build on a voxel-based sparse convolutional network, which imposes a spatial quantization not present in the raw point measurements. Point transformers remove that constraint and have been adopted for open-vocabulary segmentation indoor environments [5], where scenes are dense and bounded. Outdoor LiDAR is the opposite regime: sweeps are sparse, ring-structured, and span a hundred meters, and to our knowledge no point transformer has been trained for annotation-free open-vocabulary segmentation in it.

Lang3DSeg closes that gap with two components. We train a PointTransformerV3 [6] backbone from scratch on open-vocabulary supervision, with no geometric pre-training and no supervised initialization; and because a from-scratch backbone has no prior to fall back on and reproduces the errors present in the projected pseudo-labels, we pair it with an offline curation stage that corrects those errors at the projection step rather than compensating for them afterwards. Together they outperform every published annotation-free result on both driving benchmarks.

Prior work treats the 2D-3D projection noise statistically, by temporal voting [7], adaptive label correction [8], or keeping a vision-language model in the loop at inference [9]. Each method introduces computation or memory cost that may be unsuitable for resource-constrained deployment, and much of the error is not statistical in the first place: a point behind a car is mislabeled identically from every similar viewpoint, so voting reinforces it. We instead remove these labels at the projection stage itself. A per-pixel occlusion test does not suffice, since a point behind an object typically lands on its own unoccupied pixel inside that object’s mask; we therefore test each mask instance as a whole for points that lie beyond the surface it describes.

The contributions of this paper are as follows.

We create a new annotation-free open-vocabulary 3D learning framework, and validate its effectiveness through 3D LiDAR outdoor semantic segmentation task by training a point transformer from scratch without projected pseudo-label errors.

We identify and quantify occlusion bleed as a dominant and
systematic error during 2D-to-3D label projection, concentrated in the
foreground categories that significantly matter for class-averaged accuracy.

We introduce a priority-ordered rasterization with an instance-wise depth approach to handle this error, requiring neither registration nor cross-frame voting.

We attain the SOTA annotation-free accuracy on
both benchmarks, 52.8% mIoU on nuScenes and 41.4% on SemanticKITTI, while
keeping the vision-language model out of the inference path.

1. We create a new annotation-free open-vocabulary 3D learning framework, and validate its effectiveness through 3D LiDAR outdoor semantic segmentation task by training a point transformer from scratch without projected pseudo-label errors.

2. We identify and quantify occlusion bleed as a dominant and
systematic error during 2D-to-3D label projection, concentrated in the
foreground categories that significantly matter for class-averaged accuracy.

3. We introduce a priority-ordered rasterization with an instance-wise depth approach to handle this error, requiring neither registration nor cross-frame voting.

4. We attain the SOTA annotation-free accuracy on
both benchmarks, 52.8% mIoU on nuScenes and 41.4% on SemanticKITTI, while
keeping the vision-language model out of the inference path.

title: Reward as Observation: Learning Reward-Based Policies for Rapid Adaptation
authors: Morgan Byrd,Maks Sorokin,Robert Wright,Sehoon Ha
comment: Website:this https URL
abstract: This paper explores a reward-based policy to achieve zero-shot transfer between source and target environments with completely different observation spaces. While humans can demonstrate impressive adaptation capabilities, deep neural network policies often struggle to adapt to a new environment and require a considerable amount of samples for successful transfer. Instead, we propose a novel reward-based policy only conditioned on rewards and actions, enabling zero-shot adaptation to new environments with completely different observations. We discuss the challenges and feasibility of a reward-based policy and then propose a practical algorithm for training. We demonstrate that a reward policy can be trained within three different environments, Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing, and transferred to completely different observations, such as different color palettes or 3D rendering, or Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim, in a zero-shot manner. We also demonstrate that a reward-based policy can further guide the training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.
introduction:
Humans readily adapt when the appearance of a familiar task changes. A gamer who masters a racing game can play immediately after a graphics engine upgrade, because the underlying rules and controls remain the same. Similarly, a robot trained to navigate a corridor should not need to relearn from scratch when its camera is replaced with a higher-resolution, wider Field-of-View or upgraded from RGB to RGB-D. In both cases, the core task structure, including dynamics, controls, and reward, is preserved; only the observation representation changes. However, typical deep RL policies treat such observation shifts as entirely new problems, requiring full retraining and discarding all previously learned task knowledge, because standard policies are tightly coupled to the specific observation space used during training.

We consider the problem of transferring a policy between two Markov Decision Process (MDP) environments that share the same underlying task structure, including state space, action space, transition dynamics, and reward function, but differ entirely in their observation space. Most prior transfer work in robotics focuses on transition dynamics shift, as in sim-to-real transfer [1, 2, 3, 4]. Instead, we address the complementary case: fixed dynamics, but a completely different observation space. We impose no constraint on the relationship between source and target observations; they may differ arbitrarily in modality, dimensionality, or structure. We intentionally fix the dynamics to isolate the observation shift problem, and we expect our approach to compose naturally with existing methods that handle transition shifts.

Our key insight is that the reward signal directly encodes the task structure and remains consistent across both MDPs, and therefore serves as a natural bridge to enable rapid transfer between environments with different observations. Let us consider a driving task: if the reward stays high, the agent should continue its current behavior; if the reward drops, a steering correction is needed. This intuition holds whether the agent observes a 2D top-down view, a 3D camera feed, or the onboard camera of a Stretch mobile robot in a scanned 3D environment. This suggests that a scalar reward signal alone may carry sufficient information to address the challenge of drastic observation shift, but only if it is sufficiently dense and informative. Under this condition, the reward signal has the potential to provide effective guidance in the target environment, regardless of how the observations change.

We propose a reward-based policy as a transferable teacher that bridges source and target environments under drastic observation shifts. Training such a policy is inherently challenging, as the reward signal is only a scalar projection of the underlying state space with limited information for control. To overcome this, we adopt an LSTM-based architecture that processes the temporal history of reward and action pairs, and incorporate a guidance loss from an observation-based expert policy to stabilize training. Once trained in the source environment, the reward-based policy is deployed in the target environment as a teacher, and we use DAgger to train an observation-based policy significantly faster than learning from scratch.

We demonstrate that a reward-based policy can serve as an effective transferable teacher across environments with arbitrary observation shifts. First, reward-based policies achieve 6666% to 9595% of state-based performance across three environments. Second, they transfer zero-shot under drastic observation shifts, including 2D-to-3D rendering changes and deployment on photorealistic Habitat-Sim [5] reconstructions of real building interiors with a Stretch mobile robot. Third, using the reward-based policy as a DAgger teacher enables substantially faster learning in the target environment. Finally, reward estimation proves far more tractable than state estimation under limited data.

The technical contributions of this paper are:

We define the reward-based MDP and discuss its theoretical properties, including feasibility conditions and an optimality gap bound (Appendix).

We propose a practical implementation for training reward-based policies, and a DAgger-based algorithm that uses the reward-based policy as a zero-shot teacher to train an observation-based policy in the target environment.

We demonstrate reward-based policy training across diverse environments and validate rapid transfer under drastic observation shifts, including 2D-to-3D transfer and zero-shot deployment on a Stretch mobile robot in photorealistic Habitat-Sim reconstructions of real building interiors.

1. We define the reward-based MDP and discuss its theoretical properties, including feasibility conditions and an optimality gap bound (Appendix).

2. We propose a practical implementation for training reward-based policies, and a DAgger-based algorithm that uses the reward-based policy as a zero-shot teacher to train an observation-based policy in the target environment.

3. We demonstrate reward-based policy training across diverse environments and validate rapid transfer under drastic observation shifts, including 2D-to-3D transfer and zero-shot deployment on a Stretch mobile robot in photorealistic Habitat-Sim reconstructions of real building interiors.

title: Learning Transferable Skills using Goal-Conditioned Bisimulation
authors: Mohammad Amin Abbasfar,Farbod Azimmohseni,Mohammad Hossein Rohban
abstract:
Unsupervised skill discovery has emerged as a promising approach for leveraging reward-free datasets to pretrain general-purpose policies. However, current skill discovery methods either require access to expert data or exhibit limited generalization, failing to transfer effectively to previously unseen layouts. A key challenge is to learn representations that capture the temporal structure of the environment while remaining robust to variations across layouts. To address this issue, we present an objective for learning action-aware temporal representations that satisfy the functional equivariance property while preserving the local temporal structure of the environment. Building upon this embedding, we further propose unsupervised skill discovery using bisimulation, which learns transferable skills by conditioning the behavior of skills exclusively on the subset of state features that directly affect their execution. This enforces invariant behavior across different layouts, enabling skills to transfer effectively to other configurations. Finally, through comprehensive empirical evaluations, we show that skills learned in a given environment can be effectively applied to solve downstream tasks in various environment layouts, demonstrating strong out-of-distribution generalization. 11

        The code and videos are available at https://sites.google.com/view/usb-atr/.
introduction:
Leveraging large unlabeled datasets has substantially contributed to the advancement of deep learning in recent years. Unsupervised and self-supervised techniques such as masked language modeling in natural language processing (Devlin et al., 2019) and contrastive losses in computer vision (Chen et al., 2020) have enabled deep neural networks to benefit from vast and low-cost unlabeled data. Numerous attempts have been made to apply the same strategy in the context of reinforcement learning (RL), where the goal is to pretrain the agent’s policy using only pre-collected offline datasets (Chebotar et al., 2021; Reed et al., 2022; Park et al., 2023a; Park et al., 2024a; O. X.-E. Collaboration et al., 2024).

Unsupervised skill discovery has been recognized as a promising approach for pretraining such policies. These methods aim to learn a versatile set of latent-conditioned policies, each demonstrating a distinct behavior, such that together they cover the state space. Prior work has proposed various objectives to train such skill policies, either via behavioral cloning (Pertsch et al., 2021; Ajay et al., 2021) or by diversifying their state visitation distribution (Eysenbach et al., 2019; Park et al., 2023b; Park et al., 2024a). These skills can then be used to perform downstream tasks in a zero-shot manner, or harnessed as low-level policies within a hierarchical approach (Eysenbach et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2020).

Many applications of reinforcement learning in locomotion and robotic manipulation involve frequently occurring temporally-extended actions that appear during the accomplishment of a wide range of tasks (Hauskrecht et al., 1998; Sutton et al., 1999; Pateria et al., 2021).
For instance, in the AntMaze environment (Fu et al., 2020; Park et al., 2025), where a quadruped agent must navigate to different goals within a maze, the ability to move in the four cardinal directions constitutes a sufficient set of skills for performing any task, regardless of maze layout. Similarly, in the Kitchen environment (Gupta et al., 2019), which consists of several long-horizon manipulation tasks, a temporally-extended action such as placing the kettle from the cupboard onto the oven top should be performed independently of other environmental features, such as whether the microwave door is open or closed. In such structured environments, learning reusable skills is essential for generalizing to previously unseen configurations.

Despite the importance of such reusable behaviors in structured domains, existing skill discovery methods are not explicitly designed to account for this structure. For instance, the Hilbert foundation policy (HILP) (Park et al., 2024a), which is a state-of-the-art distance-maximizing skill discovery method, learns skills that span the state space reasonably well. However, it struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution layouts (Sobal et al., 2025). To illustrate, suppose HILP learns to move a kettle only when the microwave door is closed. In a scenario where the microwave door is open, despite being irrelevant to the task, the behavior of the kettle-moving skill may change drastically, making it incapable of completing the task. In contrast to distance-maximizing skill discovery methods, behavioral cloning-based methods offer better out-of-distribution generalization (Pertsch et al., 2021). Nevertheless, they fall short when using suboptimal datasets, as they tend to replicate the exact action sequences that exist in the dataset.

Motivated by this, we aim to extract skills that are transferable to out-of-distribution layouts, even when only a single training layout and low-quality datasets are available during training. Our method consists of two components. First, we introduce an objective for training an action-aware temporal representation (ATR) that aims to learn a structured state embedding with functional equivariance (Hansen-Estruch et al., 2022) property, while preserving local temporal distances. This allows us to enforce each skill to show monotonic behavior while retaining the benefits of temporal representations when learning from suboptimal data. To train such representations, we employ bisimulation metrics (Ferns and Precup, 2014), which have demonstrated well-established capabilities for improving generalization (Zhang et al., 2021; Agarwal et al., 2021). In particular, we use goal-conditioned bisimulation (Hansen-Estruch et al., 2022) to enforce this property for state-goal pairs that share similar underlying action sequences.

Second, we build upon this representation to propose unsupervised skill discovery using bisimulation (USB), a modification of HILP in which the behavior of skills is conditioned only on the state features that are relevant to their execution, rather than on the full state. To achieve this, we again employ bisimulation metrics to learn a state representation in which states with similar transition dynamics are embedded close to one another. Conditioning each skill on this representation encourages the learned skills to exhibit consistent behavior across dynamically similar states, even when the corresponding action sequences are not present in the dataset for all such states. In this way, we encourage skills to disregard layout-specific features of the environment and to acquire generic behaviors that improve their transferability. These generic skills can then be equipped with a planning approach or composed by a high-level controller to accomplish downstream tasks across diverse layouts.

Finally, to evaluate the out-of-distribution generalization capability of our method, we assess the learned skills in both a test-time planning setup and a hierarchical approach. By conducting experiments across environments with different layout maps, we demonstrate that our method offers strong generalization and outperforms existing state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods.

In summary, our main contributions in this work are as follows:
1) We propose ATR, a novel structured temporal representation for the states with the functional equivariance property.
2) Building on this representation, we propose USB, an unsupervised skill discovery method for pretraining latent-conditioned policies that learn generic and transferable skills.
3) We extend the popular OGBench (Park et al., 2025), a standard offline goal-conditioned RL benchmark, by adding a feature for generating random maze layouts and datasets, enabling a more thorough evaluation of the generalization ability of different methods.
4) Through experiments in several maze environments, we empirically demonstrate that USB+ATR learns effective and transferable skills across different layouts and offers strong out-of-distribution generalization.
